Accordion plaiting is mu,:ti worn this neaten' and It appears in a variety of new designs, the crepon effect being most novel. A beautiful pattern called the ondine has tha plaits in two ways; that is, the material is plaited lengthwite, while a sort of crumpled plait crosses it. and produces a serpentine effect. I saw a very pletty navy blue and white check, with a bluuze front made of white chiffon, plaited in this way. Too s'Lirr, was plain, with a Blight pannier or hip piece. The waist was cut touave effect, the sma.ll revers being bound with mavy-blue moire, finished at the throat and waist In front with soft moire rii_dion bows caupt with steel buckles._

Jet, satin, feathers, laces, and paste ornaments are all introduced in the mihinery of the hour. The colouring of a charming summer bat is brown and pink, the velvet crown and band tieing in the dark shade, vt-.ile the front smartly tied bow is of the colour of a blush rose. There again touches of black are added to i;i7e cxpretsion, awl this is managed by the bla..;k embroidered brim with jet edging which is mountd on pink satin, and again by the bunches of ostr:ch feather t pi arranged in such faleinating fasiii,in at toe back of the chapeall.

A delightful costume for afternoon and pro- menade wear shows the effect of the foothionable passementeries and lace embroideries. Tile skirt, sleeves, and yoke are of a royal blue crep m, while the corselet and trimmings are of yillow pasPe- menterie worked here and there with jet nailheads. Black satin, charmingly folded and tied on the shoulders, accentuates the charm of this very becoming bodice, and a full band of the same satin circles the throat. The bonnet shape is composed of cut jet beads, trimmed with pale blue forget- me-nots, and ripe wheat-ears, while the parasol is of blue Chine silk, banded with guipure inseri ions. An entirely black dress, arran.:ed on the above lines, would be serviceable and ladylike, while brown, green, and even red lend themselves well to such combisations. A dress of checked tweed has the skirt draped up on one side and fastened with two buttons, while the bodice and belt are very neatly hem-stitched.

Sleeves are much lower on the shoulders than they were, and very few extend over the elbow. They nearly all have a little bow of ribbon or , velvet at the band of the arm. There is a tendency I to return to tight sleeves, and to trim them on the shoulders with frills, flounces, and puffings, instead of making them of the balloon shape. In fact, a general tendency to drooping softness is beginning to show itself. The turned-up bands on the wrists of sleeves are no longer tight, but loose. Collars also no longer-stand off so s. fay over the shoulders. 'They fall in soft and graceful folds instead. Tailor-made costumes alone remain somewhat stern looking. Travelling costumes, on the other hand, axe made of sofe light cloth, and are made with a plain bell skirt, loose jacket, and foulard blouse. A stylish blouse which came under my notice recently was me.de of coral satin, gauged with tiny tucks drawn up 4nll, and trimmed with black moire ril,bons. The hat was of white Leghorn With tt./Ack wings and pale relcet zasettes.

Had it not been for the Transvaal war the master of Ditzhingliam and his wife might even now be living the life of pros- perous colonists in South Africa, and the world would have lost one of its best story-tellers. • A love for nursing seems inherent in the Queen's d •ughters, says the " Gentlewoman." Princess Alice of Hesse was a splendid nurse, the Empress Frederick ran her very clo,e in the Franco-German War, and Princess Cnristian has been, and ever will be, a positive enthus- iast on the subject of hospital nursing, as we know so well. Princess Beatrice, Lo, when her little daughter's accident caused such anxiety, proved herself scarcely less proficient. The Qtklert herself at one time had no Taste for nursing, and it is told that owing entirely to her influence the Duchess of Teck gave up her most cherished wish in her maiden days—that of becoming a professional nurse. Mn. Mary North, who lives at Avoceitha, near Rtiosllanerchrugo, Denbighshire, attained, on the 21st ult., hcr one hundred and fourth year. Mrs. North is t robably the oldest person living in North Wales. She possesses all her faculties, and is able to converse quite cheerfully with any visitors. She resides with a daugh- ter, who is of the age of seventy-five.

Tomato Eggs. , You will want says a writer in " Cassell's Family Magazine" three eggs to half-a-d,)zen medium-sized tomatoes, and the latter you must boil whole, either in water or stock, for about five n-.inutes .; then you skin them and drop them in a stew-pan, in which you have fried a small union or a couple of shalots—chopped,need I say ?—then you go on stiring for a minute or two, and put in a teaspoonful of white vinegar and a pinch of powdered thyme and bay-leaf, which makes such a dif- ference td the dish; so do not think that it is to be lightly dismissed from your calculation. Half a teaspoonful each of white pepper and pounded lump sugar are next in order, and a dust of nutmeg and a scant teaspoonful of salt. Then you add a teaspoonful of good brown gravy or stock, or, failing any on the spot, make a little with the ever-useful meat extract and boiling water. The eggs you drop in wlicle, one at a time, with a brisk stir; then you stir away for a minute or two, until a very smooth mass is the result. The dish you serve this in cannot be too hot, and the garnish should be fried bread; but for a makeshift, when not convenient to fry, dry toast will serve the purpose. For a refined edition of this, the tomatoes must be sieved after the ingredients —except the eggs—have been put in, and the freiishing off is exactly as I have told you.

div.head: Indigestion, or Dysp.ep.iia.
div.p: Indigestion, or Dysp.ep.iia.

Rightly to understand that coVtit-ion which we call dyspepsia, it is necessary to have smile acquaintance, however rudimentary, with the physi!logy of digestion. the natural process of digestion the food is first masticated and mixed with saliva, and then swallowed. In the stomach it is moved about by a kind ot revolving or churn7ng action, and is acted on by the gastric juice, which reduces it to a semi-fluid consistmce, and converts it into a uniform pulp known as " cliyme." It then passes into the intestines, where it is mixed with bile, and with the pancreatic juice. w hich is secreted by the pancreas, or sweetbread, and closely rca,embles saliva. The nutritive portion of the food is now taken up by the veins and other vessels, and is by them carried into the blood, whist the excrem entitous part, which is useless for the purposes of nutrition, is con- ed out of the body. The gastric juice is a secretion poured out br. and peculiar to, the stomach. It is an acid fluid, alai to its acid, combined with a substance known as " pepsine," it owes its solvt nt or digestive properties. The readiness with which the gastric juice acts on different articles of food is in a great mea,nre determined by their tendernessnd state of diviiou. By minute division of the food, the extent of surf ice with which the digestive fluid can come in contact is increased, and its action proportionately accelerated. A weak, dyspeptic stomach acts slowly, or not at all on solid lumps or tough masses of food. 41 knowledge of this fact affords an explanation of one of the common- est causes of dyspepsia, and ;,t the same time sn7gests the appropriate mode of treatment. Persons who are 61.1 i jecc to dyspep.,ia should never cat in a tiurry,as busy men and those of studious and sol.t:ry habits ct ten do. They should be cautioned not to 44 bolt" the ir food, liiah should be well ground in the mill of Nature's own prodding. It has been supposed, a lid the supposit hal app, ars feasible, that the increased lOngevity of nwaern generations is in some degree attributable to the capa- inlay of chewing their food which the st;ill of the dentist prolongs to persons advanced in life. I ender a,al moist substances offer less resistance to . the action al the gastric juice than do tough, laird, and dry ones, for they are thoroughly penetrated by it, 111.1 are thus attacked not only on the surface, but at every part at once. The readiness with which a substance is acted on by t lie gastric jaice is, however, no indication of its nutritive value, tor a substance may be nutrit ion,, and yet, on account of its toughness andaVier qualities, bard to digest ; arid many suit, asily-digestible bodies centaio c,onparatively little nutriment. It is obvious, however, that a substance which the stomach cannot ,clieest is incapable, of nourishing the body, and there is. therefore, so tar, a necessary connection between them digestibility of a substance and its power of .nourishing.

An extraordinary scene was, ai air-ady reprted, wit- -nessed on the comity ground at Brist )1 on Mondty in connecti'in well the Gloucestershire and Sussex cricket .match. Owing to the state of the turf and the weather, the umpires decided about half-past two that playwas impossible, whereupon an angry feeling was manifested by the crowd, which numbered about 2,000, and there was a hostile ,demonstration in front ot the pavilion. 'Pressing against the railings, large numbers of people .hoottd -Dr. W.G,Grace,and demanded their money back. The veteran, who kept. perfoptly cool throughout, en- deavoured to.pacify the most excited - of the crowd by telling them that they -could have passes Fur the next day., but this proved of no avail, although _most people iknow that there is no provision for returning money taken at a cricket gate. •" W.G." made more than one :,atteinpt to restorethe good humour of the pkople, but l-each time he appeared he had an extremely unpleasant reception. In order to-do somethiro, for the crowd, he arranged an exhibition game of Association football, including himself amongstlthe player-, but when they had donnfd their flannels, and the champion 1,,d the ,wvoy out of the pavilion,-some 700 people pa-keel them- selves in front, and offered uncompromising rtsistence. -It was clear they were in a7n sty mood, and at length -he returned to the pavillion. Twice afterwards he an- nounced that, on the umpires' decision, crick-t was ow, of the question, and Murdoch, Fr whom a big shout-had bean made, came out and endorsed the champion's re- gearks. The excitement-showed no signs of abatirw,a.nd after a lapse of twenty mimr,. cricketers made a move for the gates. ' W aud Murdock n,ing ea- cored by three stalwart !policemen. The crowd surgt d aro4ind, and there was every indication of a so riusdis- ttirbiince, but at length alter difficuty, cricketers and found their wa to he gate, and the cele- braWd players drove off. -Old sportsmen who can-re- memiaer forty years of cricizet a 1..;. more were awaited at the occurrence, which is withoiy- A parallel, at any rat' so tar-as Bristol is concerned. !I:tie most noisy section of the mob was composed tst-enders. One regNettable fact was that aier the umpires' decision people were allowed to pay at the gate and go upon the ground. The whole affair was en Monday evening es- , citedly tikicussed in Bristol spr--.-.--ng circles, and caused quite a Etir in the city.

OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
By the Author Of " DARKWOOD."
CHAPTER XXV. LORD ADLOWS RECOVERS HIS SPIRIT& If I stay, my rage Will hurry me to mischief; better leave her To certain ruin, than betray myself To danger of it. _ _ CLAPTIIOnNE.

The discovery of the continued existence of Geoffrey Trevelyan almost paralyzed Lord Adlowe. A weaker villian would have despaired at this dis- covery, but Lord Adlowe was stung to a sullen and desperate fury. "Love, fortune—all—swept from me at one blow 1" he muttered as he strode to and fro in his own room, his valet having departed to the ser- vants' hall. "My hopes of a brilliant marriage dashed 1 The prize I have schemed and waited for all my life swept from my hands 1" He glowered around him like a madman, He was silent several minutes, during which he continued his hurried strides panting heavily. "What am I to do?" he Whispered, hollowly, at length. He racked his brain for a solution of the ques- tion.

"I have it r he thought, after a pause, his face glowing savagely. "Geoffrey Trevelyan must be discovered and betrayed to the marquis, who will wreak upon him a terrible revenge I Beatrice will die of a broken heart. She is too proud to live, disgraced and pitied by those she has always deemed her inferiors. Their children must be dis- posed of. I can plan how hereafter. As to this girl—this Giralda—upon whom my uncle has settled at his death sixty thousand pounds, what am I to do with her. She is bright, beautiful, innocent, and intelligent and high-bred. 1 might marry her myself. Since I cannot have the mother, why not the daughter 7" The idea seemed to strike him favourably. "I will do it f' he mentally exclaimed, a ju- bilant thrill pulsing through his dark and schem- ing soul. "By making her my wife, I shall secure a fortune. I shall strike a deadly blow to the hearts of her parents, and I shall posses a shield against a possible disgrace and exposure. I will move quickly in the mattcr. I have no time to lose I"

He continued his musings for some minutes, his suddenly conceived project becoming a fixed deter- mination. Gradually he assumed an outward calmness, although his soul seemed on tire within him. The air of his chamber grew stifling to him, and at last he quitted it to seek the fre:-.11 air and seclusion of the grounds. In the lower hall he encountered Haskins, his valet. Motioning the maxi to follow him, he passed out of doors, making his way to the long-neglected garden, now an untrimmed wilderness of vines and shrubbery. Lord Adlowe entered a little summer-house, off a by-path, and full of dusky, slumberous shadows caused by the vines that covered it thickly. He sat down on a rustic bench, and awaited the arrival of his servitor.
Haskins made his appearance a moment later. "What has happened, my lord?" he exclaimed, starting at sight of his master's face. "You look like death !"

"I feel like death 1" was the abrupt response. "Sit down there. There is no danger of our being overheard here, as Miss Arevalo is out riding, and no one else ever comes into the gar- den. I want a serious talk with you. How deep is your devotion to me, Negwyn—that is, Has- kins ?"
--;‘-is deep as your lordship's purse," declared the valet smiling. Adlowe ft owned.

" oa can choose your words better than that," he observed calmly. "You and I, my man, must sink or swim together. Without me you will sink to poverty and disgrace. Cling to me as to your plank of safety, assist me in all my designs, help me to carry out my plans, and I will make you a rich man."
Haskins stared wonderingly at his employer. "I —I don't understand you my lord !" he stam- Inered.

"You don't? Well then, Geoffrey Trevelyan is alive !" Haskins sprang up, pale end frightened. "Alive !" he ejaculated. "Has he come back, my lord? Is he here? Is the truth known ?" "No. Sit down. He is alive and in England, but he would not dare to come to Trevelyan Park. His uncle wntilil 1-i vg. If h. LI% is in hiding under an assumed name !" Haskins resumed his seat, his alarm giving place to an expression of thoughtfulness. Adlowe was quick to read its meaning. "You will never dare to betray me !" he said coolly. "You would never dare to think of sell- ing your secret to Lord Trevelyan, or to Geoffrey! In the first place I would pay you more for your silence than tßey would for your confession. In the second place, I am not a man to brook treach- ery. He bestowed a glance upon his valet that seemed to scorch and shrivel the soul of the lat- ter.

"I have no intention of betraying you, my lord," the man said, trembling. "'ln for a penny in for a pound!' I'll stick to your lordship all through, If you'll do the right thing by me." "You may depend upon me Haskins. My plans are not fully matured yet. I must have time to think. I have but just discovered that Geoffrey Trevelyan is alive, and my thoughts an still in a whirl!'

"How did you discover it,•my lord ?" inquired the man, beginning to recover from his fright. "I saw a letter not meant for my eyes !" de- clared Lord Adlowe. "You cannot guess? This Miss Arevalo, whom Lord Trevelyan has adopted —this mysterious stranger who has worked such a change in my miserly old uncle and in the Park— 's the daughter of Geoffrey Trevelyan.l" A cold sweat broke out on the valet's brow.

"She the daughter of Geoffrey Trevelyan ?" he ejacalsted hoarsely. "I might a known it. She has got his very, eyes. What .is she a doing here, .my lord, in the very jaws of the lion ?" "She has come here for the purpose. of clearing Iher father's name," said •Lord Adlowe. "An :also to worm herself into Lord Trevelyan's heart, 'and to beguile him •of his savings ! Besides these .objects, She is bent on discovering her father's ene- anies, that a terrible vengeance inay•be wreaked :upon them !" The valet trembled to the very •depths of his ,cowardly soul. " What are you going•to do, •my lord ?" he ques tioned. "Are you going to denounce her to the marquis? Are you going to have her turned away ?" "You are all wrong in your surmises, Haskins," *lid his lordship. with .a brave and placid front, not deeming it politic to bare the weakness 11/Id anguish of his soul to his attendant. "I am going to marry the girl I" Marry her !" ejaculated the valet in astonish- ment.

"-Such is my intention. I have discovered the true state of affairs just in time, Haskins. They all think me in the dark. They are all waiting for Lord Trevelyan's death to spring a mine on me. It is here the game fairly begins. I have aimed all along at the possession of the Trevelyan es- tates. I aim at them still, and I mean to peasess them.' " But my lord," suggested Haskins, "if Geof- frey Trevelyan has a daughter, he has also, perhaps sons.' "He has enc.s—two, I think," remarked Adlowe coolly. "Then what ,are you to gain by a marriage with Ibis girl ?" questioned the hewildered valet. "The case is iust here," his lordsh p explained. "I see before me magnificient estates, yielding a princely revenue. Until this morning I have deemed them the mum as already mine. Suddenly I behold two or three persons ahead of me in the %ace for the splendid prize. Do I give up, or turn back? No. I lay snares for them. I remove them kern my path. Do you take my idea?" " Yes, my lord," said the valet in a whisper. "You look at me in horror. Yet the thing is not S e terrible. I think theac boys are not aware of their real name. I gathered that fact from an ob- scurely written senteuce in the letter that told me so much. How easy to ship them off to some other portion of the world! How easy to Provide for

Geoffrey Trevelyan where he will not again be heard of I The rest will be easy." "It's an able plan," declared the valet, recover- ing his courage. "I will go in with you, heart and soul, my lord. As long as you don't mean downright murder," and his voice fell, "I'll work with you." Adlowe smiled subtly. He knew his man thor- oughly, and knew that so long as he kept dis- played before Hs eyes a glittering reward no one could tempt the fellow from him. They were bound together by too many ties of mutual vil- lainy to nart •• It is understood, then," said Adlowe, "that you are to assist me in sweeping all bstacles from my path. You shall name your own reward when I find myself undisputed master here !" Haskins expressed his satisfaction at this prom- ise, and declared that he would be -faithful to his Lordship's interests. "How lucky it was," said Adlowe, musingly, "that I happened to look into the girl's room ! I nderstand all their secrets, all their plots now ! Miss Geradda Trevelyan—otherwise Arevalo—l am warned and armed against all your plots! You will find, poor little fool, that it would have been better not to enter the lists against me (" It was just before this critical juncture that Giralda came leisurely along the by-path, on her way to the dwelling, desiring to reach her room unseen after her ride. She had gained the very shadow of the vines embowering the summer-house when Lord Adlowe spoke her name, and she halted abruptly, transfixed, as we have said, to the spot, an involuntary listener to the remainder of his speech. She comprehended at once that her father's enemy was in possession of the secret of her identity ! A realisation of her father's peril rushed over her soul. Sick and dizzy with terror, she clutched the vines to keep herself from falling. "She shall have a chance, however, to save her- self from destruction with the rest," observed Adlowe. "I will see her to-day on the subject. We shall not be here over a clay or two, Haskins, as I want to report my discovery to the detective. It will greatly simplify matters for him if he is told at once that Geotirey Trevelyan is alive and in England, and that it is to meet him that the Lady Beatrice Hampton effects such mysterious absences from her father's house ! By Jove !" he added, darkly, "her ladyship has been living a hidden romance. I have returned to England just in time to turn her 'pretty comedy into a tragedy !" Giralda gave utterance to an involuntary moan, and grasped more closely the rustling vines.

With -a smothered Oath, Lord iidlowe sprang from his seat, and gained the door at a bound. He stood on the threshold a moment, looking at her, his eyes blazing, a fearful and deadly expres• sion on his features.

Then he waved his hand at his servant, motion- ing him to depart, and said, slowly, with a strangely evil smile: "You are just in time, Miss Arevalo. I have something to say to you. Let me assist you to a seat I " He took her arm and drew her into the little summer-house, at the same moment that Haskins quitted it at its opposite extremity. Giralda shrank from his touch in loathing, and sat down, trembling, pallid, frightened. "Quite a little adventure, Miss Arevalo," said her enemy, standing before her against the light, his arms folded, and his sinister visage glowing darkly upon her. "I do not know how much you have overheard, but you evidently have some com- prehension of the state of affairs. Permit me to explain matters to you. As I was passing up to my room I found your door ajar, and naturally looked in, the -room having been closed for many years, it having been the chamber of misguided and unworthy cousin Geoffrey. The little portable writing-de3k on the table in the baywindow at- tracted my attention. It had been GeoEfrey's in his boyhood. I looked into it; my eyes rested upon your unfinished letter; in short, Miss Arevalo, as I must still call you, I inadvertently stumbled upon your secret !" He spoke deprecatingly, as if the discovery had forced itself upon him against his will. _ _ _ _

Giralda roused herself from her drooping atti- tude, the colour glowed in her clear dark cheeks, her scarlet lips curled themselves into an eßpres- sion of haughty _scorn, and her eyes flashed and burned like living coals. She comprehended perfectly Adlowe's baseness, and the manner in which he had possessed himself of her secret, and she could not disguise her con- tempt of him. nrefigaasrhdeodf neUr anstisl, trnhpaitymaolmoveeulty butTmrl-A- the --erusuirldae spirit aroused him to the fact of her transcendent beauty, and inspired him with a sudden interest in her which was almost akin to love.

"I am not so base as you think me, Miss Are- valo," he said, apologetically. "I have not be- trayed your secret to my uncle. Lora Trevelyan is still iguorant that his hated nephew lives. It is in your power to keep him in ignorance of the fact until his death places your father beyond his lordship's hatred." "Since you know so much of our affairs, Lord Adlowe," said Giralda, with a brave seeming, but with a sinking heart, "I will own to you that I am indeed the daughter of Geoffrey Trevelyan, the man whom you have traduced, maligned and cruelly injured I You know him to be good and true. If you would, you could clear him of the foul disgrace that clings to his name. I came to Trevelyan Park not knowing my relationship to the marquis. I have stayed here hoping to clear ray father's name, and to reconcile him and my uncle. If there is any pity in your soul, leave me to my work l" Lord Adlowe sneered.

"You have succeeded very well in your work,' so far," he remarked. "As your father will in- herit the title and estates, you have contrived to bag his lordship's spare cash, to use a vulgar ex- pression, but one which is significant. Lord T-e- -velyan would look at the matter in this light, if he knew who you wore 1" Giralda shivered as with cold. She had not -thought before that such an interpretation could be put upon her stay at the Park. "The Lady Beatrice knew very well what she was about when she sent you here," observed Adlowe, coarsely. "By the by, Miss Giralda, where is this hidden home of yours? Where does your father, this noble Count of Arevalo, this Spanish grandee, live ?" "You will suffer me to go on to the house," said Giralda, arising with dignity, her clear, dark cheeks strangely pallid. "You can certainly have nothing more to say to me, Lord Adlowe." "But I have something more to say to you," said Adlowe, his anger rising. "Shall I say it here, or before my uncle?" Giralda resumed her seat.

"You do not seem to be aware of the deadly peril menacing your fath6.. continued Adlowe— " of the scandal that will tear in shreds the hither- to spotless fame of the Lady Beatrice Hampton— of the disgrace of your brothers ! Lord Hampton, your grandfather, is a proud man. How will he bear to hear of his daughter's long-concealed secret marriage, of the existence of his daughter's children, when that knowledge will come to him first from the witness-box, and from every news- paper in the kingdom? You hold in your hand a cord, by pulling which you can bring down on the heads of all whom you love an awful avalanche of disgrace and woe. Shall I show you how to save them ?"

Girolda assented, with a low, wailing cry. "Accept the protection of my name. Become my wife. In that ,case, no harm shall come to your loved ones. I will even agree to reconcile your father end the marquis ! " "I cannot! I cannot marry you!" cried Giralda, shrinking from him. "Itis to you my father owes his life-long disgrace. It is to you my uncle Trevelyan owes his years of misery. I would rather die than become your wife ! " She arose as she spoke and faced him bravely, her eyes, so innocent and fearless, looking to him like the eyes of his wronged and banished cousin. "And you would rather your father should die I" suggested Adlowe. The question shook the girl's composure. "I cannot wrong my own soul and prove false to all his teachings even to save dear papa," she said, in a faltering voice. "I will share his dis- grace—l will die with him!" " With your mother's reproaches and your brother's cries rina4l%., k your ears 1" said her pitiless

enemy. " You prefer your own girlish Tanow; tr, their happiness. Such is the strength of tilial affection?' he added, sneeringly. "Lord Adlowe," said Giralda, .4rl fudge of any sort of affection. But I will not waste words with you. I cannot go to my Uncle Trevelyan and tell him who I am, for he might judge roe as you have done, and I thould thus in- jure my dear father, instead of helping him. lam going away from the Park—" "To warn your father that all is discovered, and that he must fly? No, you had better remain here for the present, unless you wish to precipitate the very evil you dread ! ' declared Adlowe, signifi- cantly. "Once more, I offer you marriage. You know what a refusal will entail. Do you still re- fuse me 7"

"I do. I will never do evil that good may come," said the girl, bravely. "I will never marry you ! " "Then blame yourself for whatever happens to you and yours ! " cried Adlowe, savagely. "You have rejected all chance of safety. So be it ! " He turned, and stalked out of the summer- house, leaving the maiden to her terror and despair. He had not taken a dozen stelae when he ene counteii.ii hus valet, who carrunl in 1113 hand a scatuo. envelope. "A dispatch from town, my lord," said Haskins, presenting the missive. " Mr. .Black, the butler, has just come from Trevelyan village, where this was given to him." Adlowe tore open the dispatch at once. It was, as he expected, from Rush, the detective, and was as brief as significant, running as rollows "Lotto AoLowy.-1 have run the game to earth. Come at once. * Rustt."

Adlowe's face lighted up with a lurid glow. "He has tracked her ladyship ! " he exclaimed. "This is well. We will go back to night, Haskins. I mean to probe this secret to the bottom. But first," he added, with a backward glance at the arbor, "I must prevent any danger from this girl. She means to be off for home to-night secretly, to yarn her father of his danger. If she succeeds iu warning him, I shall have trouble. We must pre- vent her escape ! " "But how, my lord?" "Come up to my room, and we will see. I will devise a plan, which you shall execute, which will remove the girl from my path, and bend her to my designs. Come I " He led the way into the dwelling, Haskins fol- owing closely in his steps.
CHAPTER XXVI. A DESPERATE MOVE. No thought within her bosom stirs, But wakes some feeling dark and dread. PIREBE CAREY.

Lord Adlowe had read correctly the expression of Giralda,'s face, The maiden had indeed formed the instinctive resolution of hurrying at once to her father and warning him of his peril. The thought that she had been unconciously the means of his betrayal to his enemy filled her young soul with remorseful anguish. She hurried, with tottering steps, up to her own room, and sat down before her tire, shivering and trembling. How suddenly all her bright hopes had failed her! Her thoughts were in a chaos. Her soul was wrapped in sudden darkness. She could not weep. Her sorrow was dumb. She was consciouo only of the impending ruin and disgrace cf all whom she loved—of the deadly peril menacing her father.

And then, through all her grief, came back to her mind the coarse insinuations of Lord Adlowe that she had been sent to Trevalyan Park to win the love of the marquis, with the view of inherit- ing his savings. Her cheeks burned hotly at the insu 1 t.
" But his lordship will think so," she murmured aloud, unconsciously. "He will never know that I really and truly loved him. He will think me base and wicked."
The tears came now in a tropical shower. De- spite his faults, she tenderly loved the grey-haired, grand old man, whose vindictive hatred of her father was the cause of all her woe.

"I cannot see him again," she thought, when she had grown calmer. "His keen eyes would read my soul. I could never bear his scorn and anger. And I could never keep from him the secret of papa's assumed name and whereabouts. I must steal away from this second home as I stole away from the first, in secret, alone, and at night. I mast get back to The Evergreens, and warn papa before Lord Adlowe can see his detective."

Her brain grew clearer and her sad heart grew resolute. She arose and took nut from her desk the fatal lettpr which had wrought so much sorrow, reading it over and putting it in her bosom. Then with a feverish energy she packed away in their boxes all the costly presents Lord Trevelyan had bestowed upon her, including those he had given her in London. Her next step was to make her travelling toilet, and to secure on her person the letters she had that morning received from home, and then she resumed her seat and her despairing thoughts. For a long time she sat there in a sort of stupor, once vaguely conscious of a summons to dinner, to which she managed to reply that she was not well and would not go down. Dolly, the little Welsh maid, entered the room once, but Giralda genfly dismissed her for the day. Soon afterwards good Mrs. Pumpton made her appearance, bearing a tray of delicacies, a troubled look on her motherly countenance.

"You are not ill, Miss ? " she asked, alarmed at the pallor of the sorrowful young face, and at the hunted expression in the lovely eyes of the young girl. "You do look mortal bad, that's a fact. Shall I send for a doctor, Miss?" "Oh, no, Mrs. Pompton," replied Giralda, rous- ing herself, yet speaking with a strange languor that further frightened the good dame. "I feel tired—" " Tired ! You look that, poor dear! And if yon ain't sitting in that hard, straight-backed chair I Just let me take care of you, Miss." She deposited the tray on a small table, and drew up to the fire Giralda's luxurious easy-chair, with its white covers, gently compelling the young girl to occupy it. She placed a hassock for her feet, and then proceeded to carve the tempting little dinner, as if for a helpless little child. "My lord is distressed on account of your sud- den illness, Miss Giralda," she said. "He is as gloomy and cross as if he'd lost his best friend. Ah I he loves you, Miss, as if you were his .own kin. And Lord Adlowe looked gloomy, too, at the table. His man says that his lordship is going back on the 10.50 train. He makes short visits." Giralda's heart gave a quick bound. She in- tended going on the same train, but trusted. to escape his lordship's observation in the darkness and hurry, with the aid of a veil and thick shawl, by which she hoped to conceal and dis6nise her figure. _

-" Haskins says," continued the gossipy house- keeper, " that Lord Adlowe had a disp itch, hurrying him back to town. I suppose it was from the Lady Beatrice Hampton, that they say is engaged to marry his lordship. Somehow," she added, musingly, " that Haskins reminds me of some one I bisel to know—l can't tell who, He says he was never in these parts before. But, dear heart! You don't eat anything, Miss Are- valo !"

"I cannot eat !" said Giralda. "I am not well, Mrs. Pompton. If you don't mind," she added, gently, " 1 think solitude will be the best thing for me. Please give my love to my uncle Trevel- you, and say to him that I shall not be down to tea !"

She leaned her head back wearily, and Mrs. Pumpton, pitying her, went out softly, bearing to Lord Trevelyau the report that his ward was suf- fering from a distracting headache, and must on na aeoeuut be disturl.ed.

Ihis veport did not prevent the marquis from t,E...)ling up the stairs several times and listening at Giraida's door, his rugged features wearing an expression of tender solicitude anu yearning. The maiden had become inexpressibly dear to him, and it was With 'difficulty he could restrain himself from breaking in upon her seclusion, and offering her his sympathy and ministrations. "Poor child I" he muttered, as he hobbled down the stairs with his staff for the third time. "I would gladly bear the pain for her. I hope she'll be well by morning. The house is a desolate old prison without her !" Meanwhile, unconscious of his solicitude Giralda bore her griefs in a dumb silence. As night ap- proached she began to feel it impossible to go away without a word of farewell to his 'lordship. His affection for her, and unquestioning faith in her, demanded at least a word of explanation in regard to the cause of her abrupt departure. But shA

pitifully, for she loved. him, she wrote him a little note intending to leave it on her desk, that he might receive it in the morning when she should be far away. She began by calling him her dear uncle, and assuring him that she loved him and was deeply grateful for all his loving-kindness to her. Then she said that eircinnstances had arisen which com- pelled her immediate departure from the Park, and that she dared not see him again lest her strength and self-command should fail her. She begged him to destroy the will he had recently made in her favour; and whatever he might hear to her disadvantage when she was gone, to believe al- ways that she had loved him sincerely, and with no hope or thought of a pecuniary reward. This letter, written in a tremulous hand and blotted with tears, she sealed, addressed, and laid upon her desk. 'By this time the evening shadows had fallen. Dolly came in with lighted wax candles and re- treated after stirring the fire and drawing the curtains. Remembering the long and tiresome walk to the station, and the necessity that existed for a secret departure, Giralda put on her cloak, hat, and veil, took her shawl and travelling bag on her arm and with a last glance around the room, and at the picture of Geoffrey Trevelyan on the wall, stole down the stairs and out by the side porch into the overgrown garden. The night was mild, and not dark. Every object in the near landscape was plainly perceptible through the light, pale gloom. Giralda stole around to the front of the mansion, and halted in the shadow of a tulip-tree. The drawing-room was lighted, and the curtains were not drawn. Lord Adlowe sat at the table, a book in his hands, a watchful expression on his face. Lord Trevelyan sat by the hearth, gloomy and moody, a strange and new expression of sad- ness on his grand and massive features. Giralda regarded him a moment, checking back a sob. Then she turned resolutely away, and hurried down the avenue towards the lodge-gate; despair in her soul. She was going away from her father's rightful home, her work unfinished, her hopes all crushed. She could never come back again, she said to her- self, in Lord Trevelyan's lifetime. She need never think now of reconciling those two noble, but estranged souls. She need never dream of clear- ing her father's name of its stain of disgrace. If she could only save him from arrest, and get him away from his enemies, it was all she hoped for now. She diverted her course before reaching the lodge. proceeding along a by-path to an open part of the high wall which was under repair. She passed out through this gap into the road, and hurried along in the direction of Trevelyan She had no thought of fear as she traversed the wild mountain solitude through the night shadows. She did not even think of herself, her whole mind being wrapped up in her loved ones, and the evil tidings she was taking to them. There seemed to be no one stirring abroad, no farmers' wagons, no tramps, no vagrants. She did not meet a soul. "I shall not be missed to-night," she thought, "and by morning 1 shall be at The Evergreens. I must procure my ticket at the moment of arriving, at the station, and then keep out of sight, lest Lord Adlowe suspect my design." Her course thus marked out plainly, she resumed her sorrowful musings. • The three miles were half traversed when, tired and worn, she sat down on a stone by the wayside for a brief rest. A sensation of relief was stealing over her frame, when a rumbling sound reached her ears as of a farmer's wagon, approaching by., the route she had come. She drew back a little into the shadow of the hedge, waiting for the wagon to pass. It came nearer, into plain view. As she had guessed, from the noise it made, it was simply a farmer's light wagon, with two seats. It was drawn by two rough, strong mountain ponies, and occupied by two men, one of whom sat on either side. Giralda noticed that they looked sharply at the hedges as they came near, and she shrank back still further with a sudden sensation of dread. Suddenly, when the vehicle was nearly abreast of her, it came to a halt, and the man who was driving leaned forward, exclaiming: "Hallo there, Miss! Which way are you go- ing ?" Further attempt at concealment was useless. The sharp eyes of the driver had discovered her. Giralda answered, with pretended coolness: "I am going on to the village." "Won't you have a ride, Miss? Can take you over as well as not." "No, I thank you," replied the young girl, her heart fluttering. "I prefer to walk. At this juncture, the man on the rear seat leaped lightly to the ground, and approached the maiden. She recognized him at once as Lord Adlowe. With a cry of terror, she turned to run. In a moment he was in full pursuit. In another moment he had overtaken her and grasped her by the arm. "I see you are afraid of me," he observed, draw- ing her toward the wagon. "It is well that you should be. You thought to escape me—to flee to your home—to warn your father? You have but run into a snare! You are in a trap from which you cannot escape 1" Giralda panted in terror. "Let me go 1 Oh, let me go !" she pleaded, struggling frantically. "0, Lord Adlowe, as you hope for mercy, release me, and let me go ! Adlowe looked down on her anguished face with a pitiless smile. " Will you be my wife ? " he demanded. "Never ! Never ! " cried the maiden, despe- rately. " Oh, I cannot be your wife ! You know I cannot 1 You have no right to detain me in this manner. I demand my freedom ! " "Haskins," observed his lordship, " keep a tight rein on your horses. I will take care of the girl." He lifted her as he spoke, pinioning her arms in his swift grasp, and placed her in the wagon, springing after her. Giralda uttered a loud and terrified scream. "You had better be quiet ! " he said, in a men- acing tone, all the fiendish cruelty of his nature finding expression in his looks and manner at that moment. "Another scream like that, and I shall be compelled to gag you 1" Giralda was for a moment dumb with terror. " Haskins," said Lord Adlowe, " get out and hand up the young lady's shawl and bag. Give me the reins." Haskins obeyed, then returning to his seat. " What does this outrage mean ?" demanded Giratia, recovering her self-command. Are you going to take me to the Lady Beatrice Hampton, Lord Adlowe ?" "No. I intend to make you my wife. Your rejection of me lias no °fleet whatever upon my in- tention. You are but little more than a child and cannot know your own mind. A little prompt severity will bring you to your senses." "No severity can ever force me to marry you, Lord Adlowe! ' asserted Giralda, with quivering lips. "Then I will keep you as a hostage to be ran- somed by a sum that %ill make ine independent," declared his lordship with a heartless laugh. " Yon are my prisoner, and such you will remain for the present.' " Not long 1" said Giralda, with a flash of spirit. "Lord Trevelyan will discover my situation and rescue me! He is too keen not to find out that I

am a prisoner." "Do not flatter yourself with such fruitless hopes. I have guarded my tracks too well for that. Why, you yourself have left a note, explaining tc his lordship that you were going away. I shall return immediately to the Park and leave in an hour in the family chariot. My uncle thinks MC in my own room at this moment. How is he eves to suspect the truth ? " Giralda uttered a low, sighing moan. "I expected that you would make your escape to-night to warn your father of his danger," con - tinned Adlowe, mercilessly. "I prepared for it by sending Haskins to the village for this trap, which has waited near the Park since nightfall. I saw you as you took a last look into the drawing. room, although you did not dream that I was on the watch for you. Haskins is my man, devoted to me body and soul. His interests and mine are identical. He knows of a good place on the coast where no one would ever dream of looking for you. He went there this afternoon to make arrange- ments for your stay there. He will take you there to-niAt wljln T en on to ItThifll

Gifalda looked from Adlowe to his servant. fTrholenrethwatasstnoolidcofmacfeo,rtanodr ttoepesintaoll levy extracted ing with the fires of cupidity which his master had lighted. The recent cowardly fears of fie's' kins were all lulled now, for he had only a woman to deal with. He had embarked in Adlowe's ne- farious cause with heart and soul, as his master had fully satisfied that he would thereby serve h es, gleam- his beat interests, and save himself from possible harm. "You have no pity—no mercy?" the young girl asked, piteously. "None," said Adlowe, smiling like a demon. "If you will promise to be my wife, you shall go with me to London. Otherwise you shall staY here." 1 "I cannot promise," moaned Giralda' her whole being in an agony of grief. "Better death than such a marriage !" "Suit yourself. Such resolution cannot last long. You must permit me to guard against the chances of your escape," and Adlowe drew from under the seat a coil of rope, with which he pro- ceeded to bind his captive. It seemed as if he had read her heart. Giralda's last hope of escape left her now. Despite her struggles Adlowe, whose nerves were of iron, bound her to the seat, and tied her hands behind her. He then flung her shawl around her, pinning 1 it carefully to conceal her bonds. "Had I better gag her, Haskins ?" asked the titled ruffian, with another cruel smile. "Oh, no I" cried Giralda. "I will not cry out. I will not call for help." J "I trust to your honour," declared he who ham none. "Now I must go back to the Park. Yet ' another word, Miss Arevalo : I received a dis- patch directly after my interview with you, surn- moning me back to town. It was from a detective in my employ, and informs me that he has run his game to earth.' In other words, he has tracked your mother to your father's house. To-morroW the whole secret will be in my hands." With this last shot, which almost struck Giralds senseless, Adlowe commanded Haskins to move on. The valet turned the horses and the next moment they went speeding along the road towards Trevelyan Park. Not a word was spoken on the way. The wagon halted near the lodge gates, permitting Adlowe to alight, and Haskins then whipped up the horses, hurrying towards the sea over the road Giralda had passed so gayly that morning on Zulime's back. As they rode onward the maiden made various appeals to the valet's heart. She might as well have appealed to stone. She offered him bribes, but Haskins turned a deaf ear to all her pleadings. He deemed his present course the safest. When they arrived at the spot where the bridge had been swept away that morning, Giralda felt a momentary hope that further progress in that direction would be barred. But Haskins, after a brief glance of surprise, turned up the stream to a ford at some distance, betraying a familiarity with the scene that was surprising in one wile professed to be such a stranger in the neighbour- hood. The ford crossed, the road was regained: and tne journey progresscu swiiray. they encounterea no one. The lights of the Eagle's Eyre—the abode of the young Lord Grosvenor who had rescued Girq..lda, so gallantly that mornincr'—gleamed like stars from the high bluff, and a nest of glowworms seemed resting on the plateau at its foot where the hamlet was situated. Every moment these li,ghts became brighter and nearer. Giralda fancied that her captor was taking her to the hamlet. But he turned aside into a by-road before reach- ing it, and struck down the cost, away from the Eyrie and the hamlet. "How much further have we to go?" asked Giralda, chilled by the rude sea winds, and af- frighted at the sombre darkness setting now upon shore and sea. "Only a couple of miles, Miss. Do you see that light from the rocks away up yonder?" and Has- kins pointed with his whip to a gleam to the Southward against the darkening sky " That light comes from your future prison, Miss. Yen are expected, and the light is a signal. It'll take us half an hour, may be longer, to mount the bluff, but you'll be perfectly safe when you get there." He chuckeld under his breath, and whipped 11P, his ponies, while Giralda sank back, hopeless an° despairing. (Tob cont,:,nued).

The friends and admirers of the late Canon Liddon have committed the mistake of many other enthus- ia.4io committees who begin to erect a memorial before they have obtained sufficient money to pay for it. The canon's long connection with St. Paul's his fame as a preacher, and his position in the High Church party, should have been enough to save his memory from this indignity. There is a deficit of £5OO to make up, and of this SUM the Dean and Chapter of St. Paul's have prJmised to contribute .£lOO, leaving .£4OO to be obtained from the public. The committee should have resolutely set their faces against putting up a grander memorial than they had the means of paying for ; as when the first gush of enthusiasm or sympathy is past, the work of collecting funds invariably proceeds with difficulty. Somehow or other, of course,the money will be forthcoming.

I hear that the Postmaster General has agreed to the concession pressed on the Government by Mr. Heaton, to allow the public to use their own cards as postcards on condition of affixing a half-penny stamp, instead of being obliged to use the official stationery.

Some well-known and influential friends of the tempetance cause have set about the formation of a Barmaids' Union. It is to be a union up to date, and to aim not only at safe-guarding the interests of the girls as a class, and reducing their hours of labour, but to strive to establish a minimum rate of wages also. The movement will be supported with all the strength of the National Women's Temper- ance Association, ot which Lady 11. Somerset is the president ; but whether it will be strong enough to accomplish any of the objects for which it is intended is a different affair. The great number of unemployed girls who would be willing to accept work at less than the union rate of wages, and at Er ore than the union scale of hours, will speedily swamp the union. Barmaids, like dockers, belong to the ranks of the unskilled, and in the present state of the female4labour market, their places would be easily supplied if a strike were ordered. But girls of the class from whom barmaids gener- ally drawn are not likely to resort to such an extreme measure as a strike, which would end in depriving them, not merely temporarily, but in numberless cases permanently, of their means of living.

div.head: 1 I
div.p: 1 I
IMPRISONED ON A SHIP.

The steamship Normannia, from Hamburg, arrived in the port of New York on Saturday, Sept. 3rd, 1892,with cases of cholera on board. Many of the ship's company had died on the passage. At Hamburg and elsewhere in Europe the disease was raging. The authorities in America were alarmed lest the scourge should he intro- duced into that country. Hence they quarantined the Normannia with every soul of her passengers and crew. The writer was a passenger. It was an awful time. Death was among us and on all sides of us. Nobody knew who next would fall. We were imprisoned. Liberty never seemed so fair, nor so far. We could neither fight nor fly. There we were—hundreds of us— perfectly well, and yet bound together as with chains, that the health officer of the port might see whether the plague would not yet break out in our midst. When at last—after weeks of this—we were set on shore, men lifted their hats and reverently said, " Thank God." This was being shut up under conditions to make it horrible and harful. Yet any form of incarceration is had enough. Here is a woman for example, who says, I never moved a yard from my own doorstep for twenty weeks !" Her own house was a prison to her. Who had •entenced her ? A judge ? No ; a power greater and more pitiless than any judge. Her tale runs, thus : In April, 1882, whilst living at Lasher's Farm, Old Samford, Essex, a fire broke out, and the family were burned out of house and home. We have no call to remark on such a calamity. The very thought of it is fit to make one shiver with dread. For most of us it is like the world coming to an end to experience such a disaster. Well, what happened after that the lady shall tell in her own fashion—the ltest of all fashions, because it is plain and straight to the point. She says :—" Owing to our bedding being damp from exposure, I took a bad cold, whi ch brought on rheumatic fever. For fourteen days I was confined to my bed, and for twenty weeks I never moved a yard from my own doorstep. After a time the fever abated, leaving me weak, languid, and low. At first I had a sickening taste in the mouth and a poor appetite. No matter how simple and light the food was, I was afraid to eat, for it was sure to give me pain at the chest and sides; so I often had to loosen my corset and undress myself during the day. I could not bear the weight of my clothing. " I was constantly spitting up a sour, frothy fluid, and had a gnawing pain at the pit of the stomach—like hunger, and yet different. It was with diffitilty I void(d the kidney secretion, and my bowels, ankles, and legs began to swell. I got worse; I was in agony night and dav, and could not put my foot on the ground. Soon afterwards a husky cough took me, and my throat filled with a thick phegm. I could not sleep, and was never easy. Later on I had often to sit up in bed, for I felt as if I should choke.

"Year after year I continued to suffer in this way, growing worse and worse, until I despaired of ever being well again. But who can tell when trouble will come, or when relief ? A wonderful Providence is over all.

" One day in June a book came by post describing Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and what it had done for many poor sufferers. I got a bottle from Mr. Suckling, medicine dealer, and after taking it fors short time all pain left me, and I gradually gained strength. By taking an occasional dose I have since keit in good health, and can eat and digest any kind of food. (Signed) Mrs. LYDIA GREEN, Moor End, Great Sampford, via Braintree, Essex. Aug. 24th, 1895." Now, in order that Mrs. Green's clear and truthful statement may be of use to others (as she desires it to be), we must add a word or two. The had cold she caught at the fire no doubt" brought on" the rheuma- tic fever (as she relates), but there was something back of the cold, for a cold never causes rheumatism. The rheumatic seeds, or poison, must already lie in the blood; and that poison is always created by pre-existing indigestion and dyspepsia, whether the sufferer knows it or not. This is proved by the fact that Mis. Green's chief ailment for ten years after the fire was not rheu- matism. but indigestion and despepsia and dropsy, which is one of its results and symptons. When the digestion was finally righted by the remedy she alludes to, all her apparent maladies ceased together. Why ? Because she had but one, as we have said. Ah, yes, Disease is a stern jailor. And how sweet (and cheap) is liberty, obtained by Mother Seigel's help.

div.head: NAVIGATION OF THE WEAVER.
div.p: THE NAVIGATION OF THE WEAVER.

A compromise has how been arranged concerning future rates of carriage on the Weaver Navigation, with regard to which a large deputation interviewed Mr. Bryce a few days ago. The settlement was concluded at a conference held by the parties on Tuesday after- noon at the Board of Trade, undef the presidency of Sir Courtenay Boyle. Among those present were Mr. Brunner M.P., Mr. Walter Long, M.P., Mr. H. J. Tolleinache, M.P., and the Hon. Lionel Ashley, chairman of the Salt Union. The terms agreed upon are an all-round toll a 101. per ton for white salt, cc liether from Northwich or Winsford (being a reduction of al. per ton for salt), and 10d. per ton for alkali from Northwich, which is an in- crease of 2d. In view of this arrangement, it is now believed that the provisional order will pass on Thursday without opposition. Mr. Brunner will then move— " Provided always that the tolls from time to time ,act- nails charge shall not exceed such amount as may in the opinion of the Board of Trade be sufficient to provide for thc reasomble expenses of adequately maintainine the Navigation in the interests of the traders thereon." This provison may not be pressed if, as is expected, Mr. Bryce takes the opportunity of publicly stating that the rates will not be such as to accumulate a balance for the Cheshire County Council, who are the inheritors by statutory right of any surplus that may accrue.

div.head: 14: KA MINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1894.
div.p: THE 14: KA MINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1894.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.-TANI VISIT TO THE CLIO.
_The mitiwes of this_Glinnii7.fe? were moved by Coffn.

cillor S.atw Gr, en who said that the borough acoount, had tie-n publised in a different form than had been d ate hitherto. There was a very much improved state- ment of the funded debt of the borough, bringing down the figure at which that debt stood by the addition of cash in the bank and debits owing to the bank, showing the amount as £576,374 53. 11d. On another page would be found a consecutive list of the bonds and bondholders of the borough. Hitherto they had been placed under the departments in which loans had been obtained. It was a saving of labour,and would be convenient to those who din not want it known that they were bondholders. Pr •ceeding, he said it was intended shortly to apply to Parliament for an extension of powers in connection with the borough. As a part of that application, they had proposed to ask Parliament to extend certain of their loans and give them permission to issue stock to recoup those loans and provide capital sums. By an Act which was passed in 1890 power was given to the Local Government Board to make such regulations and assent to such alterations as boroughs might require for the diversion of their debt into stock. Although they put it in their Bill with the intention of going to Parliament the Town Clerk was advised through his Parliamentary agent, and other channels, that if they did so include it the Government through the wition of the Local Govern- ment Board, would strike it out of the Bill, and clearly it was no good to go to the expenditure of putting it for- ward with the absolute certainty of having it struck out. If they applied to the Local Government Board the Beard would make such reasonable arrangements as the circumstances might demand. In consequence of that the resolution which appeared on the minutes to .the effect that application be made to the Local Government Board was passed. Councillor J. FAIRCLOIIOII seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor Dr. CANNELL objected to the payment of £5 ss. for the expenses of the deputation from the School Attendance Committee to the Clio, and asked for the order for the raymeiat of it, because he contended that it should not cost more than £3 103. They had therefore, the handsome balance of £1 15s. for whiskey and cigars. (Laughter.) He objected to this because at the last Council meeting they passed a resolution to the effect that three members and the Clerk should go and the very next week, at the School Attendance Com- mittee, the resolution of the Council was passed over and another resolution was passed to the effect that the whole of the members should go if they liked. He moved an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the £53. 53. for the expenses of the deputa- tion.

Councillor GREENING seconded, and said hi did not think it right that the money of the town should be squandered in such a manner. Councillor SKELTON supported the amendment,remark- ing that it was not dignified for any committee to set at open defiance any resolution passed by the Council. Hear, hear.) He could not admit for an instant that £5 ss. was a reasonable sum for the expenses of three gentle- men going from Warrington to the Ship Clio. Alderman BOLTON said as one of the outside members of the Council he went to the Clio for the express pur- pose of seeing whether they got value for their money in what they paid for the boys on the ship. He paid his own expenses, and he did not think that £5 ss. was an unreasonable sum fot the deputation. Councillor BENNETT observed that the question of the actual amount did not dispose of the matter ; the ques- tion was, whieh was supreme, the Council or the com- mittee ? (Hear, hear.) In the face of a direct deci- sion from the Council he thought it was disrespectful that the members of the committee should pass a dif- ferent resolution.

Councillor BENNETT then referred to the accounts and pointed out that whilst liabilities to the extent of haifa million were shown the assets were not produced. They had some very valuable assets, including the waterworks uas works, Town Hall, Council PERCY DAVIES characterized the action of the School Attendance Committee with regard to the depu- tation as a piece of great impertinence, and as a matter of principle a. committee should not have the right of up- setting the decison of the Council. Alderman Surrov said the discussion partook some- thing of the character of a "storm in a teapot," and the sooner it was disposed of the better. If the committee decided to take others with them, and that the cost would not be inure than £5 53., he though it was petti- fogging work to object to it. Councillor MUIR suggested that it would simplify the matter if they ascertained whether the three gentlemen forming the deputation spent the 25 53. If the Borough Treasurer wbuld inform them of that it would simplify the matter.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH : I understand that this money has been paid by the Boreugh Treasurer; who is going to make it good if we pass the amendment? Councillor Dr. CANNELL Councillor Heaton will make it good. (Laughter.) Alderman FRANCOME said the only difficulty in his mind, was that at the last Council meeting-they decided that three only should go to the Clio. Personally he be- lieved that the School Attendance Committee had such an unpleasant and difficult duty to perform that if it was possible to give them a treat once a year he should only tie too pleased to give it them. But if the Council decided that only three should go, he thought that the committee should not try to upset the decision of the Council, and on that ground he should certainly sup- port the amendment. Councillor ROBERTS said that he supported the amend- ment at the last Council meeting reducing the number of the deputation to three and he therefore felt hound to support the amendment that night, until they had some evidence from the chairman of the committee, which at present they did not possess. Councillor Bennet had given them a speech which was very creditable to him. Both he and Mr. Percy Davies had contributed consider- ably to the debating talent of the Council, and he hoped they would always retain the same desire that they had shown that night to act fer principle and not for "pelt" (Hear, hear.) As usual, they had a very characteristic apology from the apologist of the Council. If ever there was a job that was not particularly savoury that wanted carrying through, their friend Alder man Sutton rose to the occasion and gave it a lift. (Laughter.) It was not a question of three or five guineas. Councillor Bennett had touched the core of the whole matter. This was a question as to whether the Council as a Council was to rsignisupreme for the business of the Corporation, or whether its decisions were to be set aside by any section of the Council. It was a question of principle. The Council was appointed for a specific purpose, to govern the town, and it was a most lamentable thing in his opinion that it should ever be considered a matter of small importance when a committee chose to etas deci- sion of the Council at defiance. The Council decided that the deputation should be restricted to three mem- bers. There was no limit to the number of members of the Council who chose to go voluntarily, and if the Chsirman of the committee could assure them that the £5 Ss. was the only expenditure of the three members then their case was at an end. (Hear, hear.) They could only take their stand on the question of extrava- gance, and having an intimate knowledge of that part of the world where the Clio was situated, he considered the sum very extravagant. It ought not to cost more than a guinea a head to take them to the ship Clio and back again in one day. As to the question of giving the members treats, surely they did net come there for the purpose of getting treated occasionally. In their elec- tion addresses they all—including himself—posed as ' " it.4imon Pores" of the town. They would never think of such a thing as taking a penny bun at the expense of the ratepayers, and yet they had a worthy Alderman getting up and suggesting the desirability of giving the Corporation a treat occasionally. Let them rise to their dignity and re member that they were the people's rep- resentatives, and that they held a high and dignified office. But he hoped they had heard the last of a desire on the part of any committee to set aside the delite race decision of the Council. (Hear, hear.) Let them be loyal to the Corporation, even if it did not please them to do so at all times. Referring to the suggestion of Coun- cillor Bennett that the assets of the Corporation should be published with the accounts, he suggested that the committee should adopt it so that those who ran might read. Although an enormous amount of expenditure was shown, he thought they had a quid pro quo in the shane of assets.
Councillor LONGTON said he would vote for. the pay- ment of £5 ss. on the understanding that it was devoted soliAy to the expenses of the three members of the com- mittee.

Councillor SnAw GREEN in replying, said that the committee accepted the decision of the Council that only three members should form the deputation, and they invited any other members who liked to accompany them. Several other members went,and he for oxe paid his own expenses. The £5 ss. was not only the expenses of the deputation, but included gratuities given to the boys.

The amendment and motion were then put to the meeting, and the voting resulted as follows : Fort he amendment: Alderman Francomb ; Councillors Dr. Cannel), Roberts, Woods, Percy Davies, Greening, Skelton.

For the motion :—The Mayor; Alder man Hutchinson, Blackhurst, Sutton, Bolton ; Councillors R. T. Fairclough, Tinsley, Heaton, Hepherd, Monks, Shaw Green, Smet- hurst, Shillcock. Flood, Wilkinson, Plumpton, Shaw, Beaman, Garner, Baird. - - - --

The motion was, therefore, carried by 20 to seven. Councillor SHAW GREEN said the observation that fell from Councillor Bennett was extremely valuable. There had never yet been published a statement of their assets. Councillor Bennett raised the question in his remarks, but it had been frequently before them. They had such a record in a certain form, and they were having it amplified. It would not be right to publish them in their entirety, and some they could not publish. The minutes were then passed.
