HEALTH COMMITTEE. -DROWNING FATALITY.
Alderman SUTTON mwed the confirmAzion of the
minutes of the Health Committee which contained a
presentment from a jury who were at an inquest in leitchford, to the effect " that the attention of the Cor-

poration be drawn to the dangerous state of the property whew, the deceased resided, and suggesting that the Corporation should take steps to have the place suffi:ti- ently protected." The Town Clerk replied to Mr. Brig- house, coroner, as folluws :—"I be to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yesterday's d ite, enclosing ver- dict and presentment herein. I fail to see in what Sense the Corporation can be considered responsible, or what steps they CE.,-71 take to have the place sufficiently pro- tected. I knew of no Act wSich gives the Corporation power to compel the fencing of a river," Aldernmn Sutton said the Corporation could not be held responeibie for the insecure condition of back premises. The Town Clerk had sent a notice to that effect to the owner of the property. The minutes were carried. _ PAVING A 111) SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. . _

Alderman WRIGHT in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the above committee said that the cost of the Padgate-lane drainage would be slightly over £2,000. As would be seen from the minutes, he and the Town Clerk and the Borough Surveyor had an interview with the m4ln Roads and Bridges Committee of the County Coun- cil at Preston on the nth ult., on the subject of the widening and improving of Warrington Bridge, and the committee were pressed to replace the present bridge with an iron girder bridge ee feet in width. They were promised a definite answer in the course of a fortnight.' Councillor LiFxrox seconded the passing of the minutes.

Councillor PLIIMPTON referred to the condition of the top of Cartwright-st., and said that in rainy weather people were unable to get to their houses except by treading over stones placed in the water. Several members of the Ceuncil called attention to certain defective streets and passages, Councillor SKELTON pointing out that he could not visit the houses of several of his constituents on certain occasions owing to the condition of several streets.

Councillor MONKS also brought up the subject of Monks-st. He said that he received numerous com- plaints from the inhabitants respacting its condition. Alderman WRIGHT, in reply to the various questions which had been raised, said that soma time ago the com- mittee made out a list of 90 streets and passages which required to be paved, and it was decided to do the old- est-and worst streets first. SeverAl of the places to which reference had been made were now under con- sideration and the work being proceeded with. The minutes were then agreed to. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
The following letter from the Education Department was read at a meeting of the School Attendance Commit-

tee ; " Sir,—Adverting to the application addressed to the Education Depirtment on the 30th June, and pup- parting to be signed by 15 ratepayers of the borough of Warrington, lam directed to request that the appli- cants will furnish ma with such a short summary of their reasons for feeling aggrieved with the notice dated 24th May, 1894, as will define the subject of the public inquiry applied for (Section 73 (2) ot the Elementary Education Act, 1870), and will enable the Education Department to settle whether, before ordering an in- quiry to be held, they should require the applicants to to give security for the expen,,eA (Section 73, 4). The summary should be forwarded to this office within one month from the date of this letter.
Councillor SHAW GREEN moved the confirmation of

the minutes ; and referring to the education question, said the committee were endeavouring so to reply to the letter as to avoid the necessity for the inquiry which was foreshadowed. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SHAW seconded the motion, which was agreed to.
CEMHTERY COMMITTEE. APPOINTMENT OF BEGISTRAR.,--.
LIVELY SCENES.

• Alderman HARRISON opened the discussion upon the Cemetery Committ:p's minutes by moving the adoption of the minutes with the exception of the portion relating to the appointment of a Cemetery registrar. To that clause he said he undoubtedly took exception. He con- tended that it wts not camp ttible with the interests of the people of Warrington that such an appointment should be made, and—

Councillor FLOOD rose to a point of or'er. Was it, he should like to ask,compatible with the duties of a chair- man of a committee to move a negative without first consulting his committee? (Hear, hear.) TOWN CLERK : It has been done frequently. The Town Clerk advised Alderman Harrison however, that it would simplify matters if he allowed someone else to move the minutes.

Councillor Fuxin then moved their confirmation, and Councillor HILL seconded. Alderman HARRISON moved an amendment to the effect that the minutes pass with the exception of that oortion referring to the appointment of a Cemetery Registrar, on the 97h July. He repeated the assertion that it was not compatible with the best interests of the people of Warrington that such an appointment as that pt ,posed should be made, as it was not calculated to add to the comfort and convenience f those who had, unfortunately to use the cemetery. What was the qual- ification of Mr. Taylor f.,r the office he sought, and which a section of the committee were very anxious be should talc—

Councillor FLOOD (interrupting) : The majority. Alderman HAIWISON, continuing, said there must have been a majority, or Mr. Taylor Would not have been sekcted, but the majority only consisted of two. There would only have been a majority of one if Alderman A4iton could have been preQent at the meeting of the committee. It was not compatihle with the hest interests of the people of Warrington that the appointment named by the Committee should be made. In the first place they did not know one word about Mr. Tayler's qualifica- tions for the office. It might be said that :he qualifica- tions could be learnt, but that took time, and many in- conveniences and heart hurnirws- might take place before a man was able to discharge the more delicate duties of the office. Mr. Young had been appointed sexton of the Parish Church, and.that position gave him considerable emolument. If the Cnutioil did•not appoint him registrar they would havo,, in pay him between £2O and £3O a year. They would have .to par that sum in sonsideration of the duties he discharged on behalf of the Parish Church. If they appointed Mr. Young regis- trar those fees would merge into his salary, but if they appointed Mr. Taylor they would still have to appoint Mr. Young. _

" At this stage of the proceedings, .there was a great commotion at the end of the room where accommodation was given to public. Several pfirsons persisted in inter- rupting, and applauding, and it appeared likely that an order would have to be given to clear the room of "strangers." After considerable diffieulty peace was restored, and Alderman Harrison continuing, admitted' that Mr. 'raptor was a respewahle man, but why dis- pense with the services of thole who had done so well, for whose who had never been tried? Councillor MUIR seconded the amendment. Alderman HUTCHINSON also supported the amendment and said that Mrs. Yonng hid done her work in a most admirable manner. He had no obpction to Mr. Taylor, who was a respectable man, and if' elected would do his level best to discharge the duties of the office with credit to himself and the committee. Councillnr HEATON contended that for the past three or four ycars the work at the cemetery had been done in a most disgraceful manner. (" No, no," and " Hear, hear.") 'there had been repeated complaints, and on the death of Mr. Leigh gardeners had to be sent from the Town Flail to put the cemetery in " sonsething like ship- shape." It was time a registrar was appointed who should be called upon to devote the whole of his time to the duties of the offi,e. Why should not the other denominations of the town have the services of their registrar as well as the Rector P Mr. Leigh's work had devolved upon his dauehter. They all knew that Alderman Harrison had written to several members of the committee asking them to resign so I that he might put a nice young man on, that took an interest in the cemetery. (Laughter.) Alderman HARRISON (warM!v): Allow me fora mom- ent. I say that Counciller Heaton is making a state- ment that is absolutely and deliberately false. (Applause I from the public, and continued interruption. The Town Cierk appealed to them to remain quiet.) Alderman BOLTON : I shall refuse to take part in the discussion if I am to be hampered by the outside public. (Hear, hear.) Councillor HEAToN (continuing) said there were 68 applicants for the vacant post, and the number was re- duced to Mr. Mason, Mr. Young, and Mr. Taylor. Mr. young got four votes, Mr. Mason five, and Mr. Taylor six. Everything at the cemetery had been going to rack and ruin, and until they appointed a registrar to look after the cemetery properly it would not be looked after. His opinion was that Mr. Taylor was the best man. There was no doubt that the " congregation " (referring to the public) had been specially brought to the meeting that night. ("No, no.") Pressure had been brought to bear upon members of the Council with regard to the appointment. ("No, no.") Mr. Taylor was the best man in Warrington for the position. Councillor FLOOD remarked that out of the 66 applic- ants for the post, 20 were townsmen. The question under discussion was creating a fever heat throughout the town. But tiler() was something behind this matter: it was the liberty of the Council, whether they were al- lowed to use that judgment and discretion in the con- duct of their business or to be influenced from outside 'against the best interests of the town. The MAYOR: Address the chair.

Councillor noon said he was not addressing the gal- lery. There was no juggling about the matter, and when the committee voted, the minority was composed of four, which included the Mayor, Mr. Muir, and Mr. Hutchinson. The other six who voted were men of honour as well as the other four.

Councillor Woos contended that Councillor Flood, in his heat, had forgotten the pith of the subject. He (Councillor Woods) found on looking over his year bock that he was only a member of one committee; and, desirous of serving his ward, he went to Alderman
LINEN LASTS LONGER In snaking and washingelothes. use HUDSON'S EXTRACT OF SOAP LINEN LASTS LONGER! or HUDSON'S DRY SIAP
LtNEN LASTs Saves rubbing I Does rot the line. 3

Harrison and askcd him if he would obj.ct to write to Councillor Wilkinson—who did not attend the commit- tee meetings as well as he might do—and ask him to retire in his (Councillor Woods') favour. Mr. Lei,di wag; not then dead, ald Mr.. Harrison was in no way to blame; nor was the speaker. The chAirman of the committee wrote a gentlemanly letter to Mr. Wilkinson, but that gentleman had not replied to it. The letter had been shown about, and even been taken to the Clio. (Laughter.) This was a personal matter, and he knew that Mr. Taylor's name was placed on the cane for the appointment of registrar long before the deatlr of Mr. Leigh. (A Voice: " Prove it.") He would do eon and in the words of a man who had spoken on the snbject that night. Councillor Heaton had in committee re- 'marked "Taylor is the man." There was no represen- tative of the Fairfield wan-ion the committee, and yet the cemetery was in Fairfield ward. Who was more suitable to be a member of the committee than one who lived in the ward—(hear, hear)-and who represented the whole feeling of the ward', and net one section ? After some further observations,. Councillor Woods said the Rector consulted his churchwardens when the vacancy became known, and they referred him to the vestry clerk, who told the Rector the law on the matter. The Rector also saw the Town Clerk, who told him "You can please yourself. What you do is an inde- pendent appointment." The Rector had'a perfect right to make the appointment, and he did not make it at all to influence the committee.

_ Councillor DAVIES supported the amendment, and con- tended that it would be a great shame not to elect Mr. Leigh's son-in-law. It was the duty of the Council to support a cemmittee if they believed their action to be right, not otherwise. Alderman BOLTON said that the accusations which had been bandied about were not fair to the committe. He hoped that when the members of the Corporation sup- ported a committee they would do it in a- generous manner. That generosity should be extended to every committee of the Council, and they should be regarded as doing their best for the interests of the town. He would not support the committee if he thought they had done anything that was not straightforward and honest. Councillor ROBERTS said he would endeavour to avoid indulgence in any personalities, that were only charac- teristic of young and inexperienced members of the Town Council. (Laughter.) He wished to ask a few questions so that he might be guided in the vote he was about to make. Up to the present moment he had not made up his mind which way he should vote, although he should have been pleased if the committee had not advertised for a cindidate, but had appointed Mr. Young, because he knew him very well indeed. He knew his wife, and he knew them both sufficiently well to say without hesitation that lie heli ved them to be both well qualified to undertake the duties of the office. With regard to Mr. Joseph Taylor, he might say that he had known him from boyhood, and could repeat every- thing Councillor Heaton had said about his personal character, fitness for the office, and respectability of the whole family. Oae gentleman had referred to the fitness of Mr. Young, and supported that gentleman's applica- tion for the office by stating that he possessed "an habitually grave demeanour." Well, Mr. Taylor's demeanour was still graver than that of Mr. Young. (Laughter.) It was said that if they app ,inted anyone but Mr. Young, the town would be put to the cost of 235 per year more. Was that true? That was rather a big order for him to swallow. He took it that they did not pay £35 a year for nothing. If they did so it was time they reformed themselves and addressed them-elves to proper questions of economy. If the appointment of sexton was held under similar terms to that of St. Paul's Church, all the Council had to do was to say: " We will recognise the position of Mr. Young as fe-xton to the Parish Church and require him to do the duties, and thus we shall not pay the registrar of the cemetery for discharging the duties, the sexton of the Parish Church performs." If the Council asserted its position it might require Mr. Young to perform to du ties of sexton to the Parish Church. He (Councillor Roberts) wish al In know whether the appointment ef registrar was bound to follow the appointment of seliton of the Parish Church, because if so it was a farce for the Censet-ry Committee to meet together to make the appointment. Their proper duty would be to fold their arms, and wait till the Rector had made his appointment, and then con- firm that appointment by appointing the sexton regis- trar of the cemetery. As Councillor Woods had said, he believed the Rector • was a gentleman of the highest ' honour, but at the same time he (Councillor Roberts) did not know how he might have been advised in the matter. There was no legal obligation upon him to carry out the agreement entered into by his predecessor, but there was such a thing as a question of honour in these matters. It was to be re- gretted the Rector should have taken the action he did unwillingly, which might be open to the construction in certain minds that he had attempted to force the hands of the Council. Was that Council never to have the right of appointing its own registrar. When was the time to come ? (Several members : " Now.") Coun- cillor Roberts said Mrs. Young had strong qualifications, but they were not appointing her. They could not re- tain her in the appointment if anything happened to her husband. Therefore what they had to look at was a person responsible to them,and that was not Mrs.Youeg, but Mr. Young. If it was considered that Mr. Young had pre-eminent qualifications for the position by all means let them appoint him. Whoever was appointed he had no doubt that the Council would be well served. He regretted that this had become a matter of discus- sion, and thought that if there was any case when a discussion might have been excluded this was one of those cases.

Councillor SHAW GREEN said no one had higher re- spect for both candidates than he had. It had been considered desirable to terminate as soon as possible all sinecures, and in the propossed Bill there was a clause whereby they hoped to limit such appointments to the lives of the men who now held them. Mr. Young had been appointed as sexton, and if he were appointed registrar they would be sure of getting rid of one life.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said the Rector asked his advice on the appointment of a sexton, and he aged the same words as Councillor Roberts had used with regard to the Rector. He told the Rector that if he hadthe ap- pointment he should appoint the man of his choice, and not allow the Council to appoint a man for him. He knew Mr. Young was a suitable man for the place,and he sug- gested to the Rector that he should be appointed. He did not give that advice with the idea of going against the Council, but he thought that the Rector would be simply acting in his own rights. Councillor SirsuroN supported the amendment. He did not like to go against the decision of the committee, but he did not think it was, any more than any other committee, infallible, and he believed that on this occa- sion they had made a very great mistake. He had failed to hear that Mr. Taylor possessed any special qualifica- tion for the post. He heard Mr. Heaton say that the work had not been done satisfactorily. That surely was the,fault of the esmmittee. If they compared the quali- fications of the two men, he thought they would agree with him that Mr. Young was the better man for the post. He would also have the assistance of his wife. Councillor PLIIMPTON, in suppor' ing the amendment, said an active member of the committee and a supporter of Mr. Taylor said distinctly that he believed, and that the cemmittee believed, that Mr. Young was the best , man but that he would not get the situation on account of the interferenee of the Rector. He thought it very hard that if Mr. Young was the best man he should have to suffer on account ot the interference of the Rec- tor or anyone else. The question was then put to the vote, the voting being as fellows :—For Alderman HARRISON'S amend- ment : The Mayor, Aldermen Francomb, Harrison, Wright, Hutchinson, Blarkhurst ; Councillors James Fairclough, R. T. Fairclough, Shaw Green, Dr. Cannel!, Woods, Muir, Longtin Bennett, Davies, Greening, Skel- ton, Tinsley, Ilepherd, I. ,mpton. For the motion : Alderman Bolton, Councillors, Heaton, Hill, Shillcock, Flood, Wilkinson, Shaw, Garner,and Baird.
The amendment was declared carried by 20 to nine, and the rest of the minutes were agreed to,
COUNCILLOR WOODS MOTION.

Councillor Woons asked that he :night be allowed to go on with the motion standing in his name, instead of leaving it until the end of the agenda. Councillor HEATON moved as an amendment that the minute be sent back to the corn inittee for further con- sideration. Alderman BLACICHURST said he thought everybody would thoroughly understand whatthey were doin,,,and it would simplify maters if the motion were dealt with at once. .

_ Councillor FLOOD seconded the amendment. The MAYOR put the question to the council, and it was decided by a large majority to go on with the mo- tion. Councillor WOODS then proposed that Mr. Young be appointed registrar, and presented petitions bearing 300 signatures, requesting that the consideration of the Council be given to Mr. Young. Alderman HARRISON seconded. He felt sure if they appointed Mr. Young it would he almo4qual to having two registrars ; for besides Mr. Young, Mrs. Young was as competent a person as they could possibly have. Alderman BOLTON ; I certainly do not like this busi- ness, to think that the Council his not confidence in its committee. (Cries of " Vote, vote.") The MAYOR: Order, order.

Alderman BOLTON (warmly) : I have a right to speak and I will speak. Continuing he thought the Council ought to have sufficient confidence in the committee to adopt their recommendation. Previously on such occa- sions, when the minutes had been overruled, the com- mittee had had an opportunity of rectifying the mistake it had made. It was an insult t, the committee to act in this way, and it had only been done once before, and that net in the memory of the present Council.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman E. Greenall) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Francomb, Harrison, Blackhurst, Sutton, Wright, Hutchinson ; Councillors Plumpton, Nionks,

Hepherd, Heaton, Bolton, Muir, Tinley, Greening, Davies, Baird, Garner, Shaw, Beaman, It T. Fair - dough, J. Fairclough, Shaw Green, Roberts, Cannel!, Hill, Smethurst, Shillcock, Woods, Flood, Wilkin- son, Longton, Skelton, Bennett : Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town Clerk) ; Fairhurst (borough trea- surer).

div.head: DEATH OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL, BART.
div.p: THE DEATH OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL, BART.

Before the business of the Council commenced, the Mayor referring to the death of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall said : There has assed away since our last meeting uur venerable and respected townsman, Sir Gilbert Greenall, at the ripe age of 88. The late Sir Gil bert.will be long remembered in the town for his benevolence and kindness. I feel tosome extent debarred by my relationship to the deceased baronet from saying more on the subject, and,l will, therefore move :—"That this Council desire to record their deep regret on the occasion of the death of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., and their sense of the eminent • public services rendered by him to the town as its representative in Parliament for nearly 34 years and as a former member of the Council ; and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to Lady- Greenall and her family the sincere sympathy and con- dolence of the Council with them in their bereavement."

(Applause.) Alderman' HARRISON as the oldest member of the Coun- cil present said that he should like to say a few words upon the subject. He was sanguine enough to believe that there was no gentleman present who would not sup- port the resolution just proposed by the Mayor. It had become their custom—he might call it time-honoured— that whenever one of the members of the Council or one of the ex-members passed away,to refer to his departure and when they came to remember that the late Sir Gil- bert Greenall was once a member of the Council, an alderman of the borough, and for nearly forty years the parliamentary representative, it almost followed as a matter of course that they should notice him on that occasion. Not only was he a irvlnber of the Council,but he was also a munificent supporter of many institutions, including religious, educational and charitable. He was ever ready and openhanded to those who required sub- stantial assistance. The late Sir Gilbert Greenall was decidedly a party man, but his politics and his patrintism were so blended together that it was diffieult to know where the one commenced and the other left off. His genial smile and kindly recognition of the humblest member ot the community were the gentlemanly instincts of a great character. In his own home he was a pattern husband, and a kind indulgent parent, and Lady Greenall's loss was very great, and they all sympAhized with her in her bereavement.

Councillor ROBERTS said he would like to represent in some measure, " the other side of the House," and join most sincerely in the words of sympathy which the Mayor and Alderman Harrison Lad so well expressed. He could not attempt to follow Alderman Harrison in his eloquent utterances, but he wished most sincerely to express on behalf of the Liberal members of the Council representing the larger body of Liberals outside the Council, their regret at Sir Gilbert Greenall's death. (Hear, hear.) He had always looked upon him as a strong party man, but they always considered him an honourable one, and he always admired consistency in the support frf the principles which a man believed to be right. He believed that against Sir Gilbert's private life, and personal character, not one word could he spoken. He therefore, joined most sincerely on behalf of other members of the Council, and the party outside, in the resolution of condolence. The resolution was unanimously adopted.

div.head: DELTH OF ALDEUMAN AsaroN.
div.p: DELTH OF ALDEUMAN AsaroN.

The MAYOR proposed the following motion of condol- ence with the family of Alderman Ashton :—" That this Council receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Joseph Ashton, Esq., an alderman of this borough, which took place on the 14. th July, and desires to record the loss which the Council has sustained by his death, and to express its appreciation of the valuable services rendered by him to the borough during a period of upwards of 21 years.- And also to request the Town Clerk to convey to the family of the deceased the sincere sympathy and condolence of the Council with them in their bereavement." (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON Said that alt hough Alderman A shton was n.)t very prominent in the council chamber as a speaker, still at the same time he worked hard on the committees, and took great interest in the affairs of the town. _

Aldorman FRANCOMB said that he had known Alder- man Ashton for something like 26 years and had always looktd upon him as a man of the highest character, and although, perhaps, he had not had the advantages which many had had in education, still he was one of nature's noblemen.
The vote of condolence was passed unanimously. MRS. MACKIE AND ALDERMAN HARRISON.

The next item on the agenda paper was a letter from Mrs. Mackie, bet previous to this being read, Alderman HARRISON said that he hoped permission would be given to him to make an explanation,as it contained a personal attack upon himself. The letter was then read as follows: " 16, Stanley-street, July sth, 1894. To his Worship the Mayor ot Warringtan.—Will your Worship excuse my troubling you on a matter that as a wife has given -me most severe pain. Mr. Harrison's defence of my hus- band, if it deserved the name, is so contradictory that it reminds me of the proverb " Save me from my friends." It was quite unnecessary to tell the people of Warrington that my husband at as the most genial and kind-hearted of.men, that he laboured hard earnestly and patriotically to do all he could, generously and justly, but why go on to state that he had detractors, and lam not going to say they were not justified. Well let these detractors state their reasons for maligning hini. I cannot fight the air. Do they find it in the forty years incessant labour for the the town generally and hia workpeople particularly, some. of whom owe their easy and improved position to his unfailing energy though they are.too ungrateful to confess it? IS it because he struggled perhaps unwisely to pay seven and a half per cent, on the " Gaardian" shares? If they think that was wrong let them return it to make up for the last seven years when they have not paid anything. I have it in his own statement that seventy-five thou- sands were paid in dividends up to the time of his ill- ness. That that illness was caused by incessant brain work, his medical attendant will testify, and that my very severe illness was the cause of his leaving home, he quite believed, for an hydropathic establishment, where he was happy as his letters sent every day proves. His only ungratified wish was that I did not go to him, and which my severe illness rendered impossible. His last words were any news of her coming,' and then immedi- ately falling asleep and his much liked attendant says he had a most peaceful end. There he made many friends, ' tor which I heartily thank God. There has nothing come to him that has not come to many others. The paralytic seizures have been very frequent lately, and though his affected the brain, and rendered it necessary for him to go, there are a thousand circumst tnces that soften the blow. May any who are so afflicted escape any eulogies from those will think his detractors were justified. Will your Worship do me the great favour of reading the enclosed at the next Council meeting and let my more than fourscore years plead for my untidy writing. I expect soon to meet my most de at husband, and I could not leave his defence to other pens.—Yours respectfully Eliza beth Mackie." Alderman HARRISON having been given permission said that he never was so astounded in his life than , when he was permitted to see the letter of Mrs. Mackie. He had written a letter to her expressing his astonish- ment and extreme regret that he should have said one word which should jar upon her feelings for a moment. No one could have sinned more innocently than he had done, and he craved that she would favour him with an interview of a few minutes when he hoped to completely disperse the wrong expression she had conceived of his remarks. However, Mrs. Mackie did not favour him with an interview and he found he had no alternative but to offer that brief explanation there. In his opinion the letter had nothing to do with the Council, but he did not fear the reading of any letter concerning him. He left the matter as it stood, and was ready to he judged by those of his fellow townsmen who thought it worth while to do so. (Hear, hear.) Another letter was read from Mrs. Mackie as follows: —" 16, Stanley-st., July :11th, 1894. Mrs. Mackie desires to express her thanks to the Town Council for their kind vote of sympathy on the death of her very dear husband. She had the satisfaction of nursing him for more than seven years, and it is a great satisfaction 'tef her to know that he was kindly nursed when she was ,unable to do it, and that his end was a most peaceful one.

The overtaxed brain is at rest, Its achings and throhhirgs are o'er, Envy and malice concealed or expressed Can hurt or disturb him no more." THE BIRTH OF THE ROYAL PRINCE. Letters were read from the Queen, and the Duke and Duchess of York in reply to the loyal addresses sent by the Council on the birth of an heir to the English throne.
ELECTION OF AIDERMAN.
The Council next proceeded with the election of an alderman in the place of the late Alderman Ashton. The election resulted in the unanimous e7ection of Councillor .Bolton.

Alderman BouroN, in reply, said: I can hardly find words to express myself in -thanking the Council for having elected me to the honour of an Alderman. I did not know I had so many friends, hut I will do all I can to deserve the honour which has been conferred upon me. (Applause.)
COUNTY COUNCIL ELFCTION.
The TowN CLIME announced that Alderman Francomb had been elected a county councillor for No. 3 division of the borough in the place of Mr. Lewis Voisey resigned.

div.p: THE COMUISSIONERS INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The Clerk reported the receipt of a notice trom the Ritricorn Improvement Commissioners, stating that it wai their d . ire and intention to discontinue the azree- ment of 1832 existing between them Ind the Runcorn Board of Go trdians as to the receipt and m tintenance of pauper patients in the infectious dise-ises hospital at the expiration of three m niths from the 2,1.1 inst.

THE NEW SCHOOL ATTENDANCE INQUIRY OFFICER. In accordance with notice of motion. Mr. firandreth moved that the resolution passed on the 29th May last, appointing Mr. Cooke 'nquiry officer for the Runcorn district without remuneration, be rescinded, and that Mr. Cooke be appointed inquiry officer as from the 16th June for the said district with remuneration to be paid by fees at the rate of is. for each new case reported by him and relieved by the Guardians —Mr. Heywood :eeonded and the resolution was eat rird.

Mr. Brandreth produced the report of the Financiii Committee which showed that £l3B was to be paid in out-relief; £B5 for Runcorn; £33 for Frodsham, and £2O for Badworth. There was a balanee in the trea- surer's hands amounting to more than £564.

div.head: VISITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: VISITING COMMITTEE.

Mr. Cunnah said the Committee wished to thank Mr. Shaw of the L. and N.-W. Ry. Coy. and also the mana- ger of the Pier Comp toy at Rhyl, the first gentleman for the efficient arrangements made for the conveyance of the children to and from Rhyl on the previous Wednes- day, when they travelkd thither on the occasion of their annual treat, and the latter gentleman for so kindly allowing the juveniles upon the pier.—On the proposi- tion of Mr. Handley seconded by Mr. Williama, the vote of thanks was carried. The last named gentleman said that he could not h-lp expressing his individual pleasure, and that of the rest of the cointnittee, in proposing the thanks of the Board to Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah for the admirable way in which all arrangements had been carried out. Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah had given as much attention to the children on that day as they would have given to their own children.—Mr. Heywood seconded the proposition and it was carried.—Mr. Cunnah on replying on behalf of his wife and himself said it was always a pl a-tire to both of them to provi le any such treat for the children, and to endeavour to ensure their enj tyment of it. He hoped that they would always possess sufficient funds to give this annual treat to the children.

div.head: FINDING OF THE MISSING ENGINEER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE FINDING OF THE MISSING ENGINEER AT RUNCORN.
INWEST.

The circumstances attending the death of Samuel late chief engineer of the steamship " Albertina," whose dead body was recovered from the Ship Canal by the dredger " Barry" on Tuesday night of last week, were enquired into on the fol- lowing Friday by Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, at the Cemeter, Lodge, Greenway-road, Runcorn.—lames Berrow, of 16, Gloucest..r-st., Cardiff, identified the body as that of James 'Higley by means of a scar on its right side which he said v ai caused during the man's lifetime by an accident on board ship.—P.C. flammersley, stationed at Weston P/int, stated that when the deceased was drowned on the 9th January, he (witness) made the m.cessary encriiries prep:a/atoll t the.holiing of'aan quest. Ile saw the man AuAustus Guise, who ws the first mate of the vessel, and who was with Tilsley when he fell into the canal. Guise told him that at 7.30 p,m. on the 9 h January, himsolf and William Pearson, second mate on the " Albertina," went with the deceased to Runcorn. They all returned at about 10.15 p.m. and when Tilsley was nearly at the top of the ladder, which was more in a horizontal position than a perpendicular, he missed his footing and fell into the canal. Guise made a grab for the falling man but could not reach him. William Poarson jumped into the water and searched at/out, but could not find any trace of him. Toe police ' officer, continuing, said that he had seen Pearson, and he had supported, in statvment, everything which Guise had told him. Questioned by a juror, witness said the ot the" Al bertna " appeared to be a very peacable set of men and he did not think for one moment that ther: hail be/ n any recent quarrelling amongst them.— The jury eventually returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned."

SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1894.

Tun war which has broken out War in the between China and Japan concerns East. England more than any other European Power, with the possible exception of Russia. A world-wide empire bring with it world-wide responsibilities, and British posses- sions are now so numerous and so wide-spread that a ditturba nce in any part of the globe is almost certain to afiect one or other of them. China is in close contact—a neighbour, SO to speak—of more than one of the dependencies of this country, and, in addition to that, the com- mercial relations withboth China iln&jap. an are of an important character, and involve mighty interests. War, too, is .Contagions. When it has ! oneebroken out iv i apt to spread like. a pesti:- lence, and no one can foretell where or when its ending will be. Fortunately, there does not seem to, be even .'a possibili4 of- this or any other European country which has interees,in the East becething' embroiled. in the present conflict. Thera i, of course, a latent rivalry between England and Russia in some parts of Asia,: but it is not at, all likely that any point of difference *ill be developed to an acute degree at the present time. It is more probable that they will find a common cause in protecting the rights of their 'own subjects against the excesses and encroach- ments of the-two belligerents. Already it would seem thht England is placed under the necessity of demanding reparation from the Japanese for an atrocious excess in firing upon and sinking an unarmed vessel carrying the British flag and hav- ing on board more than a thousand Chinese soldiers. This was done before even a declaration of war had been made, and Was, therefore, a grave offence both against international law and humanity. The Japanese Government, however, on being apprised of the mistake of its over- zealous Admiral Very promptly apologised to the British Government and offered to make all the atonement that is now possibla for the damage that has been done.
The cause of the present war, like the cause of many another war, is obscure. China and Japan seem to have been exercising a joint control in Corea and have fallen (U over their self-imposed
task. The real origin of the disi,ut3 is doubtless to ke found in the national jealousies and the race Jlatred of the two peoples. Japan is generally credited with the doubtful honour of forcing on

the struggle. It is to be feared that is another instance of the truth of the Shakespearian aphorism that the sight of means to do ill deeds make deeds done." Japan has been furbishing her weapons for a long time past probably with the intention of turning them against her colk rival. She is now credited with having an arra, of sixty-thousand men which is admirably trained and equipped, and with being able to augment this force if need be by another one hundred thousand men. Her navy, too, is supposed to be in Per' feet trim for action. Japan has, in fact, show] herself to be, in warlike matters, an apt pupil - the Western nations. It may be sospected, there- fore, that having perfected her arrangements she has been tempted to hasten a struggle which w' perhaps, considering the history and the relations of the two countries, inevitable either sooner or later. It is, of course, premature to speak Of the probable result of the war. It is generally exPec; ted that Japan will, owing to her readiness and the comparatively easy mobilization of her forces, score some successes at the outset. But these!, unless they are of a very startling description, win not decide the duel. China is a %wit" able giant amongst the nations of the earth. Her population is reckoned not by nail" • lions but by hundreds of millions, and her WO attains enormous dimensions, though it is net known how many of these troops are adequatelY trained and armed with modern weapons. It has however, been proved on more than one occasinur that Chinese troops when properly officered and led make a capital fighting material. Owing to the immense area of the country China cannot he easily struck in a vital part, and, apart from some such coup ,her resources and persistence will enable her to carry on the conflict for an indefinite periedl and may in the end wear down the resistance Of her. opponent.

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS FOR RUNCORN
div.p: THE NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS FOR RUNCORN

' CORRECTION. We incorrectly stated in our last issue that the Rev. William George, of Morecambe,in the Lancaster Circuit, would. succeed the Rev. T. Wilkes as superintendent at Runcorn. Such is not the case. The gentleman first mentioned has been choosen and has accepted the posi- tion,at present occupied by the Rev Willihm Arrowsmith which is that of second minister. The Rev. Arrowsunith will soon vacate that post take over the superintendency of the St. Helens Circuit, and the Rev. T. Wilkes will also leave this town for his new station of Superintend- ent of the Usion-street circuit of Rochdale. He will be superceded by the Rev Thomas Brackanbury,superinten- dent minister of Huddersfield. The Rev. James Hanby of Halton, has been appointed second minister for Black- pool, to live at Fleetwood. His place will be taken by the Rev W. Lile Stone, of Aberystwyth.
THE LATE MR. JAMES REYNOLD'S WILL

The will has been proved of the late Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., of Foxhill, Frodsham, hide merchant, Liverpool, who died on the 30th May last. Tne will is dated the 29th January, 1894, anti the gross value of the personalty is sworn at £71,289. Testator bequeaths to his widow an immediate legacy of £l,OOO, together with all his furniture, horses, carriages, agricul- tural implements, plate, jewels,and valuables at Foxhill. There is a legacy of £l,OOO to the. Vicar and churchwar- dens for the time being of St. Paul's Church. Heist)? ,the income to be paid to the Vicar in augmentation of his stipend, or the principal to be paid over to the Ecclesias- tical or Charity Commissioners, to be applied to the augmentation of the endowment of the church. To each domestic servant, male and female, coachman,gardener, &c., deceased leaves £5; and to those who have been in his employment ten years an additional £lO each, with a further £1 added for every additional year of service. The house and pleasure grounds of Foxhill are placed in the hands of the executors for the use of the widow dur- ing her lifetime or widowhood. .Deceased bequeaths the goodwill of his business as a hide merchant, carried on under the title of Robert Smith and Co. to Charles Banks Lucy and Joseph Bunnell Blossom, both in his employ- ment, subject to the payment thereout by them of the capital he might have employed therein at the time of his decease, and with a loan of £lO,OOO for three years. The residue of the real and personal estate and property, is placed under the direction of the trustees and execu- tors, Charles Hutchings, Charles Reynolds, and Lewis Voisev, with directions to invest £33,750, and pay the interest to the widow during heir lifetime or widowhood. In the event of her ceasing to reside at Fox-hill she will receive £BOO a year, and in the event of herfre-marriage £5OO a year. The following bequests are also made To testator's sister, Elizabeth Ware, an annuity of £300; to his niece, Alice Warren, daughter of his late sister Fanny Partridge Warren, an annuity of £5O • to Mary Sparrow, widow of the late Ben. Sparrovviof bridge, Devon.the interest on £5OO ; to Mary Northcott, widow of deceased's late nephew, Henry Northcott, the interest on £2,000; £5OO each to such remaining children. of his brother, Thomas Reynolds. as attain 21 years of age ; £l,OOO each to such of the children of deceased's late sister, Fanny Partridge Warren, with the exception of his niece, Alice Warren, as shall he 21 years of age ; £5OO each to such children of his brother, William Rey- nolds, as shall attain 21 years ; £lOO each to the children of his conein and brother-in-law, John Hutchings ; £5OO each to the children of his cousin and brother-in-law,. Charles Hutchings,who shall attain 21 years ; £5OO each to Charles Banks Lucy and Joseph B. Blossom in recog- nition of their long and faithful service ; several smaller legacies are also made to other relatives. The rest of the personal estate is directed to be divided among all per- sons who receive legacies, with the exception of the small.£lo ones, and with the exception of the vicar and wardens of Helsby and of the employ-es Messrs.Luey and Blossom, in proportion to the amount of their several legacies. In two codicils deceased revokes the bequest. of the goodwill of his business tip Charles B. Lucy and Joseph B.Blossom, and. leaves the business absolutelY to Charles B. Lucy. He also revokes the gift of £5OO to Joseph B. Blossom. Testator bequeaths to Caroline Rey- nolds, widow of his late brother, Williarn Reynolds, £lOO a year,amd makes further legacies to emplos 6s. The gift sf £l,OOO to the vicar of Helsby is also revoked, and the executors are instructed to invest the £l,OOO, and upon the occurrence of the neat vacancy in the living the pre- sentation of St. Paul's, Helsby, should be offered to the deceased's cousin, the Rev. G. F. Reynolds, curate of Matlock Bath, and whether he accepts it or not the £l,OOO, with interest, will 43 paid to the incumbent and wardens of the church for the augmentation of the stipend.
THE SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT EtUNCORN.

RESUMPT lON OF THE CORONER'S INQUIRY. The inquest respecting the death of a Liverpool unfortunate named Ann Moran which was opened by Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, on Tuesday after- noon of last week in the cemetery offices, Green- ! way-road, Runcorn, was resumed on Friday after- -110011; It will be remembered that • the Coroner adjourned the inquiry in order that the police might make further investigations with regard to the deceased woman's whereabouts on Saturday night, and to verify . the statement made by the man Sant when before the jury: Another witness, named John Barns, labourer, - of Fryer-street, was called and deposed to having first known the deceased on the Saturday night previous when she asked him between nine and ten to treat her to a glass of beer. He went with her to the Commercial Hotel, (" Glass Barrel,") but owing to her disorderly be- haviour the barman or proprietor would not serve her. They then left the house arsd he afterwards quitted her company near the Market Place. Qusstloned by the Ceroner, witness said he did net know of his own know- ledge that the woman he was with was. actually Ann Moran, the deceased woman upon whom the inquest was then being held. The reason he knew was that the ; police had evidently seem him with her and had told him who she was.—George ?oft, barman at the Commercial Hotel, said he could not remember seeing the last witness on Saturday in the hotel.—Paul Caldwell, carter lodging at the Blue Bell, Fryer-street, deposed to being • in the company of the witness John Sant on Saturday from eight o'clock until a quarter to eleven. They both • entered two or -three public houses, and had drinks in each. The Commercial Hotel was the last house they went into, the • time at. which they entered being ten • o'clock. Witness came out at a quarter to eleven and went home leaving Sant still there. Witness saw noth- ing of the deceased neither of John Burns.—P.C. Richard- son stated that since Tuesday he had made further in- quiries and had found that the statement made by Sant to the Coroner with reference to 'Mrs. Fieldes, of Irwell- lane, having permitted him to sleep in her stable was quite true. She had toll witness that Sant came to her on Saturday night, and having explained that he had been locked out of the Blue Bell asked her • to allow him to sleep in the stable for the night. To this request she atsented ; and he remained with them until dinner-time the following day. Witness had also discovered that the Blue Bail had been closed at ten Minutes past eleven on Saturday night. —Dr. McDougall testified to having taalde a post mortem . exam- ination of the body. He found no external marks of violence, but internally the appeararce was perfectly consistent with drowning. and he concluded that that had been the cause of death.—The Coroner inquired of P.C. Richardson if he had brought the woman Catherine. Bowden as a witness, who was siiii to have seen • Sant and the deceased tiorn,ln together late on Saturday night.—P.C. Richardson replied that after having made the neCessary inquiries he was informed that the woman had been sent to Knutsford aaol for attempting to drug a moan—The Coroner: Oh! I am .afraid her eVidence would not be very reliable then. The Coroner, in eon- cludina his review of the evidenee said that as to the unfortunate man George Sant, whose testimony had been brought s,tnewhat into question, no guspicion whatever now rested upon him. It had been ascertained that the st,tement he had made reaerding his whereabouts on he Saturday night mentioned was perfectly correeteand It was enly fair to the man to thus allude to it. He (the Coroner) advised the jury that it would ho the .test c.orse to return the open verdict " Found drowned," so ;hat the police, if they were at any time put in the pas- of imoortant evidence aeuring upon the case, would la able to re-open it- Such a. verdict would not prever t. further investigation bring made.—The jury accordingly recorded a verdict of " Found drowned."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1894.
WA.RRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Board room on Wednesday morning. Mr. Wm. Houghton occupied the chair, and there were also present: Rev. G. F. Roberts, Dr. Patterson, Means. G. Pilling W. Balharry, J. Clarke, W. Gill, R. Heaton, J. Hill, A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, T. Mather, J. Muir, G. Rat- cliffe, W. J. Shaw, J. Turton, J. C. Sutton, (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (master),and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate schools).
A DEPUTATION TO INSPECT FIREWOOD._

On the iminutes of the House Committee being read, Mr. Mum raised an objection to an item of expense in- curred by a deputation of the board to Acton Grange to inspect some firewood on sale there. It was explained that the deputation consisted of three members of the Board and the workhouse master. Mr. Muir said he did not think it was necessary for such a number to go. The CLEM( stated that the expense to the Board was really the cost of the conveyance. Mr. MUIR said it was not a matter of cost but of principle. The matter then dropped.

div.head: CASE OF SMALLPDX.
div.p: THE CASE OF SMALLPDX.

The following letter written by the medical officer of health (Dr. Gornall) to Dr. Braide respecting the man who presented himself at the workhouse suffering from smallpox the previous Wednesday, was read : "2nd August, 1894, Dear Dr. Braide,—The case admitted from the workhouse is undoubtedly smallpox. I ascertained last night that though he had lived in Warrington four months, he nude various journeyings, which included Northvrich, where he slept at a model lodging-house on the 17th ult., staying there until the 21st. I wrote to Dr. Fox the medical officer of health, and received the enclosed reply : the Cross, Lymm,—We had a case removed from a model lodging-house in Northwich on the date you mentioned (July 17). I had as many of the occupants re-vaccinated as possible, but many had fled leaving no address. It was undoubtedly smallpox, but is doing well. I have not heard of any other case.— Yours etc.. Dr. Fox.'—This proves our case up to the hilt.2Yours sincerely, .1. H. Gornall?'

• THE lATE SIR GILBERT IMEENALL. The CLERK read the following letter he had received from Lady Greenall. "Walton Hall, Warrington, July 30, 1894, James Sutton, Esq.—My Dear Sir,—Will you be so good as to convey to the Board of Guardians, our most sincere and grateful thanks for their kind condolences in our great sorrow, and accept my thanks and my chil- dren's for your personal sympathy in our bereavement. Believe me, yours Very truly, Susie G reenall." THE VISITINU COMMISSIONER'S REPORT.

The report of Lieutenant Colonel Irving on his visit to the workhouse on the 7th July on behalf of the Local Government Board was read. It was as follows: There were at the time of my visit 22 inmates classed as of unsound mind-7 Males and 15 females. Of those seen by the last visiting commissioner two men and four women are dead and three women have been discharged. Two men and one woman were reported to be epileptic and there was one inmate of each sex in bed. I saw all 22 inmates, and heard no complaints from anyone. The clothing was clean and tidy, the bedding in good order. All with two exceptions seemed to be cases suitable for a workhouse, but the man Winstanley who has constantly recurring fits would I think be b4ter looked after in an asylum, and the woman Worrall, if she continues to be troublesome will probably require more efficient control than she can receive in the .Union. I commend these cases to the medical officer. No" tell tale " clock has been introduced so that there are no Means of knowing that the duties of the night watchman are properly per- formed. It was decided to refer tf.e matter to the House Committee.
THE ACTION AGAINST THE GUARDIANS AND OTHERS.

Mr. SurtoN read a communication giving reasons for the action taken by Henry Miller against the Board of Guardians, Basil Shearer, Samuel Hunt, and Inspector Bowen for alleged false,and malicious imprisonment at Warrington on the 13th. April for which he claims £lOOO damages. Mr. Sutton said he would take such steps as were necessary on their behalf. Mr. Muir wished to know whether they were retilly guilty. Mr. Gill thought it wotild be better for the matter not to be discussed at. present, and the Clerk was of the same opinion. The subject was, thereupon, allowed to -drop. .

div.head: NOTICE OF MOTION.
div.p: NOTICE OF MOTION.

Mr. SHAW said he wished to give notice that at the next meeting of the Board ho would move that they pro. vide for the •Catholic children of Padzate schools, Catho- lic bibles. It was stated that this was a matter which the Committee should deal with. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of the Rrincorn Rural Sanitary Authority was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Workhouse, Dutton, Mr. J ohn Mclntyre pre- siding. There were also present Messrs. J. Bran- dreth, T. Baxter,C.C.,J. M. Williams,li. E. lie:ovood E. Aaren, J. Knowles S. Woodward, T. Lewis, C. T. Whitley, John Vith itlow, J. Weir,Joh4 Ashton, clerk, and J. Farrington, nuisance inspector.

div.head: REMUNERATION OF THE CLERK
div.p: REMUNERATION OF THE CLERK

The Clerk reeorted the receipt of a letter from • the Local Government Board, written on the 28th ult., .sanc- tinning the payment to the-Cleric of the Rural Sanitary Authority of the various amounts -recommended by the members for his services during the year as clerk to the Parochial Committees: of Frodsham township, Apple- ton, Halton, and Frodsham Locdship. 'ITIE ALLEGED OFFENSIVE TRADE AT CLIFTON. . A letter dated July 27th was read from Mr. Jacob Commas, of Liverpool, referring to the alleged nuisance at Clifton, and expressing regret that the medical officer had reported that the trade which he carried on was of- fensive. .There might be a little smell from oil in hot weather, but an oil smell was not an offensive one. However he should be more frequently at the works himself during the summer months, and would try to prevent any smell whatever.—ln a later letter on the 3rd of August, Mr. Commas stated that the premises pre- vious to his occupation . were used as . a patent Manure works, whip!' business must of necessity be more ellen-. sive than the present one. Further,having laid out a large sum of money in furnishing and fitting up the neces- sary plant to manufacture this oil ,should hebe compelled to lose this, it would be a manifest injustice ; and again, looking at the situation of the works (the nearest house being a quarter of a mile away ) any offensive smell,and that a-minimum, would be" imported" before it could become a nuisance. The complaint. .in this .instance arose from the bursting of a barrel of .the raw material whilst in transit. This was purely an accident which might not-occur again. In future it would be anxious care to prevent any cause for complaint, and trusted to the authority's favourable consideration of the matter, which to him was of the, most vital importance. Mr. Farrington remarked that 'there was a-house in the yard adjoining the works. Mr. Aaron suggested that Mr. Comins be brought before the Authority.—Mr. Heywood thought- the matter • should be left as it was. If Mr. Comins came before the Board, he.aliqht think that he had a licence to continue his manufacturing. He thought that as long as the nuisance was not repeated the mat- ter might be kept in abeyance.—The nuisance inspector said he thought there would be no smell when the weather became cool again. It was only during the very hot weather that the smell arose.—The Chairman said that the Course suggested by Mr. Heywood could be followed, and in time meantime the inspector would keep the mat- ter before hitn.—This was agreed t

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB ANNUAL SPORTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB ANNUAL SPORTS.

The tenth annual festival of the Warrington Foot- ball Club was held on the football ground in Wilderspool Causeway on Monday afternoon. The weather in the morning was very threatening, and. it appeared to be likely to set in for rain, but to- wards noon, tfie sun shone out, and the weather proved to be everything that could be desired. As a consequence of this, there was an enlrmous "gate," the number being estimat.ed at about 5,000. The arrangements were carried out in a very satis- factory manner, and the ground was also in excel- lent condition for sprinting and also for bicycle riding, and it may be mentioned that in the bicNcle races, there were only two "spills." The following were the officials in charge of the arrangements; Clerk of the course, Mr. T. Bowers; starter, Mr. F. Baldwin;, judges, Messrs. P. Davies, J. Evans, W. Lomas, and R. Andrews; committee, Messrs. W. Hewitt, W. Speakman, T. Barnes jun., Fair. Turner, S. Wright, E. Gilbert, T. Davies, G. Smith, J. Boyle, and W. RAndles ; handicap- pers, Messrs. J. H. Hardwick, and H. P. Ellis; hon. treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton; hon. sec. Mr. J. E. War- ren; assistant hon. sec., Mr. S. W. Jeffery. There were eighteen events inclusive of the competition for the Northern Counties Gymnastic Championship, on the programme, and some excellent races were witnessed during the afternoon. The first event was 100 YARDS PLAYING MEMBERS' RAC,E.

There were four prizes for this event whick was run in two heats, the first and second to run in the final. In the first heat, J. T. Massey, the scratch man failed to gain the necessary places, and after a good race, T. i Cunningham came n first and .1. Thornton, second. In the.second heat H. Webster made a welcome re-appear- ance before a Warrington crowd, but he was too much handicapped to "pull cif" the race which was won by P. Carey and Fair. Turner, Carey winning easily. There being four prizes, each of the winners of the heats of course gained one, the order being, P. Carey, T. Cun- ningham, J. Thornton, and Fair. Turner. Carey and Cunningham were very close at the end, but the latter's handicap preyed too much for him. Carey's victory however,_proved Very popular with the crowd. 100 YARDS HANDICA.P (OPEN). There were 32 entries for this event, although several failed to put in an appearance. The competitors ran in six heats. In the first Archer (Nottingham) was an easy winner, although heavily handicapped. Goodhind (Sheffield) was the successful runner in the second heat in which J. T. Massey of the Warrington Football Club received his quietus. H. Webster gained a popular vic- t9ry in the third heat. The fourth heat resulted in a dead heat between J. Shannon (flindley Football Club) and T. Horan (Warrington), but on the two running again later' in the afternoon, the Hindley man was suc- cessful over his rival. There were three Warrington men, Hockenhall, Asnip and Smallman, in the fifth heat but not one of them came in first, the winner being T. W. Daniels of Nantwich. Tne winner of the sixth heat, rejoiced in the name of Noble Morton who hailed from Wigan, and among his followers were Carmine= and Houghtonsof Warrington.. There was therefore only H. Webster left in the final to uphold the hononr of War- rington, and he also failed when the final did come off. The final resulted in a victory of Shannon, and his immediate followers were Noble Morton and Goodhind.

div.head: ONE MILE BICYCLE HANDICAP.
div.p: ONE MILE BICYCLE HANDICAP.

There were 21 entries for this event which was decided-, in two heats. In the first heat were Buxton, Dutton and Charnock, of Warrington, the latter being 15 ears of age, and also Spreckley (Manchester) and Jackson (Altrlncham and Bowden Harriers). A capital race Was the result, and it was not until near the end that any idea of the winner could be ob- tained. Buxton, sTackson,and Spreckley kept very close company, almost all thcs way, but near the end, Buxton by a grand " spurt "got past his two brother cyclists and ran in an easy first. The other two came in in the order above mentioned. There was only-two of the com- petitors of the secOnd heat who came from the Warring- ton district, viz., A. Forster of the W.C.C., and J. A. Watson (15 years) of the Sankey Harriers, Flotigkinson of the Wigan C.C. ran in first, Tomlinson (Hough Green) second, and J. P. White of the St. Helens C.C. third. most exciting race ensued at the final. Buxton was Df : course the favourite with the crowd, and he was con- tinually changin!: his place. At the-last lap, however, he suddenly out-distanced his rivals, a-tad appeared to be a certain first, but Hodgkinson suddenly adopted the same tactics as Buxton, and just passed him at the finish, Buxton being compelled to take the sdeond place. An obstacle race for which there were three privsi caused much a:nusement. The competitors were c.;tri- pelted to perform all kinds of ridiculous feats. After running a few yards, they had to run 'round three barricades, then - under a sail cloth fastened on the 'ground, then more , barricades followed by a dive. through a tub - suspended from a beam. - They than ran up some Planks, at the top of which was a gate. After climbing or tumbling over the gate, they ran down another set of planks. The3e feats had te be done twice, and when they returned to their starting place the second time, they had to wheel a child's, barrow, fil!ed with potatoes, fora distance of about 20 yards. If any of the potatoes dropped out,the comp-=t- tor had to stop and pick them up again. This last per- formance caused .roars of laughter among the spectators, for the mta.toes were piled up so that the least'shake would cause them to drop out. There were 10 campeti- tars for this race which was run in two heats. In the that Horrocks, of Leili, was an easy first until he came to the potatoes, which alnrest cause&his downfall. The second winner was Wnittield of Warrington,and third J. McDonald of Heaton Norris. In the second heat, Gibann of Warrington, fairly ran away from the rest, the second being Groin atld tins third Boyle, both of Warrington. In the final, Gibson attain woo easily. div.head: ST. HELENS
div.p: ST. HELENS
ROBBERY FROM THE PERSON.

At St. Helens Police Court,on Tuesday, Ann Monaghan Who made her 90ch appearance,was charged with stealing a purse, containing 4s. ed., from the person of Robert Ellison, a labourer. The prosecutor was counting his money in the street,when the prisoner came up.snatched his purse, and ran away, Information was given to the police, and she was afterwards apprehended.—She was sent to prison for a month. OBTAINING MONEY BY FALSE FRETENCES AT ROBY.

at Prescot Police Court on Tuesday, Charles Percival, hailing from Dewsbury, was charged, on two informa- tions, with obtaining money by false pretences at Roby. The prisoner visited several houses in the district, and falsely represented that he had been authorised to col- lect subscriptions and donations on behalf of the Huyton and Roby Cricket Club. He obtained a guinea from Mrs. Earle, of Edenhurst, and a similar sum from Miss Pilkington, of Roby Hall. He was committed to prison for a month with hard labour. • SAVAGE ATTACH ON A POLICEMAN.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Edward Carey, of Cowley-street, was charged with assaulting Police-constable Smith on Saturday night. A number of men attacked the constable in Gerard-street, and inflicted serious internal injuries upon him, he being unable -to appear. At the court on Wednesday the officer deposed that on Saturday night the prisoner was creating a disturbance at Gerard's Bridge, and on refusing to go away he took him into custody. Carey then commenced to kick witness, who was knocked to the ground. Pri- soner and his companions then kicked him about the body and legs until he became unconscious, and had to be carried into one of the houses in the locality. He had since been under the care of Dr. M•Nicoll.—Prisoner was fined 255. and costs, or 28 days' imprisonment.
CLAIN FOR COLLIER'S WAGES.

At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Shand, William Birch, collier, residing in Crank-lane, Windle, claimed seven days' wages from Messrs. Glover, Urmson, and Glover, of the Phcenix Colliery, St. Helens, In lieu of seven days' notice. Mr. J.P. Mearns appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. •0. Swift for the defendants.—When the case was called,Ddr. Swift applied for an adjournment on the ground that one of his material witnesses could not attend.—Mr. Mearns said he agreed to the adjournment, but the piesident of the miners' society and the organiser were present to go on with the case. There was a resolution on the books that the case should be taken that day.—His Honour: It does not matter to me if there are a hundred resolutions. —Mr. Mearns said the question might be asked why the case was not heard that day. He asked his Honour to say that if the plaintiff ultimately succeeded he should have the casts of that day awarded.—Mr. Swift con- seated, and the case was-adjourned.

div.head: FATALITY AT A COLLIERY.
div.p: THE FATALITY AT A COLLIERY.

On: Wednesday, Mr. S. Brighouse, -county coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hail, on the body of Robert Hutchinson, 31 years of age, collier, of 34 York- street, who was killed by a fall of roof at the St. Helens collieries of Messrs: Pilkington Brothers, on Saturday morning. Mr. J. O. Swift appeared on behalf.of the firm, and Mr. H. Hall, Government inspector of mines, also attended.—Henry Harrison, collier, deposed that he and deceased were working togethor when the fall oc- curred. A lar:ze stone fell upon Hutchinson, who was dead when extricated. The roof was supported by bars a yard apart, Pesting upon props. Witness attributed the occurrence to a box of coat having•left the rails and knocked down one of the props. tie saw a box off the rails after the accident.—Eloch Carter, fireman, stated that he had examined the. roof at the spot where the fall occurred, an hour before it happened. It then appeared all right and .perfectly safe.—Mr. Hall, Government inspector remarked that on examining the spot he fouxd that the rails were only about 6in. from the foot of the prow supporting the roof: In reply to one of the jurors, he sail the Coal Mines Regulation Act did not stipulate that props should be set at stated distances from the rails It was optional so long as there was an absolute clear- ance for the boxes.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death " With a recommendation that there ought to be a greater space between the rails and the props.

div.head: THELWALL MILKDEALER iN TROUBLE AT MANCFIESTER.
div.p: A THELWALL MILKDEALER iN TROUBLE AT MANCFIESTER.

• At the Strangeways Police Court án 'Wednesday, before Mr. Yates, Q.C., . stipendiary, henry Cooke, farmer, Thelw-all, was summoned for selling. milk to the prejudice'of the purchaser at Old Trafford on . .July 22, there being in it nine per cent. of water. Mr. Brookes \Cr Acon and Craven) appeared for the eansaaution, end Mr. Arthur B:owne defended. •Mr. Brookes in hie opening statern-nt sail that Inspector Keys on July 22nd, watched for the arrival of the. defen- dant's and others' milk at Old Trafford. On its arrival he took a sample and when sent to the analyst it was discovered to contain 9 per cent. of added water. Mr Browne here asked Mr. Brookes under what Act of Parliament the proceedings were taken, and Mr. Brookes replied that it was under section 3 of the 1879 Act.— Inspector, Keys then gave evidence corroborating the Solicitor's opening statement, and produced the analyst's certificate.—Mr., Browne submitted to the. inaistrate that he had no case to answer inasmuch aathe evidence of the ease was not the charge on the sumrnons.—Mr. Brookes admitted that the proceedings were taken under the 1879 statute, whereas the summons was under the 1875 statute. Mr. Yates agreed with Mr. Browne, but Mr. Brookes applied that the summons should be varied, Mr. Yates asked if he knew the summons was bad, and Mr. Brookes replied that he knew four days before when the matter was put into his hands, but he did not give notice to the defendant. Mr. Browne thereupon asked for the dismissal of the summons. Mr. Brookes pressed , for the amendment of the summons, but Mr. Browne pointed out that it would be an amendment Of substance which could not be done. Mr. Yates thereupon dis- missed the case.—After a consultation between the two solicitors, it was arranged that a fresh summons should be issued against the defendant to save him coming a second time. Mr. Browne then addr,ssscd the court for the defence. ' He said that his client and his , father before him, had been on the farm for 5) years.- No complaint had ever been made , against him until then. Tne defendant would swear j that he had never put any water into the milk, nor had ' ordered any of hl3 servants to put any water in. rhe only explanation which could be made of the matter was,that the consignee had reel:tested the dairymaid to havethe cans filled with a couple of quarts of cold water over night, and possibly the milkman had • teemed the milk into the cans with the water in, Mr. Browne further painted out that the added water only gave a profit of 4ii. to the defendant.—Evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement was given by the defendant:—Michael Bligh also said that he never saw Mr. Cooke ,or anyone else put any water in tbe milk.— Ralph Steele,loreman porter, Old Trafford station, said that he had seen Mr. Cooke's tniqr coming, to OA "Traf- ford for 18 years and had never heard a single complaint about it before. One man named Schofield had had his milk from defendant for over eight years and another for over four years, and various other places for a con- siderableperiod.—Mr. Yates said that there . was no doubt that there vvas.water in the milk, tut it was not clear how far the defendant was to blame. He was however, liable far it, and altboarla he believed that defendant personally had nothing to do with the trans- action. he was obliged to fine him in the mitigated pen- alty of 203. and costs.
POISONED BY SPIRTS OF SALTS AT WARRINGTON.

A painter' named William Richardson, 47 years of age, who had been living apart from his wife at 63, Chorley-Street, Warrington, committed suicide on Satutday by drinking some spirits of salts. An in- quest was held in the Parade-room on Tuesday evening by lir. Brighouse, coroner, touching .the death of the dectad. Evidence. .of identification was given by Joseph Thomas Pichardson, son of the deceased. When he saw his father a week previ- ous to his death witness said deceased then seemed in his usual good stats of mind. Drink W,19 the cAuse of the deceased's 'separation from hi 4 wife, but since ' Christmas deceased had been temperate. Witness spoke to deceased a short time, previous to his death, and asked him whether he was not sorry for the rash act he had committed, to which the deceased replied " I am in one sense, but not in another."— Fjizabeth Worrall, 63. Chorley-st. stated that the deceased was hefnephew,and he commenced to lodge with her a few weeks before Christmas. On Saturday morning be wot up a little be- fore six o'clock. Shortly afterwards sriebeard deceased shouting " Mother, mother." Witness went downstairs, and he told her that he had poisoned himself. Tim bottle produced containing spirits of salts was by his side. He used it in his business, and kept it in a shed near the house.. She had never noticed anything strange in his conduct, and be had never said anything about taking' away his life. He had been very steady since Christmas. Inspector Bowen gave evidence as to ques- tioning the deceased before he died. Witoess aske;l him whether ,he had taken it by mistake or whether he had taken it wilfully. Decea.ed that he .had taken it wilfully as "he couldir't s'andat any longer." He said he met one of his lads in the street, and offered him a two-shilling pieee. He refuse it, saying that his mother told him tlia t. he must not speak to him, and this had preyed upon his mind. He was tired of ty!ing senarated from his family. "Ehe C.roner commented npoo the folly of potting chil:lren against their parents.—The jury returned a verdict of " Suiede whilst temporarily in-ane."
