div.head: A.R.U.
div.p: THE A.R.U.
BY HR. H. WK/TRAM.

No doubt before this letter is published most men who care to be abreast with the times will know what the above letters stand-for. The American Railroad Union stands before the world as the strongest combination of Labour as opposed to Capital is has ever seen. It may possibly happen that the trouble now making itself felt in the States will be transient, and peace be soon restored, but under any and all circumstances a very big lesson is being taught and the pupils are numerous and apt. A month ago the public press were silent on the question of State ownership of railroads. All the great possibilities SO often and so persistently put forward:by the great socialist party were so many tabooed subjects not to be dealt with by a respectable and responsible editor; to-day the rush int o these subjects is general. Not a newspaper, in California of any standing but is now demanding, day after day, that the Government ownership of all highways is the only way to solve the problem. The biggest strike the world has ever seen is now on, and who can wonder? A state of things litas grown up here, that bids fair to rival all tte worst features that obtained in England before Factory Reform was started. Ment• now see clearly that millionaires at one end of the beam means beggars dangling in thousands at the other end, and the word is going: forth to call a halt, and make a change, whoever foots the bill. My God, if only the little I haie seen and scrutinized could be fully coml prehended by those who sit at home at ease it would call forth full sanction to a state of anarchy compared to which, that depicted in "Caesar's Column "would be mere child's play. While in New York recently I devoted two days to a study of the tenement house system. Two nights I slept in a room just large enough to hold the bed, not large enough to undress in ; we had to get on the bed to do that. No windows, and no ventilation of any kind. It was like getting into an oven. The living room, or kitchen was separated from it by a latti wall. And yet, in this, a man with live' grown-up children lived, (there was no wife) and at nights kept up a lively struggle for supremacy with the bugs. Nine shillings a week was 'Aid for the stye. Think of the thonsands who stand this kind of Thing the year round, and all within a few blocks of princely mansions the owners of whilh merely make them temporary abodes. My previous sketches must have prepared readers of the " Examiner " for the terrible state of things now obtaining here. The labour world has for years been so fully charged with electricity that the flash and the report have been hourly expected. It only needed the recent action of Pullman, the great car builder, to precipitate matters. I have often talked with men who have worked in the model town of Pullman. The owner of this place is a many,naany, many times millionaire. He, like Carnegie, poses as a philanthropist. That is, he robs his workmen With his right hand, and git es to God with his left. Very many good' and kind men find this an easy way to still the small voice within them, hopintz, perhaps, that the Great,Searcher will not find every corner and nook in their beastly carcases. I coulcint possibly tell the tale of Pullman. As a model town it would ~trike the mere sight-see'er as something very good and nice,like your own Saltaire. As a mat- ter of fact, it contains within it all the evils fore- told as sure attendants on sociali-m. The Pullman Co. own the gas, the water, and all the stores. They charge for the first two what they like, and all pur- chases must be made at their stores. All the work- men of the town must work under the Co. at one job or another. The Truck system is in full swing and a large majority are in debt to the Co. Quite a number of the men are supposed to be living in • their own houseq, really, what theybare saved lain the hotpes, but the houses are owned by the C. Our individualist friends should take n trip to Pull- man to learn lessons in Individualism. They would there learn the great. truth SJcialisrs put forward, that this 'lgni of which they are so-fond, and which we do not di,ipise, can only be of value when it has a fair and honest chance. At prei cot it is one- sided.

Thirty million-dollars are suppasel to be invested in the Pullman plant. Upon this, recently,two per cent. was declared. o.3mpetent authorities say that when all the "water" is taken out of these millions eight per cent. per annum is the real truth. Air. Pullman says he cannot afford to pay the Wages he has been paying and so offers the men the slight red action of seventy per cent. Tii& ulali'S anxiety for the prosperity of the Christian charities he is connected with, and which, of course, he wishes to support, not being shared by his workmen, as a matter of course they strike. At the present time of writing, one universal strike Setlis to threaten the land ironi Paciff 3 to Atlantic. Everyone is anxiously sUggesting or urging arbitration. The Pullman Ca. decline to arbitrate, insisting that their demand shall be accepted, merely changing their seventy per cent. into one of thirty-tee and a half. The railway Co. say they have nothing to submit to arbitration. The demand of the men, they say, is Unreasonable. The A.U.U. declared, at the time of the Pullman strike, what is known here as a sympathetic strike, which took the practical shape of a boycott against all Pullman sleeping cars. The men offered to ran all trains passenger, freight, or mail, if made up without the Pullman sleepers. The railway Ca. on the other hand insisted upon putting a sleeper on all their trains even where they had not usually .done so. The position or the railwrix companies is this,they decline arbitra- tion on the grounds that the dispute is one between Pullman and his men, and should not sfLet their business, the Co. contending that the sleepers are in a number of cases their property. Of course the central idea is that the Pullman Co. have an immense income from the sleepers running all over the American Continent, and to be successful, lab- our must cut this off. Semething very much. like martial law reigns over the several :states affected. That the men are in earnest there can be no doubt. That they have the sympathy of a large majority of the people is true also. All classes of people, repre- senting all the different shades of opinion, reform and otherwise, are holding meetings and. passing resolutions in condemnation of the stand taken by the Pullman and Railway companies. It is well to keep in mind that the men employed at the car works and on the railroads are all English speakers, and the very best class of men to be had or seen where. To prove how much in earnest they were, these men with their wives and children met an , incoming" scab" train by prostrating themselves, some Hundreds in number, across the lines in front of the train. The train pulled up when close upon their bodies.

It happens in this strike, as in moat others, .there are elements which •make for discord and defeat. The engineers and conductors are not on strike. It is the firemen and switchmen incliiding other bodies and societies caring to strike for the sake of sym- pathy and principle. The engineers and conduc- tors are highly paid men. They are without donbt. the finest class of men this world has in it. F'or courage, endurance, and calm judgement their equals are not td be found. They are the aristo- crats of the line, and as F uch are known. Anyone who has travelled over the American continent a time or two will endorse what I say o£ these men, and yet, the only stand .they take in this mighty struggle is that of refu,ing to run with "scab" fire- men, or non-expert brakesmen. If these two clksse.s of men could be made to join the A.R.U. the whole of American commerce would at once be brought to I standstill. _

I write now, news has come that the militia ha S been disbanded, having refused to. fire upon the strikers: We must not loose sight ot the fact that the Pullman and railway disputes are not the only ones going on. These, indeed, represent a law abid- ing, and as I have said, an EngUsti speaking class of people, hut away in Illinois and Pennsylvania there are to be found a great army of. workers made of lfuns, Poles, Belgians, and Italians who know noword of the language. Worse than this, they have no respect for law and order. At Spring Valley and Spokune they have just looted the towns, destroy- thousands of pounds worth of property, empt.v- in2 the salo ins of beer,they have held high carniv.al in the streets. No thrill of sorrow runs through my • Veins as I read these reports. Under the conditions of life now obtaining in Sicily the brothers of these men rebel end are shot down like (1,.;s wit hout.one word of protest from Christian Europe. This some class of men are scooped teL, ther from the most degrade . and least civilized yet most church-riibkn parts of Europe andbrought here to compete with it ' higher and better class amen. Fine promises are made to nem ,by agents accredited by the c-mal and iron barons. This land is- painted as one overflow- ing with milk and honey. They COMO, and find things different, Oh so different. In. the mint....s of Pennsylvania they find they are in very fact nei her more nor less than slaves, with no other comfort or solace in life but the beer keg. Condemned to work work, work, and yet in most cases never see the colour of money. It must be further understood that these coal districts in nearly all cases are own2l by the; railivay

syndicate, and combine are producing their natural fruits—anarchy individualism run mad is hurrying competition to its doom. As I am so unsettled and kn-iw not what a day i :t S may bring forth, 1 wish my letters, papers &c., addressed : care of Miss A'ntharn, letizie, an Rafael, Marine Company, Caliioraia,

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WA ItitINGTON.

It has been a stock argument by the supporters of the contracting out clause which the house of Lords insisted upui inserting into the Employers Liability Bill of last session, that the raiiway men were almost .unanimously in favour of it. They quite overlooked the fact that the congress of rail- way servants had declared against P.:. A meeting of railway men wa, held in the Co-operative Hail on Bunchy list week, it large proportion or whom were employes of the London and North Western railway, who are supposed to be specially interested in the contracting out clause. Notwithstanding this fact, there was not a single hand raised against against a resolutioncondemning the Rouse of Lords for inserting the clause. The resolution wns passed with complete,unanimity. Mr. Edward liar- ford, the -general secretory of the kna!gornated Society, of Railway Servants, in a Labour au 1 Radi- cal candidate for Northampton.

The simplrters of the Clergy Daughters' institu- tion at Warrington reqiiire a little "shaking for at the annual meeting of the Committee last week, only ten *. were 'present. Of course the downpour of rain which occurred that day may have had some effect, but, still that was a very pal- try number to attend such a meeting. One of those present was rather severe on the bishops for not put- ting in an appearance. Ile said that it appeared aa if they made a point of being absent on thoe occa- sions. Perhaps after that hint, they will attend to their duties a little better. The finances do not appear to be in a very finirishing condition. True the recent. Navas have given a balance to tbe good, but'unless a Special effart is made eleh fifth year, there will be a deficit. The chief offender of the three dioceses i Manchester, which receives more than twice as much as it contributes. The clergy of that diocese should bestir thetustlves and wipe' out the reproach from which the sUff,•r. It was stated at the meeting last week that ,if £1 per annum were received from each church in the dio- cese, it would he sufficient to cover the. expensea.of the schools. . This is a very small sum for such a rich church as the Established Church .aud there ought to be no difficulty in raising it.

. The Speech day" at the Grammar sc!tool last week passed off very successfully. The heel master, the Rev. l. J. Wilcocks had a most sati.-factory report to give of the school during the past year. Not only had a large number of the poplis gained honours at the school, but ex-pupils who had,gone to the Universities at. Manchester,Oxford, ard Cam- bridge, had also ,Made headway in their new sphere of life. Special aim-ion was made to R. ' "UNDER AND OVER." At the Borough Court on Ttwsday, James Bartin, described as a rogue and vag,ib ,nd, was charged with playing a game of chance called " under and over" on ttft Football Ground, Wildersp)ol-road on Monday. D.S. Monaghan gave evidence to seeing the defendant plty- ing the above named gime at the sports on Monday. On being told that Monaghan was watching hini,the defend- ant tried to get away but was arrestel by the officer. Monaghan questioned the defendant who said that he came from Wigan. The ma.,ristrates inflicted a penalty of 203. and costs (£1 43. 61. in all) or one month's imprisonment. The defendant also forfeited his paraphernalia.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the chair), Councillor B. Roberto and Mr. S. Wright. _ .

DAMAGING WHEAT.—Four lads named John Hardman (11), ; George Bate (9). Hardy-st. ;William Hill Hardy-st.; and Joseph R:chardson (8), Hardy- street, were summoned for having on the 29til July, at Warrington' destroyed a growing crop ot wheat, the property of Stephen Dean, the Poplars, Orford, doing damage to the extent of ss. Defendants all pleaded guilty. P.C. Loxham said that on Sunday at about four o'cloek he was going through some fieldi from Man- chester-lane to Padgate-lane when he saw the four de- fendants in a field of wheat. They were plucking wheat as fast as they could. Witness ran alter them and Ztaught Hardman who gave the names and addresses of the others. The lads dropped the wheat as they ran. The fence was pulled down in three or four places and a Considerable amouut of damage dooe.—Mr. Dean, The Poplars, Orford, said he had suffered great damacve through boyspulling the wheat. He wanted to put-a spot to it. Mr. Hunt said the police had nit power to summon people for trespass, or there would be more Cases up. When they caught anyone at it they sent their names and addresses to the owner,who summoned them if they wished.—The Cl.airmln said it was a criminal offence to steal wheat and was just as bad as going into a shop and stealing a loaf. If a fine was im- posed the parents would have to bear the punishment instead of ale boys. They were cautioned as to their future conduct and dismissed on payment of costs,3s.6d. tticspay, —Before Mr. F.. Monks (chairman). Alderman Francomb and Mr. T. Bwhall. A DESERTER Fnom riaE NAVY.—William Fletcher, a youth, was charged with being, a deserter from Her Maj,sty's ship Ganges, stationed at Falmouth, since the 12th January last. Prisoner pleaded guilty. An officer from Orford Barracks stated that or. Wednesday morn- ing the prisoner came to the barracks asking to be enlisted. lie was taken to the guard-room, and after his clothing had been examined, he admitted being a deserter. The magistrates handed the pris.me.s.r over to an officer of the Naval police who was present in

Court. • THEFT OF A Pam OF TRorszas.—Florence Henderson pleaded guilty to stealing from the house, 573, '<nuts- ford-road, on the 9th June, a pair of men's trousers, value 55., the property of James Williams. The Chief Constable informed the bench that the prisoner was fined 20s. the previous week for stealing some articles of clothing from the same house. Since then a pair of trousers and other articles were missed, and Mrs. Williams gave information to D.S. Monaghan. On Sat- urday evening D.S. Monaghan met the prisoner and on being charged with the effence she replied " I did take them, and told Mrs. Williams that I would take them out." The Chairman asked whether the theft had taken place since the previous Monday. The Clerk stated that it occurred en the 9th of June, but it had been discov- ered since the last prosecution against the prisoner. The magistrates recorded a conviction against the prisoner, the Chairman remarking that they were inclined to think that there was a little persecution in the matter, and they would therefore discharge her. ASSAULTING His WlFE.—Thomas Hughes was charged With being drunk and disorderly in Williamson Ceurt, at eleven o'clock the previous night,and further charged with assaulting Sarah Hughes at the same time and place. P.C. Corbett stated that from complaints received at the Police Station he was instructed to go to Williamson Court. He thare saw the prisoner's wife who told him that her husband had been beating her. The prisoner was very drunk and he knocked the woman down in witness's presence. Mrs. Hughes said she did not wish to give any evidence against her husband. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for one month's hard labour. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor H. Roberts in the chair, and Dr. T. Starkey-Smith. Dricaat AND DISORDERLY.—The following were fined for this offence :—Louisa Green, in Church-st. on Sun- day fined 54. and costs; Thomas Taylor, in Orford-st. on the 20th July, ss. and costs; Sarah Jarvis, in Silver-st. on 31st July, was dismissed on promising to abstain; Hate Hinds. in Hill-st. on the 31st July, ss. and costs. USING OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—WIIIiaM BottoMley, Kat 3 Bottomley and Mary Ann Whittaker were charged with making use of obscene language in the Market-place on the 28th July last. The two Battomleys pleaded not guilty, and Mrs. Whittaker guilty but under great pro- vocation. P.C. Clough said that at quarter past eleven on the night in question he was in the Market-place when he saw the defendants quarrelline and using most filthy language. P.C. Berry and a Mr. Topham both corroborated. The three defendants were each fined ss. and costs.—Elizabeth Dutton and Jane Johnson for com- mitting the same offence in Silver-st., were fined ss. and Costs in each ease. P.C. Bell proved the case.—For using obscene language in the Old-road on the 29th of last month, Catherine Saltnon and Catherine Carey were, on the evidence of P.C. Turner, fined ss. and costs or Seven days. CTITIHNEY ON FlRE.—Bridget Higgins was charged with Committing this offence on the Ist of August, but on proving that it was accidental she was dismissed. FIGHTING.—Peter Carroboy was charged with commit- ting a breach of the peace by fighting another man on Pinner's Brow on the 31st July last. P.C. Lexham said that on the date named he saw the defendant fighting with another man on Pinner's Brow. He separated them, but after he had gone away they commenced again. The defendant was hound over to keep the peace in a surety of £5 besides his own or in default,one months' imprisownent. ANOTHER &vans DOG.—A youth named Herbert Stanley was charged with having on "the 28:h July, allowed an unmuzzled dog to run about the streets. P.C. Taylor stated that he had roeeived information that a man named Donnellan had been bitten by the dog,which is a rough-haired terrier. Cn making inquiries lie Learned that three little children had been bitten by the same dog, and these children also gave evidence An order was made by the magistrates for the animal's des- truction.

Mr. J. H. Fleming.

IN ARREARS.—WiIIiam Flannigan was brought up on a warrant for the non-payment of arrears. The case !ic as adjourned for a fortnight on the defendant promis- ing to find the money. TUURSDAY.—Before Mr. S. Chandley (chairman) Alder- man Sutton, and Councillor James Fairclough. A HUSBAND IN TROUBLE.— Edward Livesay, 2, Buck- ley's yard, Old-road was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Prince-street at 11 a.m. on Wednesday. P.C.'s. Turner and Wheatley proved the case. The defendant's wife gave evidence as to the defendant using threats to her, stating that she was afraid to live with him. The magistrates committed him to prison for one month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly, and ordered him to be bound over in two sureties of £5 each to keep the peace towards his wife, or in default a further term of imprisonment for two months. &Hoot. CASES.—Mr. G. Riley prosecuted in the fol- lowing cases of irregular attendance at school: Alexan- dra Algie, forgeman, 25 Hoyle-street, 53. ; John Crad- dock, railway man, 172, Battersby-lane, 5.3.; William Dagnall, tanner, 16, Warburton-street, 55.; Richard Tranter, forgeman, 2, Warburton-street ; John Fidffler, spelter works, 118, Pierpoint-street, boy ordered to re- ceive twelve strokes with the birchrod.

RUNCORN PETIY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Philip Speakman C.C., Thomas Handley, and F. J. Norman. TEMPORARY Areraorum—The following licenses were temporarily transferred :—From Samuel May to Joseph Hall, the Mariners Hotel, Percival-lane; from John James Linton to William Faulkner, the Navigation Inn, Canal-street; from William Faulkner to Samuel Hough- ton, the Wheatsheaf Inn. INDECENT BEHAVIOUR.—Mary Murphy, an old offender was charged with being guilty of indecent behaviour on Waterloo Bridge on the night of the 4th inst., and Robert Parr, seaman, with aiding and abetting Murphy, in the offence,who had been several times previously convicted of similar offences, was sentenced to three months imprisonment, whilst Parr was fined ss. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A YOUNG MAN.—Henry Hayes of 36, Princes'-st., Runcorn, was charged with having committed an assault upon Sarah Marsh, aged 30 years, a single woman. of 7, Cross-st., on the 6th inst.—The prosecutrix, who is supposed to possess a weak and de- tective intellect, stated that whilst her parents were away on Bank Holiday afternoon, at about 3.30, the prisoner came into the house and asked her if her parents had gone to Manchester. She replied that she thought they had not, and added that she expected her brother back soon. Prisoner then sat down on a chair and after more conversation touched hr on the shoulder. She felt annoyed and went to the kitchen door and even- tually into the yard. Afterwards she re-entered the house, passed through the kitchen into the parlour. The prisoner followed and caught hold of her. She resisted him and a struggle ensued in the course of which a table and chair were knocked over. At this juncture Mrs. Emily Morrison, a neighbour, having heard the screams of the prosecutrix, entered the house as the prisoner was in the act of committing the offence complained of. She spoke to him and he went away. In answer to the magistrates she said that the prisoner appeared to be under the influence of drink. She had not asked the prisoner to come to the house and remain with her.— Mrs. Morrison and Mrs. Dutton, having given evidence in support of the charge, Sergeant Gill proved appre- hending the prisoner at his own heuse. When charged with the offence he replied "I am not guilty of assault." The prisoner was finally committed to the next Knuts- ford Quarter Sessions, he being admitted to bail in his own recognizances of £4O, and two sureties of £2O each.

div.head: ST. HELENS LIBEL CASE. SWIFT v. ST. HELENS BILLPOSTING COMPANY,
div.p: A ST. HELENS LIBEL CASE. SWIFT v. ST. HELENS BILLPOSTING COMPANY,
LIMITED.

This was an action at Liverpool Assivs on Monday, by Lionel Swift, b,ker and flour dealer, of St. Helens, to recover damages for libel. Mr. Pickford, Q.C., and Mr. T. Swift were for the plaintiff and Mr. Bigham, Q.C., and Mr. M'Conkey and Mr. Lorraine for the defendant. It was stated that in May last a dispute in the baking trade arose and the plaintiff refused to be dictated to by the Union established in St. Helens. Placards were issued presumably by the Union, and the defendants posted them. The placard invited people to support Union shops, of which a list was given, and in red ink there were set out two names—Lionel Swift and Ernest Swift—as persons who employed non-union men. Then followed a statement that a deputation had waited upon the plaintiff, " who refused to meet them, and left his son to treat them with the utmost contempt."—Upon the suggestion of his Lordship a settlement was arrived at, defendants paying 403. and plaintiff's costs.—Mr. Bingham explained that as soon as the defendants' atten- tion was called to the character of the bills they covered them up with white paper. There was a second action by Ernest Swift, and in that case it was agreed to pay a similar sum.

div.head: ACTION TO RECOVER TITHES AT ST. HELENS, IMPORTANT JUDGMENT.
div.p: ACTION TO RECOVER TITHES AT ST. HELENS, IMPORTANT JUDGMENT.

His Honour Judge Shand, at St. Helens County Curt, on Wednesday, delivered judgment in the action for the recovery of tithe rent on sixteen acres of land in the business quarters of St. Helens, the buildings upon which include the present County Court. The claimants were the provost and scholars of King's College, Cambridge, and Mr. Reed, agent for the Rev. H. Mitchell, rural dean of Prescot ; and the defend- ants were the trustees for the Society of Friends. The tithe rent was claimed from the defendants as owners of the land, but the defendants contended they were not liable, inasmuch as Ulu had granted the land on leases for terms of 999 years, and the holders under such leases were to all intents and purposes the owners of the land. —His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiffs.—Mr. Smith applied for costs on the higher scale, and his Honour granted the application.—Mr. Chorlton said he would not oppose the application, as his clients were going to appeal to a higher court.

div.head: "UNCLE."
div.p: "UNCLE."

Pawnbrokers do not send more than they can help to auctions, for such sales are proverbially unsatisfactory; and they stand to lose on the transaction. They gen- erally enter into an agreement with some dealer to take all their goods at so much per cent, more than they have advanced ; and it may be taken for granted that pawn- brokers seldom advance more than a quarter or a third of the real value of the articles left with them. A large number of the labouring classes are, says " Cassell's Family Magazine," in the habit of patronising the pawn shops every week. The wife, for example, pawns her husband's Sunday coat for five shillings. On the follow- ing Saturday she redeems the property. The pawnbroker receives his five shillings back, plus three half-pence interest; having already received a half-penny for the ticket, which costs him practically nothing. The weekly pawners are not so much drunken, dissolute people, as respectable but thriftless folk. All the wages are spent by them as soon as received. The wife remembers that she must buy something else, and so the coat is "pop- ped "up the spout. An amusing story is told of a nor- thern country town where strikes had caused much depression. The pawnbroker's shop was burnt out on Saturday ; and it was noticed that very few of the labouring men, who were regular attendants at Divine service, worshipped in public on the following day; while the local preacher,generally dressed in irreproach- able broad cloth, mounted his pulpit in his week-day working clothes. The inference is obvious. The stories of poor people paying in interest a hundredfeld more than the value of the goods pawned are somewhat exag- gerated. Let us imagine that A pawns her husband's coat fifty-two times in the course of the year at five shillings a time. She will pay for the use of the bor- rowed money during the twelve months six shillings and sixpence, and two shillings and twopence for the pawn tickets—eight shillings and eightpence in all ;or not half the value of the coat. The pawnbroker, on the other hand, has to have five shillings ready every week, to purchase printed pawn-tickets, Stn., to pay rent and wages to assistants to keep accounts, and to preserve the articles pawned in good condition. If small leans stash as these were all lsis revenue, the pawnbroker could not become a very rich man, unless he had an enormous business. But "uncle's "resources are not so easily exhausted. I have already pointed out that pawners seldom take the surplus on the sales of their pledges. Pawnbrokers also en joy ordinary traders' profits on the goods they sell to the public, and this 1 brings me to the" weekly payment system." Suppos- ing that I want to buy a chain hanging beneath the "gilded pills." It is marked £2. I have not that money at my disposal, but pay the pawnbroker a five shillings' deposit. I get a receipt, and on the form is printed : " Payments must be made weckly, or the deposits for- feited at the expiration of four we(ks." I pay a second sum of five shillings in the following week, but then am unable to raise any more money. The pawnbroker eventually pockets the ten shillings which I have already paid him, and I have not the slightest claim on the chain that took my fancy.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAAHNT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAAHNT.
MONDAY.

En the House of Commods on Monday, Mr. J.MORLEY, questioned as to whether any further proceedings were to be taken againcit the militia officers implicated in the Birr case, said the Crown Solicitor had been instructed to send up a bill at the next quarter sessions against the four officers as to whom the magistrates were evenly divided at the late investigation.

In reply to a question as to a possible interruption of the movements of neutral vessels owing to the war between China and Japan, Sir E.GREY said the Japanese Government had promised that no warlike operations would be undertaken against Shanghai and its ap- proaches, and upon that condition the Chinese Govern- ment would not obstruct the apprcaehes to Shanghai. The contending Powers would have, speaking generally, no right to interfere with neutral vessels, except in the event of an effective blockade with due notification, or in a case of contrat•iand of war. It would be a danger- sus and unusual course for the Government to undertake to define by a general statement what was and what was not contraband of war. Coal had been held not to be contraband of war as a general rule, but it was possible that it might, in certain cases, become so. The House afterwards proceeded to consider the Evicted Tenants Bill as amended in Committee. In ac- cordance with an undertaking he eave on Thursday last, Mr. MORLEY moved a clause providing that in case a petition was presented to the arbitrators jointly by the landlord and the evicted tenant, or in the case of a new tenants by the new tenant, stating that a voluntary agreement between the parties for the reinstatement of the evicted tenant had been enterod into,thearbritrators might make an order for carrying the agreement into effect. The clause was adopted. Mr. MORLEY also moved a clause providing that in cases in which new tenants objected to the reinstatement of evicted tenants the land Commission might acquire land for the purpose of providing other holdings, and sell that land to evicted tenants on such conditions as they thought expedient. This clause was also agreed to. An amendment, pro- posed by Mr. MORLEY, giving the arbitrators power to award a reasonable sum to a tenant who objected to an order for reinstatement was passed.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, in reply to Mr. WEIR, repeated his statement that if the Crofters Act Amendment Bill could be taken as an unopposed bill the Government would be glad to pass it. In answer to Mr. WOODS, the CHANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER said he hoped to be able to introduce a bill next session dealing with the payment of members. The third reading of the Evicted Tenants Bill, having been formally moved by Mr. MonLEv,the rejection of the bill was moved by Mr. BRODRICH, who said the Opposi- tion denied that the bill was equitable, doubted whether it was safe, and knew that every Irish member in the House believed it would not be effectual. Mr. W.O'l3lllE-EN urged that not a single Irish landlord had said a word ot concession -in the debate. All they had said had provel that they were just as vindictive and irreconcilable as i ever. All the giving had been on the side of the Irish party. They were willing to make any reasonable sacri- fice in order to create genuine peace in Ireland, so that legal changes might be carried out in a constitutional way, and even at that moment they would not stick at trifles if there was any desire on the part of the• Oppos- ition to make a genuine response to Mr. COURTNEY'S memorable speech. Up to that moment, however, they had had nothing but declarations of hostility and insult and the landlords appeared to be anxious to press the country into a state of disturbance which should be a discredit to the administration of the CHIEF SECRETARY, If the bill was thrown out a national emergency would be created in Ireland in which every man who had Irish blood in his veins would think of nothing but how to pay back the past. Mr. 'l'. W. RUSSELL thought the speeches of Mr. BRODRICK and Mr. O'ButEar had removed all hope of compromise. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the bill had been brought in to deal with a social administrative difficulty. On the second reading it was quite evident what line the Op- position would take. The Government might have had a voluntary arrangement in the nature of the 13th clause of the Act of 1891,ansl this would have met nine-tenthe of the cases of the tenants. The Government, however, instead of agreeing to a voluntary arrangement, the moment they found that was the only thing the Opposi- tion would agree to, closured all debate, and as a result it had been absolutely itnpossibin to discuss an atnicible settlement,. The responsibility for the present state of things therefore rested in the first place with the Govern- ment, and in the second place with the Irish members who refused to make any sign of inclination to agree to a settlement. After a suggestion that the debate should be adjourned, made by Mr. DILLoN, in consequence of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S speech, Mr. DILLON went on to say that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had stated that the future of Ire- land depended on its people learning that they were not to look to attaining their ends by violence and crime. That was a sentiment. he himself had frequently ex- pressed. By the admission of all parties the Irish people had for the past two or three years been quiet beyond all previous periods in their history, and if the future depended on teaching the people they would receive justice and consideration when they were quiet and patient,now was the time and now was the opportunity. Mr. MORLEY, in closing the debate, said he thought the rejection of the bill would do something to make the maintenance of the present tranquillity in Ireland tri ore diffftlt. He did not fear the responsibility of facing whatever might hapnen, but he entreated that House and all those •in " another place" not to make the wretched Irish peasants the pawns in their party game. The House then divided. There voted for the bill 199 and against it 167, giving the Government a majority of 32.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The Committee stage of the Equalisation of Rates (London) Bill was concluded in the House of Commons OH Wednesday, and the bill, ad amended, was ordered to be reported to the House. The consideration of the Building Societies (No. 2) Bill was then resumed, and the bill was read a third time. The Scotch Local Gov- ernment Bill was considered on report, and when pro- gress was reported at half-past five four pages or amend- ments out of nineteen had been disposed of. Mr. W. H. HoLLArirPintroduced a bill providing for a second ballet in cases where no candidate had received a maj)rity of the recorded votes, and for the payment of returning officers' expenses out of the rates. The bill was read a first time, and the House then rose.

McConQuonAnn CHALLENGE Cup.—The final far this cup (played for between the various offices of McCorquodale and Company Limited) was decided on Monday at Newton on the Newton Cricket Club ground kindly lent by the ccmmittee for the occasion. In the first round for this cup, the Cardington-st. club proved victorious over the team at Messrs. McCorquorlale's other London rffice (the Armoury), on June 161). Consequently they journeyed to Newton to play in the final. The match between Leeds and Newton at Leeds on June 2nd was abandoned owing to rain. Leeds therefore visited Newton and played the match on Mon- day morning. The winners playing the team from London in the afternoon. Newton won both matches and thus hold the Cup for the 2nd year in succession. After the matches the teams adjourned to the Pied Bull Hotel where an excellent dinner was provided. After the cloth had been removed, the chairman (Mr. W. H. Bindley) proposed the health of the donor of the Cup, Mr. G. F. McCorquociale, which was drunk with musical honours. div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

SPEAKS FOR ITSELF—Phonograpl/4 • OSTRICHES feather their owner's nestt TEACHER: "Johnny, what is memory ?" Johnny t " The thing you forget with." "JUDGE not a man by clothes he wears !" Poor phrase. Judge rather by the clothes for which he pays.

IF some men were to lose their fortunes in the same way they gained them, they would insist on somebody going to gaol. 31AC BOOZER: "You know, according to Bacon, reading makes a full man." MacFoozer : " Well, you must be often at it, then."

IIOLMER: "What qualifications has he for a diplomatic position ?" Jefferys : " Well, he has been for years a successful portrait painter." "PLEASE, ma'am," said the boy, "can't you help me." " You ? Why, you're not old enough to be married." " No; but me father is. It's his wife and three children I has to support." FRIEND: "Your sou played football at college, I am told." Fond Mamma: "Yes." Friend : "Quarter-back ?" Fond Mamma : "Oh, he's nearly all back ! He lost only au eAr and a hand."

LUCKY MAN !—Blink?: "Lucky man, that fellow Jones." Winks: "I don't see how you make it." Blinks : "Why, he took out a life insurance policy f,,r a thousand pounds and died six days before the company failed." " WHAT," exclaimed the accomplished and fashionable Fitzwiggle to the exquisitely lovely Miss de la Sparrowgrass, "what would you be, dearest, if I should press the stamp of my love upon those sealing-wax lips?" "I,' reponded the creature, "should be—stationery."

WHAT HE WAS GOING To WORK AT.—" My dear boy," said a lady to a precocious youth of sixteen, "does your father design you to tread the intricate and thorny paths of a profession, the straight and narrow ways of the ministry, or revel in the flowery fields of literature ?" "No, znarm ; dad says he's a-going to set me to work in the 'tater-field."

A BROAD HlNT.—Mistress : Now, "Bridget, about that letter to your sweetheart—what do you wish me to write ?" Bridget : " Och, shure, ma'am, an' iv yer leddyship would just wroite that iv it's more wages the misthress will be givin' me, it's Patrick an' messel', shure, will be married when its the nixt year !" AN APT ILLUSTRATION. —Teacher—" Will some one explain what is meant by disappointment?" Small Boy—" I kin, ma'm." Teacher—" Well, Tommy?" S rail Boy—" It's when the fish wriggles off the hook when yer sure you've got him."

A GOOD PLEA. —A pathetic plea for a holiday was put forward recently by the Baboos emp!oyed in the Government Geological Department, at Cal- cutta. They asked the supreme authorities to eose the office because "they were suffering from perspiration and a want of enthusiasm for their work."

INGENIOUS SCAVENGERS. —When one of the late Emperor Alexander s visits to Warsaw was announced, there was no time to clear the street of a quantity of mud which had been scraped lip in heaps by the roadside. The police (Russians) ordered the windows on the ground floor of the houses in these streets to be opened, and threw the mud into the rooms !

AN UNFORTUNATE QUOTATION.—Avoid quota- tions unless you have well studied their import and feel their pertinence. Mr. Brownlow, a short time ago, whi'e looking at the skeleton of tin ass which had been dug out of a sand-pit, and admiring and wondering at the structure of that despised animal, made a very ?naladroit use of one. " Alt" said he, with the deepest humility "we " are fear- fully and wonderfully made A BOY'S ESSAY ON " PINS."—A schoolboy having to write an essay upon the subject of " Pins," pro• duced the following : "Pins are very useful. They Lave saved the lives of a great many men, women, and children—in fact, whole families." " How so e" asked the puzzled teacher. " Why, by not swallowing them," replied the boy. This was equalled by the boy who defined salt as "the stuff that makes potatoes taste bad when you don't put on any."

THE KING AND THE PLUMBER. —When Hatfield shot at King George 111. at Drury Lane Theatre nearly a hundred years ago, Mr. Holroyd, the king's who sat next him, caught his arm, and thus probably saved the king's life. Soon after, while he was inspecting some repairs at Windsor Castle, he was deservingly _commended by the king himself for his promptitude z,nd cool- ness on the occasion. "But don't think, Holroyd," said he, in a jocular way, "that I imagine you were actuated by more than your usual loyalty— you were only determined that no one should serve the king with lead but yourself."

SETTLING THE SERGEANT. —SOMe recruits were being drilled at Al iershot by a very impatient cavalry drill-serg :ant. After about an hour of hard drilling at the sword exercise, the sergeant gave the or.!er, "Stand at ease " No sooner were the men standing at ease than the sergeant com- menced to complain of their altitudes, and wound up by saying, "Why, you f, llows are like a lot of dummies; I can get smarter soldiers than you at a sliNing per box.'' After about a minute's hesita- tion, one of the recruits remarked, "I suppose there would be some serge.ints amongst them."

A DEVOTED FAMILY. -" Yes," said the principal of the young ladies' seminary to the proud parent, "you ought to be very happy, my dear sir, to be the father of so large a family, all the members of which appear to be so devoted to one another." "Large family? Devoted ?" gasped the old gentle- men in amazement. " NVliat on earth do you mean, ma'am ?" " Why, yes, indeed," said the principal, beaming through her glas,es. "No less than eleven of Kate's brothers have been here this winter to take her to the theatre, and she tells me she expects the tall one with the blue eyes again to- morrow."

WHAT HE WANTED. —A confirm9d old bachelor, of roost exemplary habits, living in his own house, recently advertised for a servant girl. He received many letters, and finally selecting one which seemed to him about right, he invited the writer to call, and a very substanti 11 woman of 40 responded. "You see, I want a careful woman in my house," he explained. "I understand," she replied. "She must cook, wash, and iron, clean up the house, attend to my clothes, sew on buttons, do repairing, do the marketing, attend the door, pay the bills as they come in, and kindle my fire in the morning." "Oh," she said, as she rose to depart, "you do not want a servant girl; what you want is a wife. Good morning I" and she very pleasantly walked out. A Row IN THE HousE.—A foreign gentleman at a musical evening a few weeks since expressed a great wish to hear " Home, sweet home," which he had been told was a striking example o! musical pathos and expression. A well-known professor of music having been asked to play it, sat down to the piano and dashed into Thalberg's variations to the air, to which the foreign gentleman listened with deep attention, becoming, howexer, a little bewildered at the complicated passage to the fina;e. At the conclusion he rose, and gravely shook hands with the professor, saying, "I thank you, sare. I think me understand now your Home, sweet home '—nice and quiet to begin with, but at the end, oh, what a row in the house ! "

ODD DEVICES. ----In order to soften the heart of an offended lover an Austrian maiden has had her- scif photographed in a coffin, dressed in grave. clothes. So far from the device being successful it has driven her young man out of his mind; and, indeed, it strikes one that she might have rendered herself more attractive. This is not, however, always the object of a photograph. There is a story of a young gentleman who dis- torted his features so horribly while his portrait was being taken that he frightened the operator. "You are not a criminal," he remonstrated, "compelled to be photographed by the police, and anxious to avoid identification, are you?" "No," said the other, "but I want to get off my engage- ment with Mary Ann. I've told her I am still hers if she wishes it, but I've had a railway acci- dent which has rather blemished me." "Very good; when she gets this you will be a free man,' said the photographer.

Lord Londonderry opened a Conservative working- men's club at Sunderland on Monday. He said that per- sonalty was able to evade the Budget, but land was not. The Budget could, however, be evaded by buying land in America, and the colonies, in the names of trustees, and by insuring in foreign offices. Lord Londonderry is a member of the party that claims a monopoly of patriotism.

div.head: WARRINGTON CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCELOOL.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCELOOL.
ANNIVERSARY MEETING.

On Thursday last week the anniversary meeting of the Warrington Institution for the Clergy Widows and Orphans.and Clergy Daughters' School was held at the school. The usual business meet- ing was held at the Training College when the chair was occupied by the Dean of Manchester (Dr. McClure), and there were also present—Archdeacon Woosnam, Canon Postance, the Rev. F. W. Willis (recto' of Warrington), the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, the Rev. David Morgan (Oldham), Mr. Henry Greenall (treasurer), Mr. James Tinsley, J.P., and Mr. W. P. FuHagar. Apologies for non-attendance were read from the Bishops of the dioceses, Dean of Chester, Archdeacon Anson,Mr. Fox, and Bishop Cremer Roberts.

div.head: WIDOWS AND ORPHANS FUND.
div.p: WIDOWS AND ORPHANS FUND.

The Rev. Canon PENRHYN (hon. secretary of the clergy widows' and orphans' pension fund) presented the fol- lowing report :—" As usual in presenting their annual report, your committee have to deplore the loss of some of their colleagues. Last September, Canon Hopwood, rector of Bury, who had shown the greatest interest in our institution, and proved himself a most useful mem- berof the committee,was called away in the prime of life, and we have now with sorrow to record the death of 'another member of that family to which these institu- tions owe so much. Sir Gilbert Greenall, who was formerly an active member of our committee,and though of late through age and increasing infirmities unable to attend, continued to the last to take a warm interest in the charity. Canon Robin has also tendered his resigna- tion. Your committee would suggest that the vacancies thus caused should be filled by the Rev. Foster Black- burne and Mr. J. Charlton Parr, and that of the late Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne by his son, and Canon Maitland Wood in place of Canon Robin. No fresh nominations having been sent in to the secretary; the retiring members have been selected, subject to the confirmation of this annual meeting :—Chester, Canon Heron; Manchester Archdeacon Anson; Liverpool, the Rev. J. W. Willink and the Rev. E. F. Srnethwick ; Messrs. W. Fox, John White, W. H. Hornby, M.P., Cle- ment Royds, Dr. Watkins, and Mr. Herbert Woodcock. This year there are no less than ten applications for grants from the diocese of Manchester, five widows and five orphans; from Chester one widow, two orphans; and from Liverpool, two widows. The annual meeting will be asked to sanction pensions, donations, and pay- ments for free scholarships at the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2,110, and if the recommenda- tions of your committee are approved ; there will be upon our list—from Chester 19 widows and ten orphans, Liverpool eleven widows and ten orphans, Manchester. 33 widows and 22 orphans; and free education in the Clergy Daughters' School is provided for six orphans— two from Chester, two from Liverpool, two from Man- chester. The income of the charity for the year ended December, 31st, 1893, was £2,111 15s. 10d., made up as follows—Special donations, £36 10s.; interest on capital, £719 7s. ;collections, £504 2s. 11d. ; subscriptious,£733 19s. 10d. ; unappropriated fund, Chester and Liverpod, £ll2 103. ; hank interest, £5 6s. id. ; as against in 1891, £75 135., £670 15s. 2d., £476 16s. id., £749 Os. 10d., £B2 17s. 2d., £l4 17s. 7d. These figures on the whole are a slight increase on the previous year, but it is still much to be regretted that the subscriptions continue to diminish and as old subscribers pass away new ones are not forthcoming to take their place. We have been disappointed in the hope of increased support from the diocese of Manchester, the total contributions baying
fallen from £335 to £3-01. Unless larger funds are sup-- plied it is impossible te make them the liberal grants for which they make request."
THE CHAPLAIN'S REPORT.

The report of the Chaplain and Hon. Secretary to the Clergy Daughters' School (the Rev. F. W. Willis) ~was as follows :—" During the past half year, that is from Ad- vent to Trinity, while the school has been in residence, I have taken as the subject for my Bible classes the Gos- pels for the Sunday. From Trinity up to the present we have been reading the chief events in the history of the ivanderings of the children of Israel in the Wilderness, and we shall continue this subject next term until Ad- vent. I find it a good plan thus to master the two parts of the Christian year with a portion from the New Testa- ment bearing on the life of our lArd during the first part, and a book or books of the o,d Testament during the second. It is perhaps right that I should mention that I have received strong expressions of feeling from a few of the parents as to the advisability of removing the school owing to the recent illnesses. There may be reason on this and other grounds, but it may be reassur- ing to point out that the epidemic of smallpox which visited the town last year was imported by a tramp, and was almost wholly confined to those whose habits ex- posed them to attack ; that the outbreak of measles this term was also imported by one of the pupils from herown parish, and that the outbreak of scarlatina last term, whio could not be accounted for, was confiß.d to the three or four girls who inhabited the same room, and on the dispersion of the school was not taken by anyone in the College adjoining, which seems to point to some extraneous source as the origin and not to the conditions of the place. The general tone of the scho@l is satisfac- tory. I believe that a high standard is aimed at, and that a right feeling pervades the scholars, namely, a conscientious desire to do the best, and of real happiness. TREASURER'S REPORT: A GLOOMY OUTLOOK.

Mr. ernxitNALL said they were out of debt at the pre- sent moment, but they would be in debt five years hence if the same conditions continued. At the end of the year 1892 it was found that the adverse balance which had been growing for the past few years had reached the large sum of £745 14' s. and it was felt by the committee that au attempt should be made by means of baz iars and by special appeals to taise £l,OOO, in order to place the institution in a better pc.sition. A special committee was appointed, meetings were held, and it was decided to hold separate bazaars in each eio- cese, in addition to the one at the school. This plan was carried out, realizing in the aggregate, with the aid of several handsome donations, the satisfactory sum of £1,162 is. 7d. While the ab3ve sum had been sufficient to pay off the old indebtedness,and to add a slight addi- tional amount to the vested funds of the institution, the growth of an adverse balance would•be recurrent so long as the annual collection, donations, and subscriptions continued to be less than the annual expenditure of the school.
THE EXAMINER'S REPORT.

The Rev. Franck H. M.inley, M.A., Exeter College, the examiner,had forwarded a report upon the examina- tion of the students of the school. He was much pleased with the order and discipline and all the arrangementa made for the examination. The papers were done care- fully and neatly, the handwriting and spelling being good, and the answers well expressed.

div.head: HEADMISTRESS'S REPORT.
div.p: HEADMISTRESS'S REPORT.

Miss BEAL presented herreport,Which was as follows: —" I have great pleasure in'presenting to you my report of the school during the term now Jost ended. There are 66 girls in the school—nineteen Chester,two orphans, 2 PT., cuts S.T. ; 16 Liverpool, four orphans, two P.S, ; six extrivdiocesan. one orphan. Two girls have been absent during the term, one from illness, the other because of the death of her mother. There are eight girls leaving—Mary Harris, Nellie Atherton, Earle Hasle- wood, Edith Philiipa, D,..tra, Thomas, Eveleen Wigg- Gilbert. Fl ‘relice Diserden, and Mary Baron. There are ,no applications for admission. Cissy Cottingham will take Mary Harris's place as student teacher. The health of the girls has been good with the exception of an out- break of measles. The conduct of the school generally has been good, including the girls h Ading the various exhibitions. As Florence Duerden is leaving, one of the school exhib:tions is vacant, and a second of the first year exhibitions is also v leant-, as Eveleen Gilbert is leaving. The Rev. J. H. Manley is recom- mending two girls for the last two vacancies. In May, 16 girl t entiated for the South Kensington drawing examination, six freehand, ten model. THE EXAMINER, SAI URDAY AUGUST 11, 1894.
ALLEGED ILLEGAL DISTRAINT.
IMPORTANT CASE AT THE COUNTY COURT.

) At the Warrington County Court last week; before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, Robert i Lowe, auctioneer, sued Alfred Pemberton, Winwick street, for £25 damages, for illegal distraint upon some furniture which plaintiff had purchased from Win. Hargreaves, 16 Oliver-street,Warrington. Mr. Herbert Woods, solicitor, who represented Mr. Lowe, in his opening statement said that on July sth, the plain- tiff purchased the goods in question from Mr. Hargreaves who was a tenant of the defendant. On the same day, Mr. Lowe went to see the defendant to ask him what rent was due, but did not succeed in finding him. On Saturday following, he saw defendant's wife, and she handed him an account of £2 es. 2d. He examined the account, and found that she had included the current week's rent, and another week in lieu of notice,which he declined to pay,and made the legal tender of £1 118.10 d. —His Honour : That is no legal tender. It must be to the defendant himself.—Mr. Llwe then proceeded to say that he called in his man Jackson, to witness the tender of the money, and Mrs. Pemberton after some hesitation received £1 us. 10d., and signed the receipt produced with the words" rent up to date." Witness had adver- tised the sale for Saturday afternoon July 7th, and he went to conduct the sale, when he found a great commo- tion at the house, there being ,a large number of women present. He saw the defendant who asked him for 14s. 4d. belonging to him for rent due, and further told him, be would not allow the sale to go on until it was paid. Mr. Lowe asked him for his distraint warrant, but he replied that he did not getone. He asked him fur- ther for his certificate under the Distraint Amendment Act, but the defendant replied that he had not got one. The plaintiff thereupon told his man to take out the goods to sell outside, and when Jackson was removing the first article—a table—the defendant tried to prevent him by taking hold of it. The plaintiff sent for a police- man, but before a policeman arrived, he proceeded with the sale which was a very poor one and the articles sold very cheaply.—Asked by his solicitor the cause of it, witness replied that it was the conduct of the defendant. The people were afraid to bid for the furniture because they thought it would be taken from them. He would have realised £lO or £l2 if the sale had not been inter- fered with by the defendant. The balance of the £25 , was that claimed as recompense for damage to his repu- tation as an auctioneer.—His Honour remaiked that that could not be claimed under the present action.—Cross- examined by Mr. Arthur Browne, the solicitor for *the defendant: Witness admitted that he only gave £5 103. for the goods and that they realised £8 165., printing and posting of placards cost 10s., and that he had de- bited commission of 19s. 91 for conducting the sale.— His Honour said that that could not possibly be, inas- much as plaintiff had bought the goods at his own risk to sell again.—The plaintiff further admitted making a 50 per cent, profit, and that the sale was only advertised the day before, on a small bill: It was not true that the sale was only delayed four or five minutes. Ho did not know that a number of people living in 011iver-st. worked in Dallam and Bewsey furges,and that the forges only worked two or three days per week, and had been so for the past five or six months. The best article sold was a dresser which realised two guineas. In

his opinion he ought to have realised tS 10s. He had heard some of the goods were on the hire system. He had issued a pamphlet giving a report of a case in which he had succeeded as defendant at the County Court a few months ago, in which goods were claimed under the hire purchase system from him. The reason he had issued the pamphlet was for the pm- pose of advertising liiinseff.—Mr. Browne asked if it wis not with the intention of indirectly telling the public that when they had got goods on the hire system, he you'd purchase them so long as they not tell him they were obtained on that sygtem,—Mr. Woods obj,Tted to the question but, his Honour allowed it as a matter of credibility—Mr. Lowe replied "Certainly n',t "—Again pressed by Mr. Browne as to his obj,ct in having the case printed, he said that it was only to advertise him- self.—Evidence was given to corroborate the statement that the sale was afff cted ty the conduct of the defendant. It was admitted that Mr. Lowe was an hour and a quar- ter late in commencing the sale, and a witness named Gandy said that the goods went " neither very cheap nor very dear," and money was not very plentiful in the neighbourhood. Mr. Browne for the defence submitted that the plain- tiff could not sue for illegal diAraint, inasmuch as he was not, the tenant. .

. His Honour said that he quite agreed that the action had been brought in the wrong form. Mr. H. Woids endeavoured to convince his Honour that it was right, but his Honour non-suited the plaintiff, and ordered £2 paid in the court with denial of liability to be repaid to Mr. Browne's client.

div.head: ABSENCE OF LORD CROSS,
div.p: ABSENCE OF LORD CROSS,
The CriAIRMAN read a letter from Lord Cross who was unable to be present, as he is chairman of a committee of the Rouse of Lords which had to consider an import- ant Bill.

MORE AID FANTED. The CHAIRMAN commented upon the fact that in many large towns and parishes there were no collections made in church whatever on behalf of the institutions. If all clergymen were as aggressive as Mr. Morgan they would be in a better financial condition. (Hear, hear.) He know no one who was more aggressive in this respect. A vote of thamks to the Chairman for presiding brought the meeting to a close. Service was subsequently held in the Parish Church, when an excellent sermon was preached by tbe Right Rev. Bishop Pearson, Vicar of Leek. A dinner was sub- sequently held in the Clergy Daughters' school. In addition to the members who were present at the Committee meeting, there were also present at the dinner Bishop Pearson, Hon. Miss Cross, the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, Captain Withington, Dr. White, Dr. Sherratt, Dr. Watkins, and Councillor A. Woods. Dean McClure presided in the unavoidable absence of Lord Cross. After the usual loyal toasts had been drunk, the health of the bishops and clergy of the dioceses was proposed by Dr. White, and was responded to by Archdeacon Gore. The" preacher" was given by Dr. Watkins, and responded to by Bishop Pearson. "The Warrington Institutions" was proposed by Archdeacon Woosnam, and responded to by Canon Penrhyn. Cap- tain Withington proposed "The town and trade of War- rington," and the Mayor in reply said that Warrington compared favourably with other towns in many things. There were proposals to widen the streets and also for providing open spaces for the poorer localities. In no place were the sanitary laws more rigidly enforced, the death rate being 17 5 per thousand. The proceedings of the anniversary then terminated.
EXCURSION TO HA.WARDEN CASTLE FROM WARRINGTON.

A grand fête and flower show will be held at Hawarden Castle on August 14, 15, and 16 under the distinguished patronage of the Right Hon. W. E. Glanstone, M.P., and Mrs. Gladstone, with the object of clearing off the building debt on the Hawar den Working Men'is Institute, and to complete it according to the original scheme, and also to assist in making the necessary alterations in the building of the elementary day schools of the parish. During the week, there will be excursions from various parts of the United King- dom, and on Thursday,August 16th an excursion organ- ised by the Liberal Association of Warrington will leave the Central Station at 10 a.m. The route to Hawar- den by the C.L.C. passes through the most beautiful scenery in Cheshire, as it goes past Delamere Forest and Mouldsworth, and is the only line which goes into Hawarden village. The village is a very pretty and picturesque one, and the park by itself is well worth a visit. It is a very extensive one, and despite Mr.G:ad- stone's feats at tree-felling,it contains thoucands of trees. At the highest point in the park are the remains of the old castle,which have tolerably well survived the ravages of time. From the top of the castle a very extensive view can be had of Cheshire and Nwrth Wales. Mr. Gla- dstone will be present at the fee, and he,of course,will be the centre of attraction to all Liberals who make the journey. It is not known whether he will address the excursionists: In addition to the attractions of the park ' and grounds, the beautiful surrounding scenery,and the associations connected with the now historic village, there will be a large number of events to entertain the thousands ttitt are expected. There will be a number of celebrated military bands present, including Her Majes- ty's Royal Horse Guards (blues), under the conductor- ship of Mr. Charles Godfrey, R.A.M., the Denbiehshire Hussars, &e. By special permission, there will be a grand exhibition in the library af Hawarden Castle, of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone's numerous, valuable, and inter- esting presents and mementoes of their life's work, including many objects of historic interest. The annual Hawarden and Buckley Horticultural Show will also be held in the park. There will also be aquatic sports on the lake, illuminations of the park, old cattle,and village dancing on the lawns, and in fact there will be a day of continuous amusement for the visitors. Tickets for the excursion from Warrington can be obtained from Mr. Mitchell, at the Liberal club and also from members of the committee.

THE INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY. Sir,—The Independent Labour Party having coma into. existerce in WarrinJon, has b,:en a great surprise to many, plev(A not a few, and caused sorrow to some. °then there are who do not know what the ',L.P. intend to de. It is not my intention to-day to say what the I.L.P.'s programme is ass National programme, I will only speak as to cur local i:.rogramme, a 4 it concerns Warrington now and henceforth. It is our intention to get for the working men the,r f irsh,are of r-l.resentat ion on the local governing bodies, the Town Council and the Board of Guardiani, and, it occasion arise. the School Board. In choosing candidates we will so tar differ from the existin, systsm that we will have men of merit, no matter what their creed.may be, and no matter what their position in life, whether they be rich and poor, if they are good men. We have many means to ascertain our candidates' standa..d of righteousness, and we shall make good use of thein. I wdl not he sufficient for a man to say, "lam a Liberal, and wq. do all things well for you." We do not recogniz,a Liber- als any nacre than Tories. We do n( t slespise any one,. but we will look to the interesfs of all. Workingmen have interests whrcia can he bebt served by having their fair share of representation on the gov,rnitin• bodies. The higher class of paid officials Un getting no weh paid. and the wages of the poor sca.venc,ers and carters of the corporation are too low. The privileged class of Corpor- ation employes can and do have holidays, without . stoppage of pay. If stricken by. illness their pay is not litepped, but carters and scavengers have no holidays, nnd if ill for a day or two not only lose their pay but their place is taken, and when they recover from their illness they find themselves out of work. It will be said that the labour department of the Oorporatisn ia ruled by the law of supply mid demand. If so, why not the higher class of employment? When2ver we get the besttalenrobtainable for moner,th-n we get good value but not unless. Our working department is .too badly paid and the higher classes too well paid; hence the deficit in our finances. The struggle will be a hard one. Workingmen will have to be true to eath other and to themselves. A good many men are prevented by fear of loss of emploment from speaking their nfilds or acting openlv. Even.if they dare not openly j',ie the 1.L.P., they know that the ballot is secret. Another thing will be seen to tw 1.L.P., and that is as far as possible to detect bribery, undue influence and corruption. The time is certainly short. Twelve weeks only to work and do our best, and we shall be in the thrws of the Council and Board of Guardians elections. I would advise shop- keepers and all whom it may concern, that their interest lies with lleg more than with those who have made it possible for the rates to be 7s. in the £ in the near future with so little to show for the expenditure. Yours, 10.,
A. BROLICH EMI TE.
19, Friars Green.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

At the monthly meeting of the above auth miry, held at the Workhouse on Friday, there were pre- .sent, the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman). M-ssrs. R. Heaton, A. Jolley, W. Houghton, Mather, G. Rat- •cliffe, S. Sutton (c lerk), W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. 2ephton (medical officer), and F. Herfoot (nuisance .inspector). DRPUTATION TO TUB lEBALTEL CONGRESS. The CLERK read an isteresting account ot his visit to the Health Congress recently held in Llndon. Mr. Beaton Ells) spoke on the same suite_ The Clerk ob- served that it was an oversight on tie rart of the Board that Dr. Septiton h,d not been invited t.) attend the Congress as ttAere were many questions upon which his opinion would be valuable. RR-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS. The CLERK reported that Dr. Sephton, and Mr. Kerfoot Itad been re-appointed MPCIiCAI offi(!er and nuisance in- spector respeetivey by the Local Government Board.

RIXTON BURIAL BOARD. The CLERK reported that he tri.d accepted, as author- ised by the Board, I he tf ndc-r of John flaFes, Ri xton, for boards, &c,, for the Bixton Burial ground, for a :,urn of £5 103.

COMPLAINTS AGAINST TEILSHIP CANAL. The Ctilar read a letter he had received from Dr. -Gornall as follows :—" Dear Sir,—As a resident in the vicinity ot the Ship Canal, I wish to substantiate the truthfulness of the enclo,sed letter. The stink from that portion ot the canal nvar th Knutsford-road during the - past fortnight has been a seriouS nuisance, and prtju- dicial to the health of the district. Yours truly. John B. Crernall." The following is the letter enclosed "20h July, 1894, Dear sir,-311 this wa-ek. the Etnich from the-Mancliester Ship Canal at F 4 Grove hiss been almost unbearable. Last night it or in. the house, and two or three of the family are complaining of sickness. This morning it was quite as bad, and if you could possi- bly do anything in the matter. I slyalld be ()Weed as well as everybody else who lives on the Ship 'Canal banks. I ma-de some inqniries at th,. bridge, and they informed me that they had been flushing the locks from the sluices. What this means exactly, I do not know. If some action is not taken in the in Ater, I shalt have to -Commenee it myself.. Awaiting your roply, yours, etc., Percy Davies."—The Authority derided reff,rt the :matter to the Mersey and irwelt .k.int Committee. ~ . A complaint was received f!om Mr S. Chandler, of 'Latchford, with regard to the amount of Hack sin,ke - emitted by steam( rain the Ship Canal. It was point d out that this was a matter for the police authorities. HIGHWAY MAIMS. A letter was received, from the Court? Conneils of - Cheshire and Lar,raAiire allowing the HiL:liway Boards to continuo-in existence for three years longer. • MEDICAL DEF/CER.S REPOT. The-rnedical officer reported that during the month `there had been 21. births and 12 deaths. The death rate was eilual to 10 3 per 1,000, a:Airist 13-5, the average for the last three months, and 251, the corresponding period _of last vear. The leath rate from zyinotin diseases was- ll'per 1,000, aueinst 143 the average of the last three Months, and 12.5, the corresponding month last year.

-A LOAN- FOR EIIRTONWOOD. The CLERK read a lo_te•r from the Local Govern- ment.l3card, giving power to the Rural SAnit-pry A,1910.. rity to borrow the sums of £2,400 and 2480 for the purpose of sewerage of the township of noTtoropcond. There was a deduction of £l2O for surveyor's chares, as they did not consider Fueh items sliou/A properly be ehargeablernpon a loan account. The CLERK said that this meant that the charges wculd be upon the gcneral fund.

SERVEYnR.S REPORT. The SERVE-MR rennrted that durirg the rronthonspee- tions have been made of the Collins Green Colliery Co's houses in Burtonwond, and Mi?:I TinslWs house at Penketh. The following plans- were submitte!..l and ay. proved, Mr. E. Bywater, six houses and a jiner's ,shop; Padgate; Merev White Lead Company, adt'ition „to works at SAnk(T-firidges. • • - DIIRTONWOOD DRAINAGE. The SuavEvott repnrterl that' the plan. tl te drainage of Burtonwood were reviFtd as rtqu.l. hy the Local

Government Board, and made to embrace the land on the North side of the brook, and these plans together with the revised estimate approved by the Board had beetf forwarded to he Local Government Board, and were now approved. He would require the Board's in- struction to proceed to obtain estimates.

PAD-GATE AND ORFORD WATER SUPPLIES. The Surveyor reported that on July 7th, he wrote the 1 following letter to the Town Clerk of Warrington: "Dear I sir, re Padgate Water Supply. At a meeting of the Authority, I made a full report of what took place at the meeting held at my office on the 25th ult., when it was resolved with respect to the watersupply of Padgate that the authority wmild guarantee st per cent. per annum on the actual cost of a 6in. main from Padgate-lane to Finger Pest-lane, and a 3in. main from thence to Fearn- head-lane end,and on the condition that the Corporation lay a 61n. main for the whole distance. Re Orford Water Supply. With respect to the Orford Water Supply,'-it was also resolved that the present agreement with the Corporation to guarantee £35 per annum be rescinded, and that the Authority would guarantee fici per cent. per annum on the actual cost of the mains already laid up to the schools,and 8i per cent.on the actual cost of a 3m. main down Long-lane for a distance of 650 yards, and a 3in main towards Marsh House-lane for a distance of 350 yards.—lt is fully understood that the cost would be as low as it can be with due regard to the material and workmanship being of the best character and that should not exceed the accounts which have been computed by the Corporation and stated by you to the Authority. Yours, Sze., William Owen."

At an adjourned meeting of the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity held at the offices of the Surveyor on the afternoon of Friday the 6th of July, the estimates for the new streets off Liverpool-road at Sankey Bridges were opened when it was resolved to accept the estimates of Mr. J. A. Ewart, 11 Palmyra Square, Warrington, for Wright-st. £3OB 93. Bd. ; Howard-st. £635.43. 6d.; Barnard-st. £338 163. 3d.; Clare-st. £232 53. id.; Gatewharf-st. £l9B 103. 9d.; total £1,713 63. 3d. A reservation was ordered to be trade by the Surveyor in the case of Gatewharf-st. until the question raised by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. and Mr. Busill as to its being a public highway was settled. It was also resolved to accept the estimates of Mr. J. Burnham, of 6 Okell-et., Runcorn, for Dale-st. £185; Owen-st. £156 18s. 9d. ;total £341 184. 9d. The total amount of the accepted estimates is £2,055 53. Mr. Ewart is now engaged in forming Howard-st. and Barnard-st.—All the reports were adopted.

Oh I tis sweet to muse, be jabers On the charity of neighbours, And the very kindly sentiments folks for each other feel ; So, what follows ponder duly, And you will see how easy, truly, Tie, while steering down life's rapids, to pre- serve an even keel."

if of drink you see the folly, And wont quaff a glass so jolly, You're a snivelling teetotaler, an anti-social "stick But if at all you're noted The least fond of drink, you're voted A reprobate, a drunkard—going headlong to old Nick! If taciturn your bearing— Hating tattling, jesting, swearing— You're a dull and dry o:d humbug, witless, mopish and inane; But if your tongue's loose-jointed, And you utter puns fine-pointed, You're a g0531p, bore, and meddler, you're imperti- nent and vain!

If retiring, in society, Full of modesty, propriety, Towards the fair sex, you're /a muff, a Mollycoddle, an old dame; But if you ogle, flatter, And amuse them with pert chatter, You're a libertine, a scoundrel a deceiver void of shame!

If you are a careful man, sir, Saving all you fairly can, sir, To provide 'gainst future hardships, You're a miser and a " screw " ; But if free and open-hearted, Eas'ly from your money parted, A reckless fool, a prodigal, a spendthrift mad are you.

If, to sate some poker-wielding, To your wife you're somewhat yielding, You're a poor old henpecked duffer, lacking miknly pride or grit ; _ But. iugt practise the diversion Of a mastery-assertion, And you are a brutal tyrant, u. wife-killer, gallows; fit !

If a man, with heart love-laden, Weds a poor and lowly maiden, He's a thundering ass, imprudent rash and reckless, all agree;. But if, in her own right, sir, She has lands and kopees bright, sir, An artful fortune-hunter, soulless, mercenary's he ! If you join some speculation With successful termination, You're a model of discretion, prudence, wisdom,and all that ; But if, in like circumstances, It. proves bad for your-finances,- - You're a silly fool, ,a witless tool, a gull, a dupe, a flat!

Oft a man with talents, learning, Noble parts, and honest yearning, Must neglected and despised remain, if friendless be his fate; While a brainless, useless codger, Who may be an "artful dodger," Or has friends to push and puff him, is exalted, cheered, made great.

If church-going you're inclined for, Praying, fasting, have a mind for, You're a Pharisee, a hypocrite, a fraud in every way; But if duties appertaining - To religion you're disdaining, You're a heathen, moral leper, public scandal, fcaks will say! Warrington, August, 189 t

LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

On Monday about 160 of the scholars of the Latchford Wesleyan Sunday School had their annual Walking Day treat. The field chosen for the occasion was lent by Mr. Ashley, and is situated near the Baptist Chapel in Wash- lane. To this ' place the scholars repaired at two o'clock, and indulged in games &e., till about four,when they returned to the schoolroom and partook of a sub- stantial tea. After tea the field was returned to, and the various enjoyments re-commenced. Though the pro vious two or three days had been very wet, the after- noon in question was everything that could be desired, and at nine o'clock the scholars returned to their homes, heartily satisfied With the afternoon's enjoyment. THE WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY. • A meeting of this society was held on Sunday after- noon and wee largely attended. Mr. W. Jeffery occu- pied the chair, and in the course of a short address ho said they were engaged in a grand and noble work. It was only right that men should come forth, men of power and ability, to lead the people, because after all, what was the superstructure of a nation like England, if the foundation were dead and rotten? The working classes were the bise upon which the prosperity of the ; country depended, the wealth producing class, and what they needed was right leaders. Mr. Summersgill, San- key Bridges, delivered a powerful address. He based his rPmarks on the text "If ye can find a man," Jere- miah 5n., lv. Two solos were excellently Sum, by Mrs. .T( fiery, and a duet was exceedingly well rendered by Mr. F. R. and Miss N. Roberts. The Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. J. Irish, and Mr. C. Bristow also tank part in the meeting.

• • SUDDEN DEATHS. Jane Hastell, 45 years of age, was found dead in bed on Wednesday morniug at 9, Shepherd's-row, off Orford-street. She went to bed about nine o'clock on Tuesday night, and about eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning she was spoken to but re- turned no answer. Dr. Peacocke was called in, and he pronounced life to he extinct.—Catherine Far- rington, widow, 60 years of age, who resided with her SOD, John Farrington, labourer, 71 Wellfield- street, died somewhat Rtuldenly on Wednesday night At five o'clock. On. Sunday night she com- plained of pain at her chest but appeared in good health on Tues,lay night when she retired to ben. The following morning at Weven o'clock she said "I am near dead?' Dr, Jo:4Th was sent for, but she died at the 'time stated. The doctor is of the opinion that the deceased had a fit.
