SHIP CANAL.
MEETING OF CANAL SHAREFIOLDERS.

A large meeting of Ship Canal shareholders was held' on Tuesday ciening at the Gentlemen's Concert Hall, Manchester, as a:preliminary to a conference to he field' in the month of October. The Right Hon. Jacob Bright, M.P., who presided; expressed his belief that traffic on the canal would grow month by month, and that each ! year would mark a large advance. The case- presented to Parliament ten years ago, he said, had not been dis- turbed. It was clearly proved then that the canal was u-antedarn.l that it would pay, and in the meantime the case had 'rather grown stronger than weaker. In regard to the proposed conference, which had for its. purpose the furthering a the commercial ititerestA of the Canal, he thought it cculd do nothing but good:- Mr. Bri.ght moved a reAutiOn affirming. unabated confidence in the commercial value and economic importance of the can.,l and approving of the -corning conference. The resolu- tion was adopted with heartiness. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 11, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY AUGUST 11, 1894.
NOTES ON GAMES AND TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT ATHLETICS. RUNCORN. ENTHUSIASTIC PROCEEDINGS.
CRICKET.

To judge from last Sa—t.;;;Ci-a:;;-; match, "holidaying" appears to agree with the Warrington team immensely. They travelled to Llanduduo to meet the team of that favourite NI elsh watering place, and performed a feat which scarcely another team has accomplish,td this sea- son by defeating them. They did not do it in a half hearted fashion ei:her for after tumbling out the home team for the paltry sum of 32, they went in and piled on the formidable total of 262. They were in fact tak- ing the opportunity of showing to the cricket world what they were capable of if they were given half a chance. Their detractors will require a great amount of reckoning to explain away this victory. The team was minus tfiree good men in S. M. and J. J. Crosfield, and W.rdsworth, but R. Smith was present and he let the Llandudno men know it, But more of this anon.

The Welshmen won the toss, and they had raised the score to 20 before any separation could be made. Smith was the first to break the partnership, and this was the first of a series of disasters. Two more fell without a qinele extra run, while five runs later still another fell aid the remaining seven cguld only raise the score to 32. Out of the 32 runs, 22 were obtained off Bates for four. wickets. R. Smith was simply unplayable. He sent down 14 overs, 11 of which were maidens. Out of the three remaining overs only six runs were obtained, and these were obtained for five wickets, Smith's average there• upon being 1.2 runs per wicket. The fielding of the Warrington tea n was very brilliant, and very few liber- ties were allowed to their opponents.

Warrington had thus very little required to score a victory, and only Bibby was lost before theit opponents score was equalled. The stand of Clerk and Callon was the event of the match. They carried the score from 33 to 106 before Clarke was out with individual score of 50. Callon Continued however until the score had reached 166. His score of 60 was made up of a six' three fours, and four threes besides singles. R. Smith. the captain also claimed 20 as his share of the spoil. Clark the wicket keeper had hard lines indeed, for he was only two short of his half century when he fell a victim to a player of the same name but with an extra " e "at the end. Others players worthy of mention were Adamson who scored 25, Voisey 16, and Worthing- ton, 13. Needless to say, the Llawiudno bowing showed a very marked contrast to the other side. The best average was Halstead with three for 60.

The next fixture which Warrington have to fulfill is with Manchester. As the Warrington team have a sneaking fondness for taking down this club, being the only club to accomplish that feat twice last season, a good game will be witnessed. Of course the Manchester men are on their own native heath, but that made no difference last year, and ought not to do so this year.

The Cheshire Lines Engineers had the satisfaction of defeating the Sankey Wire Mills, by 10 runs, on Satur day. The teams had met earlier in the season when the Wire Mills proved victorious by 9 runs. Only one man in the match obtained double figures, W. Brown 11 runs for the winners. The plucky batting of Irvine and W. Nevins literallv pulled off the match,these men played a very Atubborn and plucky innings, although only scoring 10 runs between them before Nevins was run out. Harrison 5 wickets, 9 runs, and Monks 4 wickets, 16 runs, dismissed the Wire Mills team. Simpson for the losers bowled exceedingly well. •

Walker's Brewery had to play socorid fiddle to Penketh Wesleyans on Saturday, and on their own ground too. che Penketh club is only a young one, but still they can do some smart things sometimes. The match of Satur- day was a bowlers' match, for the scoring was very low indeed, the highest individual score being six, which three of the Periketh team succeeded in obtain big. The Brewery men were dismissA for the small -sup of 22. This was due to the excellent bowling of Wilkinson-and Dunabin, the former taking six wickets for as many runs, and the lett. r, thre for five.

The Cain-street Unity payed a visit to the pictures village of Arley on Monday. They not only had the satisfaction of seeing the beautiful scenery, but also scored a victory of 82 to 39, over the Arley Park team. Towards their high scar, Peers contributed 28, Brown 24, and Hampsonls. Crompton was the most success- ful bowler with live wickets for 19 runs.

The Y:M.C.A toams of Warrington and St: Helens tnet togethei on the Warrington ground on Sittt rday, and a tight match was the result. The Saints managed to rotire victors hy one run. After the match, Mr. J. Fulton Smith provided a tea for the member of both teams, who had a jolly time of it. Mr. Smith, of course, was cordially thanked for his kindness.

The Sankey Wesloyans* gained" their seebild Vietor v this season over the Warrington United. They succeed- ed in scoring 80 for the 1033 of eight wickets, toward which Watkins made 22, Peers 20, Bennett 19, and Light 14. Against this, the United could only mike 38 from all cut. The whole of the United- wickets were shared between Bailey and Watkins.

The annual demonstration of the Runcorn branch of the Sons of Temperance, was celebrated on Bank Holiday in most propitious weather. The proceed- ings in reality began the previous day, (Sunday), when at two o'clock in the afternoon, in spite of the unfavourable atmospheric conditions, a number of members assembled in Devonshire-square, and an open air service was conducted by Mr. S. M. Temperley, and Mr. Thomas Cooke. Finally the 'members were compelled to adjourn to the new Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, in consequence of the rain, where brief addresses, were delivered by Mr. Wm. Shaw, and Mr. James Moores. A service was afterwards conducted by the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, who preached an admir- able sermon on temperance. The congregation was a large 'one and the special musical programme sustained by the choir of the chapel was much appreciated. The following day, Birk Holiday, the members of the Order again assembled in the schoolroom, and at about 1.30 marched in processional•order down Greenway-road, Station-road, Lowland's-road, over Waterloo Bridge into Waterloo-road, through Rutland-street, Ashbridge-street, and Lord-street into Church-street. Here they halted at the house of Dr. MacLennan, who is the medical officer to this branch of the Order. The Widnes Subscription Prize Band, which headed the procession played selec- tions during the stay. The march was then resumed along Church-street, down into King-street where an- other stop was made outside Dr. Robinson's house, dur- ing which musical airs were rendered by the band. Church-street was again entered and the parade was re- sumed along this thoroughfare into Bridge-street, and along Halton-road as far as the Crane. They then re- turned by way of Bridge-street to High-street, and another halt was made outside the Ternperance,Hotel of Mrs. Lea. The Band again went through a short pro- ! gramiiie of music after which the processionists con- tinued their j ,urney over Savage's Bridge, up Greenway road, to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. William Banks, cabinet maker,of High-street. The order in which the procession was marshalled was as follows: —Widnes Subscription Prize Band, the beautiful silken banner of the Order, Messrs. George Sutton and George Holt carrying the charter of the adult section followed by the adult members, headed by Mr. W. Huddart M.W.P., (Salford) Mr. Edward Hallsworth, M. W.A., (Manchester) and Mr. Edward Hughes, G.W.P. (Chester). Then came masters John Bis- brown, Albert E. White, and T. Wilfred Whyte with .the juvenile charter, the rear being brought up by the juveniles. The members who acted as marshals were Messrs. George Sutton, T. R. Whyte, S. M. Temperley, T. Clarke, D. Bisbrown, S. Temp:qley junr., George Holt, Thomas Holt, with the secret tries Messrs. Edward Key and Thomas Cooke. One especially pretty feature of the procession was the four little girls, all dressed in white, and named Misses Bessie Weight, alphie Rovlet Ettie and Maggie Bartlett carrying tie smaller silken cords of the banner ; whil.t four young ladies, all very tastefully attired and named Misses E. Alice Cooke, Lydia Mathews, Lizzie Bisbrown, and Lizzie Leath wood, carried the larger cords. In many quarters of the town there were displays of bunting as well as the flags cf various nationalities. Large numbers of persons collected on the footpaths of the streets through which the members passed, and many favourable criticisms were made by the former 'regarding the appearance of the latter. Upcn arriving at the -field, sports of all hinds were participated in with a great amount of zest, the elder members doing their utmost to add to the pleasure of the juveniles. • Shortly before five o'clock tracks were made for the schoolroom again where a capital tea was served, the under-mentioned ladies kindly administering to the requirements of the hungry: -Mesdames S. M. Temperley, T. Heesom, T. Cooke, D. Bisbrown, J. Pmcilebury, P. Leathwood, W. Hough, Shingler, Gibson, and Killeress' Misses Bisbrown, E. Alice Cooke, Boyle, Killcross, Hillidge, and Polly Hillitlge.
THE EVENING MEETING

Immediately after tea, the Toolll was cleared, and pre- parations made for the evening meeting. These having been completed the persons were admitted ,and in a very short time the room was crowded. It was found neces- sary to throw open the small class rooms also on each side of the large room, and they were soon full. Indeed the attendance was so numerous that many persons could not get inside the • building at all and were forced to go away disappointed. The gentlemen on the plat- form were Mes,rs. Wm. Iluddart, P.M.W.P., of Salford. Edward fiallse,vorth, M.W.A., of Manchester, Joseph Nixon, Manchester, Thomas Cooke, Daniel -Bisbrown, T. J. Holt, G. Sutton, S. M. Temperley, and T. R. %V byte. Mr. T. Cooke said that he had to apologise for the absence of Mr. Corringe, of London, who had promised to take tile chair that evening. That gentleman had had to return to London, but although they had lost Mr. Corrings,t hey had been successful in securing Councillor 117 m. fludilart of Salford, who would, he was sure, make an admirable chairman. The Chairman in tne course of his remarks said that the order of the Sons of Temperance was a Society organ- ized and conducted on the sanie lines•as many of their friendly societies were. The difference was that whilst the other friendly societies took in all classes of human- ity, the Sons of Temperance only took in those indivi- duals who were pledged abstainers from intoxicating• drink. Hence, if anyone present was thinking of joining ! the Order, he or she would have to become a teetotaler. The society was first instituted in America, and, like a great many more good things, was sent across here to the old country. The society was not carried on here exactly as in America, •as they in England had adopted the benefit principle and the Americans had not. The organization was a very flourishing one inasmuch as the total membership was 140,000. It was known in a great many parts of Europe, as well as in many parts of the United States, Canada, South Africa. Australia and New Zealand. In this country they were in the front rank of benefit societies, the membership of the United Kingdom being 31,000 adults and 12,000 juveniles. (Anplause.) They had paid something like a quarter of a million ! sterling in claims since the beginning of the society in ! the United Kingdom. They served a very .useful pur- pose, being able to relieve their members when in distress! and sickness; and he thought he could safely say that of the claims which had been made against them in the United Kingdom, 99i per cent. had been paid. He knew of no better protection for anyone than that of being a member of the Sons of Temperance. Instead of spend- ing his time in the public-house he could visit the rooms of the society and engage in conversations which could not fail to benefit him. Speaking of the probable amount which the average workingman spent in beer, Mr. Huddart said that if the money that was spent yearly in intoxicants was only expended in the necessaries of life, there would be no poverty. (La ud applause.) Mr. Edward liallsworth in a stirring,address said that there was a time in the history of the temperance move- ment when the church would not open its schoolroom doors for the purpose of any meeting in advocation of the temperance cause. He was glad to say that such was not the case now, and he was also very glad to say that the Primitive Methodists were the first religious body who opened their doors to the advocates of tem- perance. (Applause.) The Sons of Temperance were one of the most democratic organizations in existence. The officers or the order were elected by the members, the funds wore controlled by the members,and they were the greatest enemies of the publicans. Be hoped that the parents present would allow their children to join the society, and the members would endeavour to fortify them for life's struggle. (near, hear.) Mr. Cooke in a few observations said he was proud of being a member of a society such as the Sons of Tem- perance, the membership of which in Runcorn was 280 adults and" 100 juveniles, making a total of 3.80. (Hear, hear and applause.) If only twenty young men out of the audience would now make up their minds and join the society that night the membership would thus be raised to the grand number of 400. Referring to the cadet section of the Order he remarked that it was sel- dom they had a funeral in connection with it. For a proof of this he might say that whilst they had paid £3OO in sick pay, they had had only two deaths in the whole Order. In a later address he thanked the choris- ters of the Primitive Methodist Chapel on behalf of the Committee for their services on the previous day. During the evening a programme of instrumental and vocal music was rendered,the Widnes Subscription Prize Band supplying the former. Miss Heatherington so ad- mirably interpreted" flome Sweet Home" that she wat encored very spiritedly. She responded Iv repeating the last verse. Mr. Worrall sang " The sailor's grave" very satisfactorily-, whilst Miss Alice Cooke created roars of laughter by her comic contribution " I persuaded him." For this item she was recalled and pleasing sang " Alabama Coon" in response_ A recitation entitled " The Little Girl in White " was given by Miss A.Rogers hich she rendered with tasteful expression, and for which she has recently gained a silver medal. Miss Heather ington again pleased the audience by her singing of " Corning threugh the Rye," and Mr. G. Lacy very amusingly sang " The Domestic Pets." After this item had been rendereo the audience joined in the singing of Vie Doxology which closed the proceedings.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.

• The chief local event of the present week in the athle- tic circles,has heen the Football Club annual sports. The club was extremely fortunate in the weather, for not- withstanding the constant rain of the previous days,they were favoured with an almost cloudless sky. As a con- sequence the number of spectators was very large being estimated at between 5,000 and 6,000.

The compc.tition for the Nwthern Counties champion- ship lasted the whole of the afternoon, arid some wonder- ful feats were performed by the ten competitors. Evans of Hulme performed in a capital manner, although he was lame, and he fully desereed the silver medal. For all-round excellence however, Stanley, of the Manchester Y.M.C.A. was pre-eminent, and he was accordingly pro- claimed champion.

In the sports proper, the chief event was the re- appearance of Webster who has been amongst the home rulers lately. He did net appear to he in form however, aud was not successful in his competitions. Carey showed his running powers to advantage in the member's race, and was without doubt, the ft,etest of the various mem- bers. The open hundred yards handicap was disastrous to Warrington competitors, for not a single local man Cams in for a prize. La the 220 yards handicap,the Warrington- ians were more successful,for Cunningham and Robinson were first and second respectively. The " bobby" was in good form on Saturday, and fully deserved his prize. Warrington is not deficient of long distance runners for the half mile race was won easily by Price of the Orford Harriers.

In the bicycle races, Buxton was the' only local corn netitor to achieve success, which he did in both the one and two mile race, coming in second on each occasion. Several good riders were absent, among whom was Daintith. The honours of the obstacle race were almost entirely won by Warringtonians. The first and second were natives, and although the third was a" foreigner," he was only about a yard before another native. The arrangements of the sports were excellent, and great praise is due to the committee who formed them. The various events were run without the slightest hitch, with the result that there was no long waiting to irri- tate the public. .

At the Birkenhead Rangers C.C. meeting, nnSaturdly, A. J. Mottram, Warrington Gymnasium, with 91 yards, captured the premier prize in the 100 yards race. J. Cunningham, also of WarrinF,,,ton, took third prize in. the 100 yards at the Royston C.C. Sports. Cunningham had a start of 91 Frlris.

div.head: CANAL FATALITY.
div.p: CANAL FATALITY.

'A boy named Joseph. Harrison, aged eight years, son of Mr John Harrison, Regent-street,Earlestown fell into the Sankey Canal on Monday=afternoon, and was drowned The boy left home about two o'cicck, and in company With several others pro- ceeded to the canal fEr the purpose of fishing. After being. there about two hours, Ilarrison accidentally fell into the water. His companions gave the alarm and called the assistance'7. of two men who were home hu-nciro yards away, but on their arrival at tire 'scene Of the accident, the poor lad bad disap- peared and it is said never rose to the surface after fallinc!. in. The body Was subsequently 'recovered. —Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, conducted an inquiry relative to the death of the deceased at. the Griffin Hotel, on Wednesday evening. Evidence of iden- tification was given, and the facts above related were borne out. John Sankey deposed to finding the body. A v-erdict of "Accidental death " was refurnect

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

ANNUAL MEETING: LIVELY PROCEEDINGS. The annual meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Church- st., Runcorn, Mr. J. Betney presiding. There was a crowded attendance of members, the gentlemen on the platform being Messrs, T. Watsom, W: Rhodes, T Riley, R. Royle, J. Rogerson, Holt, W. Cropper, Edwin Yates (representing the Co-operative Whole- sale Society), Jonah Evan., general manager and cashier, William Upton, secretary, &e. The Chairman, in a short address congratulated the members upon the balance sheet which had been pre- sented to them that evening. It was apparent that they were making progress, but in some instances they were going backward. By referring to the past records of the sales he had found that they had only exceeded by £2,000 the sales of ten years ago. However, he had no doubt that it the members would all unite and do the best they . could the society would soon increase its strength and perhaps prove mere beneficial in the future. Although the meeting was the largest he had ever beheld in connection with the society' he thought it should be a peaceable one; and hoped it would be con- ducted with order and propriety. THE SIXTY-FOURTH HALF-YEARLY REPORT. Toe Secretary having read the minutes of the previous meeting, which were confirmed, the report and balance sheet were taken as read, and submitted for acceptance. The report stated that the sales for the past half-year amounted to £44,304 63.2d.,an increase of £223 165.10 d. on the half-year previous. The amount disposable, after charging all expenses, including depreciation and interest On capital, deducting the cheques purchased, reducing Ship Canal shares £lOO. special depreciation land, buildings, and fixtures £lOO, leaves the nett amount £7,057 183. 7d. We' recommend a dividend of 3s. in the £ on £44,420 of cheques,account books brought in, which will amount to £6,663, leaving a balance of £394185. 7d. to the reserve fund." The cash account showed that the balance in hand at the end of the last half-year was £2l 17. 7d. The grocery sales amounted to £33,911 18. 104 d. ; butchering, £2,574 95. 9-0.; drapery,£3,sso 33. W.; boots and shoes.£l,2ls 185.5c1.; boot and shoe repairs, £613 us. 6d.; and 'coal, £2438 4s. 21; 1. The amount paid in share contributions was £5,587 13s. 8.1.•, penny bank, £290 4s. 10d.; advances repaid, £941 103.7 d.; interest on advanees,£29l 123.7 d.; interest and dividend on investments, £6O 124.91.; bank withdrawals, £50,185 163. 4d.; which with other small items made the total on the debit side £lOl,BOO 7s. 11d. On the .credit side of the same account appeared : pur- ehases and carriage, £32212; productive wages, £651 14s. 6d. Expenses : wages,£l,7lB 18s. 3d. ;.committee's fees, £l6 ' • deputations of the latter, £3l. 103. 2c1.; re- pairs, £282 53. 441. Other minor amounts brought the expenses up to £2,543 143. 4d. The other figures of im- portance on the credit side of the sheet were: dividend and interest, £7,060 133.1 d. ; share withdrawals, £5,202 93. 3d. ; ponnv bank withdrawals, £ ' 695 and hank deposits, £51,526 1e.8d., the cash in hand being £l2l 3s. 3-0. The auditors certified that the statement was correct, and added "as to the value of the stocks we have relied upon the figures appearing in the stock hooks which have been certified by your committee and officials." .Mr. Cosier asked if the secretary or anyone else could inform them of the reason why Runcorn was decreasing in some instances so far as its sales were concerned. Could the committee assign any cause or suggest ariy means of bringing about an improvement ? The Chairman explained that the slackness of trade in Runcorn would account for the falling off in some of its sale's. The trade in Runcorn had been for some time very bad, even worse in proportion than in Widnes. Mr. Clarke called attention to the item £3l 103. 21., which the committee had incurred by deputations and asked if the Committee could explain what benefit the society had derived through those deputations. After the secretary had read out the names of those places visited by deputations from the society, he re- marked that concerning any particulars as to the profit gained he thought it was a question which should be put to one of the Committee, as he himself did not feel in a position to answer it. Several of the members seemed to be of the opinion that the ieputations did not benefit the Society,and that they should entirely cease. The Chairman observed that if the Committee were to gain knowledge whereby to improve the society they had to search for it. (Hear, hear.) The deputations wore anxious to know what was going on in the co-oper- atiee world, "and they accordingly visited the various conferences with that view, and if the society could not pa.s for them it might just as well shut up the prem- ises.

. _ Explanations concerning the benefit derived through deputations visiting various places were then entered into by some of the Committee, in the course of which many propositions and amendments were brought for- ward by the members. Mr. Dyer moved that all deputations cease with the exception of the one which attended the conference of the Manchester Wholesale which was held quarterly,and this proposal was carried by 162 votes to 69. Mr. Worthington then raised a question on the land buildings, and fixtures account shown on the balance sheet. He enquired the reason- why the committee had accepted a tender for the cottages in Halton-road which was £3O more than another tender.—This subject pro- voked a somewhat lengthy discussion in the course of which disorderly interruptions, • especially at the rear of the room, were frequent, and remarks of a very irrele- vant nature were passed. Eventually Mr. Holt explained that some time previously i similar piece of work had been given to the sa;me contractor and which he had carried out very well at a loss to himself in consequence of the recent coal strike. The Committee thought, there- fore, in the face of this that they ought, in duty bound, to give him this contract, and so let him have an oppor- tunity of slightly compensating himself. THE OFFICIALS UNDERPAID. Mr. Cosier, in referring to the expenses account asked if the officials salaries were included and being answered in the affirmative, saii. he thought they were very mach under paid. The Chairman : So do L think so. Mr. Cosier, continuing, said he understood they had some trouble with one of their shop managers a short time ago. He thought the wages question had a great deal to do with the matter and begged to move that the general manager and seeretary be each remunerated with 50s. per week. The proposition was seconded but on being put to the meeting was defeated. INCREASE OF DIVIDEND. Mr. Worthington proposed that instead of paying 3s. in the £ as dividend, it should be 33. 31 The Chairman thought that their reserve fund was none too large, and that it would not be advisable to pay the extra 3d. in the £ at the expense of the sum which had been transferred to the reserve fund. Mr. Fitzpatrick in a lengthy speech against the pro- posed increase of dividend said that in these times of de- pression in trade, the principle of a good reserve fund needed no demonstration. He advised that the mem- bers should rest content with 3s. in the £, and, in the future things might possibly brightenand then the extra dividend might be paid with safety. Mr. Harper seconded Mr. Worthington's proposition which was finally carried by a large majority amid much shouting, and stamping of feet. The balance sheet was then adopted as altered. FEBRUARY MEETINGS TO BE HELD II WIDNES. Mr. Fitzpatrick moved a resolution to the effect that henceforth all February half-yearly meetings should be held in Widnes.—Mr. Preston secouded.and it was agreed to unanimously. THE RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. The Chairman announced that •lie had that afternoon received a letter from Mr. Wiswall, the Chairman of the Runcorn Technical Institute Committee, —(Cries of " Lay it on the table," " Put it under the able," &e.)—asking for a donation towards the Institute. If it was the wish of the meeting that he should read the letter he would gladly do so. (Renewed interruption and a voice : Put the money to the Reserve Fund.) After a few moments pause the Chairman read the letter, and stated that the committee of the Society had made a recominendation to the members that the sum of £2OO be given to the scheme. Mr. Cosier thought they had no right to take such an action. It was not legal. Mr. Worthington expressed himself as favourable to the payment of £2OO towards the object. If not that sem at least £lOO should be given. (Interruption, which lasted for several moments.) The Chairmareremarked that he was in sympathy with the object of spreading technical instruction, amongst the poorer classes especially,and he would have supported the recommendation to give the £2OO but Mr. Werthington had taken the stumps from under him by hie actin concerning the increased dividend. They could have well afforded to have given £2OO if they had not paid 3s. 3d. instead of 33. in the £ dividend. (Re- newed uproar.) Mr. Walter Worthington : It is the feeling of the meet- ing that the letter should be" shelved," and why don't you shelve it. One of the members proposed and ar.other eeennded that £lOO be given to the Runcorn Technical Institute. This proposition was met by an amendment that noth- ing be given to the object. The Chairman put the amendment first and it was carried by a large majority in the midst of a great uproar. ELECTION OF OFFICERS. Mr. Evans was re-elected general manager and cashier, and Mr. Upton secretary. The auditors were aLso re-appointed. .The four gentlereen retiring from, but eligible for re-election to the committee were Messrs. T. Riley, R. Royle, T. Watson. and J. Rogerson. Mr. T. Watson informed the members that it was his intention not to seek re-election. The nominations were then pro- ceeded with, those nominated being Messrs. G. F. Dan, James Sayles, J. Rogerson, Edward Guest, Edward Key, Edward Aston, Thon.as Riley, W. Dudley, D. Worthins,, ton, IL Reyle, Bradbury, Boadinan and Cosier. The election, which lasted about half-an-hour, ended in Messrs. Sayle, Rogerson, Dudley and Worthington being appointed their respective votes, numbering 109, 84, 93, 78. The meeting, which had commenced shortly before eight o'clock, then terminated', it being nearly talf-pastl eleven.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday tle Provisional Order Bill relating to tolls and charges on the River Weaver came up for consideration, and a number of amendments framed in accordance with the compromise arrived at by the repres-ntativea of the various interests concerned at the conference held recently at the Board of Trade were inserted.

In answer to Mr. HEALY, Mr. Jo rrN MORLEY stated that there were 24,000 evictions in Ireland between October, 1881, and September, 1887, and 8,975 from October, 1887, to June, 1894. A great many had been merely formal evictions. Questioned as to the cost of the police guards for persons on the Clanricarde estate, Mr. MORLEY said that last year it came to £2,098. On that estate there were nine persons under constant police pro- tection, and 14 persons were afforded police protection by patrols. No fewer than than 92 constables were en- gaged on protection duty. Mr. BRYCE, replying to questions put by Mr.CHANNINO, said the Board of Trade had no power to prevent rail- way companies from increasing the hours of their em- ploy6s, but if it were represented by the men that the hours increased were -unreasonable the Board of Trade would use the powers given them under the Railway Hours Act, 1893. In consequence of the action of the Board of Trade the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway had . undertaken to reduce all the twelve-hour signal- boxes on the Brighouse and Norrnanton section to ten hours,and two ten-hour cabins were to be brought down to eight hours. There were busy boxes on other sec- tions of that railway in regard to which complaints had been received, and the Board of Trade were using the powers of the Act in the manner which it contemplated. _ _ _ .

The House afterwards proceeded to consider the Local Government (Scotland) Bill as amended. It was agreed that the bill should come into operation next April. When the House adjourned twenty clauses of the bill had been disposed of.
GOLD DISCOVERIES IS AIISTIiALIA.

The accounts received by the Government at Perth of the discoveries of gold in Western Australia are astonish- ing. Gold is being found in large masses in the outcroP of a reef near CooLrariii4. In one of the local batiks there were to he seers about four hundredweight of " sPeci- mens " which yielded more than two hundredweight of gold. Toe qu.sr,z is even richer than that found at Londonderry Reef, another place near Coolgardie Which yielded enoren,us returns.

div.head: NEW POSTCARD ARRANGEMENT.
div.p: THE NEW POSTCARD ARRANGEMENT.

Mr. Henniker Heaton writes to the "Times " with reference to the new postcard arrangement : After a seven years' struggle with the Post Office I have the pleasure of announcing a substantial success for the public. Henceforth a person may take any plain card of the proper size, write a letter upon it, affix a halfpenny adhesive stamp, and have it transmit- ted through the rost. The Department has, I admit, made a gallant fight. The officials paid £283 per million for the material of their postcards, whereas the adhesive halfpenny stamps only cost them £l6 per million. Nevertheless by charging 6d. for ten cards and selling single cards at /I. each they have contrived to make a clear profit, on the material alone, of £22,000 a year. To safeguard this profit they even raised the cost of stamping (impressing) stationers' sheets of postcards from 93. a gross to 154. a gross (the actual cost being about is. per gross). This abuse of a letter-carrying monopoly,in order to injure trade, justifies my reiterated contention that the Post-office has no legal or moral right to enforce a. profit from the sale of stationery. It% now the stationers' turn. We may hope to see postcards sold by them in all our cities as on the Continent, bearing tiny and attractiye pictures of interesting buildings. monuments, and scones of natural beauty. Although we are grateful to Sir John Hibbert and ,the Treasury for this boon, our real work is only now beginning. We must never rest until the. Post-office sells a postcard at its bare stamp or face value as in foreign countries and in every British colony, from Gibraltar to New Zealand.

div.head: -WESTON.
div.p: -WESTON.

BOATMAN DROWNED AT WE'iTON POINT: INQUEST.—Mr. J. E. Worley, c3roner, on Friday afternoon, conducted an inquiry at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point relativeto the death of John Henry Walker, 23 years of age, of Knutsford-road, Latchford, who was drowned on th.. previous Wednesday night, in the river Mersey at the entrance of the Weston M,rsey Lock of the Ship Canal, Weston Point.—Frederick Walker, brother of the deceased, said that he was captain of the flat " Enter- prise,"which travelled between Manchester and Liverpool and on which his brother has assisted him as mate. On Wednesday night, at abalit eleven o'clock, witness was steering .the boat as it was making its way for the Wes- ; ton Mersey Loilk through which it had to pass to. enter the Ship Canal and while passing through the lock they collided with another boat. The deceased was at the front of the flat and at the time of the collision was evidently.placing a fender down the side of the boat in order that the cra,ft.might not be damaged. When the boats collided witness's brother fell over the side, having been appar- ,ently jerked from his position by the shock. Witness and several boatmen immediately made efforts to find the body, but the search was fruitless, and witness gave it as his opinion that his brother had been .crushed between the two boats and consequently had sunk at once. The night was-dark,a nd the tide was a very high one. Questioned by the Coroner witness said that as soon as it Was known that his brother had fallen over- board, a small boat was launched, and the search .livits made by the aid of lamps. Lifebuoys were also thrown i out. The next morning (Thursday) the body was recovered. —Tne Coroner remarked that he shared the same opinion as witness namely,that the deceased ,when he had fallen off the boat, had been crushed and so being, had sunk itntnediately.—Peter James Murphy, master of the Weston Mersey Lock of the Manchester Ship Canal at Weston Point, also gave evidence, during which he expressed the same opinion as the brother of deceased about the latter having probably been crushed. The reason why he held this opinion was that. when be went down in a boat with a lamp to search for the body, he thought he saw a quantity of blood upon the surface of the water. The collision which occurred was not pre- ventible, and was by no means an unusual occurrence. The utmost care had been observed whilst entering the lock.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned."

div.head: HA.LTON.
div.p: HA.LTON.

CHILDREN'S ANNUAL SCHOOL TREAT.—The youthful scholars belonging to the Halton Wesleyan Sunday school, on Bank Holidai7 had their annual treat in the Duke's field, Halton. There were upwards of 300 in- cluding the teachers, and the party were accompanied by the Revs. James Hanby. and J. Jub3on, the senior superintendent Mr. Hugh Rowe; and also Messrs. J. H. Gamon, and James Looker, the remaining superintend- ents. After spending a pleasant afternoon in the field, they adj3urned to the schools where an excellent tea was pa rtaken of and enjoyed by all.

DEMONSTRATION OF ODDFELLOWS.—The biennial demonstration in connection with the Rising Sun Lodge of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows Halton and Runcorn district, was held on Bank Holiday at about 9 30. in the morning the members (100 adults and 36 juveniles) assembled in the club room at the Halton Castle Hotel and having been marshalled into processional order marched through the village to Runcorn headed by the St. 'Paul's Church (Warring- ton) Brass Bind, and the banner of the Order. Whilst parading Runcorn they paid friendly visits to the Star of Freedom Lodge of the same order at the Egerton Arms, and to the house of Dr. MacLennan. Also to the Earl of Chester's Lodge of the Independent Order at Norton Arms, Halton. The processionists arrived back at Halton shortly after one o'clock, and adjourned to the Castle Hotel where they partook of a substantial repast. The evening was spent in dancing and other pastimes were participated in. The St. Paul's Church Brass Band, Warrington, rendered the musical programme for dancing.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF AN INVALID.—SOIDO excitement was occasioned in the neighbourhood of Frodsham on Friday when it became known that Thomas Hughes, of Overton Frodsham Lords hip,who has been incapacitated from employment tor sixteen years, had made an at- tempt to take his life by cutting his t hroat with a knife. He appears that Hnghei was suffer ing from delusions a littje before six o'clock on Friday evening and thought that someone was coming to the house to remove him. At about this time his wife left the house for a few 'minutes and when she returned she was horrified to find him in the act of hacking at his throat with a knife. She interrupted him and took the weapon away: Dr. Selby, of Frodsham, was then summoned and stitched up the wound which the man had inflicted upon his throat. Fortunately it was not of a very serious nature, and is vickly healing.—On Saturday at the local police court, before Dr. Steele, Hughes was charged in custody with attempting to commit suicide in the above mentioned manner on the previous evening. —Dr. Selby appeared and deposed to being called hito the house to attend to the prisoner's injuries. Witness describ ed the nature of the incision and afterwards stated that the man's intel- lect was weak and defective so much so that he advised his removal to an asylum.—The prisoner was discharged and an order was subsequently made for his admission into Chester Asylum.
